2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shammai rules that a woman without a fixed cycle is impure only from the moment she sees blood.
Hillel rules that impurity reaches back to the last self-examination, even if that was many days earlier.
The Rabbis reject both views and set the period by combining the twenty-four-hour limit with examination-to-examination.
A woman with a fixed cycle is impure from sighting; examination cloths used around intercourse count as examinations.
Asks for an example illustrating the preceding ruling.
Example: a woman sitting on a bed handling pure items who sees blood is impure, while the items she touched stay pure.
Although the Rabbis made a woman without a fixed cycle impure retroactively, a woman with a fixed cycle counts only from sighting.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Shammai's position.
Shammai holds that the woman stays in her presumptive state of purity, since presumptions are kept unless shown otherwise.
Hillel's reasoning: a presumption stands only when the item itself gives no cause for doubt, which does not apply to a woman.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Because her body constantly sees blood flow, the presumption of her purity cannot be applied to her.
Asks what distinguishes the woman's case from that of a ritual bath.
Cites the mishna on a ritual bath found short, which makes earlier purifications retroactively impure.
Objects that this mishna conflicts with Shammai's view on retroactivity and with Hillel's view on certainty.
Explains that in the menstrual case the teruma is suspended, whereas in the ritual bath case the impurity is certain.
In the bath case the impure item's presumption can stand, since the bath was not validly immersed.
Objects that the bath's presumption of validity should stand instead, since it was not previously short.
Replies that the bath is lacking before you now, and this offsets its presumption of validity.
Objects that the woman likewise shows blood now, so her earlier presumption of purity is equally offset.
In the bath case the water could have drained gradually, so the bath may have been short long before.
Objects: can we say the woman saw blood, stopped, and saw it again, repeatedly?
Replies that the woman too may have seen the blood depart bit by bit, so the same possibility exists.
Answers that the bath carries two weakening factors, while the woman's case has only one.
Asks what distinguishes the case of a barrel that turned to vinegar from the ritual bath case.
Cites a baraita on a barrel: wine is certainly such for three days before the check, and uncertain afterward.
Notes that the barrel ruling of uncertainty poses a difficulty for Shammai's view.
In the barrel case the untithed produce's presumption can stand, since the wine may not have been properly amended.
Objects that the wine's presumption of being untithed should stand instead, since it had not turned to vinegar.
Replies that it has turned to vinegar before you, so the presumption cannot hold.
Objects that the woman likewise shows blood before you, so her presumption is similarly offset.
Replies that in the barrel case too it may have turned to vinegar only just now.
Answers that the wine was turning gradually, so it could have turned to vinegar long before.
Objects: can we say the woman saw blood, stopped, and saw it again, repeatedly?
Replies that the same possibility exists for the woman: perhaps she saw the blood depart bit by bit.
Answers that the barrel carries two weakening factors, while the woman's case has only one.
Raises a contradiction: why is the bath's impurity certain while the barrel's status is only uncertain?
Rabbi Hanina of Sura resolves it: the barrel ruling is Rabbi Shimon's, who treats the bath as uncertain too.
Cites the bath mishna again: earlier purifications in a short bath are impure retroactively, in private or public domain.
Rabbi Shimon's position: in the public domain the items are pure, while in a private domain their status is uncertain.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis derive the bath rule from the sota case: an uncertain bath is treated as definitely deficient, like an uncertain sota.
Objects: if the bath is like a sota, it should also be pure in a public domain, as a sota there is pure.
A sota's seclusion cannot occur in public, so the analogy fails; the bath's uncertainty stems from lack of water, regardless of domain.
Objects that any uncertain impurity in a public domain should be pure, so all such bath items would be pure.
Rejects that: two factors weaken purity here, a currently deficient bath and an item presumed impure, so it counts as definitely impure.
Rabbi Shimon's view: like a sota, an impure item immersed in a deficient bath in the public domain is pure.
Asks why, by the sota analogy in a private domain, Rabbi Shimon does not treat the items as definitely impure and burn teruma.
A sota was warned about this man and then secluded herself with him; no such basis exists for certain impurity in the bath case.
Alternatively, Rabbi Shimon derives the end of impurity from its beginning rather than from the sota case.
Analogy: uncertain contact with impurity in a public domain is pure, so uncertain immersion in a public bath is likewise pure.
The Rabbis distinguish: the man who touched remains presumed pure, while the immersing man is presumed impure, so the cases differ.
Asks what distinguishes this case from that of a carcass found in an alleyway.
Cites the alleyway mishna: a creeping animal carcass found in an alleyway renders items impure retroactively to the last examination.
Two sources of carcasses in the alleyway make two weakening factors, so even Shammai agrees the impurity is retroactive.
Alternatively, Shammai's reason: a woman feels her own flow, so if she felt it only now it began now; Hillel says she may have mistaken it for urine.
Asks: is there not a sleeping woman who would not sense her flow, contrary to Shammai's reasoning?
A sleeping woman would also awaken from the discomfort of her flow, just as one awakens to urinate.
Objects: there is the case of a mentally incompetent woman who might not notice an earlier flow.
Replies that Shammai concedes for the mentally incompetent woman, who is impure retroactively.
Asks: the mishna teaches all women, which apparently includes the mentally incompetent.
All women means all mentally competent women.
Asks why the mishna did not simply teach women instead of all women.
The word all excludes Rabbi Eliezer, who listed only four women with sufficient time; the mishna includes all competent women.
Objects: the mishna on blood stains implies that Shammai's view is not followed for stains.
Abaye replies that Shammai concedes in the case of stains.
Asks for the reason behind Abaye's view.
She did not handle a bird or pass butchers' shops, so the stain must have come from her last menstrual flow.
Shammai's reason: earlier blood would have emerged at once; Hillel holds womb walls might hold blood back, which Shammai denies.
Asks what can be said about a woman using a wad contraceptive, since Shammai's reasoning seems not to apply.
Abaye: Shammai concedes that a woman using an absorbent wad during intercourse is impure retroactively.
Rava: even a loose wad lets earlier blood out, and he concedes that for a tightly packed wad Shammai agrees the impurity is retroactive.
Asks what difference exists between these explanations of Shammai's view and the earlier one.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that only on the presumption reasoning do the barrel, bath and alley cases conflict; the other versions avoid the contradiction.
Asks what difference lies between the two versions of Shammai's reasoning.
Abaye: the versions differ in a wad case; Rava: they differ only with a tightly packed absorbent cloth.
Cites a baraita with the version that Shammai reasons earlier blood would have emerged at the outset.
Hillel challenges Shammai with the basket case: items placed in one corner are impure if a creeping animal is found in another.
Shammai concedes that the earlier pure items in the basket are retroactively impure.
Hillel asks what distinguishes the basket case from the menstruating woman, who is impure only from that point.
Shammai answers: the basket has a base where a creeping animal could have lain unseen; the woman has none.
Rava: Shammai's reason is concern for abandoning procreation, since retroactive impurity would deter intercourse.
A baraita reports Shammai's objection that retroactive impurity would cause Jewish women to neglect being fruitful and multiplying.
Asks whether, on Rava's version, the mishna conflicts with the reasoning that earlier blood would have emerged at once.
Hillel misunderstood Shammai's reasoning as the emergence argument, which is why he raised the basket objection.
Shammai replies that his reason is abandoning procreation, and that the basket answer holds even on Hillel's reading.
Asks the reverse: on the emergence version, does a baraita not state the procreation reasoning?
Hillel: the emergence reason has merit, yet a safeguard should be enacted, as the Sages enact safeguards throughout the Torah.
Shammai objects that this safeguard would cause Jewish women to neglect procreation, which Hillel too would bring about.
Hillel replies that he rules her impure only regarding ritually pure items, not forbidden to her husband.
Shammai counters that even a safeguard affecting only pure items should not be imposed, lest a husband's conscience lead him to separate from his wife.
Mnemonic for the ensuing discussion: base, examined, covered, in a corner.
Presents the basket case: pure produce placed in one corner, and a creeping animal later found in another corner.
Hizkiyya holds that the earlier pure produce remains pure.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that the earlier pure produce is retroactively deemed impure.
Asks: Shammai and Hillel agree that the earlier pure produce is retroactively impure, so how can Hizkiyya rule it pure?
Shammai and Hillel agree only for a basket with a base; Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan disagree about a basket without a base.
Asks the reasoning of Rabbi Yohanan for ruling the produce impure when the basket has no base.
The basket has no base but an inward-curved rim, which might have held back a small creeping animal.
Objects with a baraita: when water is drawn pail to pail, only the pail with the carcass is impure, not all of them.
Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai: the baraita applies only to a pail without a rim; with a rim all the water is impure.
Asks whether Hizkiyya therefore disagrees with Rabbi Yannai, since he ignores the basket's rim.
Water is slippery and need not be fully overturned, so a rim could hold back a creeping animal; produce is not slippery.
Alternatively, one is not particular about leftover water but is particular about produce, so the basket is fully emptied.
Alternatively, Shammai and Hillel agree only for a basket that was not examined, where the produce is presumed impure.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In an examined basket, Hizkiyya holds the animal entered after removal, while Rabbi Yohanan holds it fell in as the hand withdrew.
Asks: is the basket not taught as similar to a woman, who is considered examined?
The woman is treated as unexamined because blood commonly flows from her, so the basket case resembles her unexamined state.
Alternatively, Shammai and Hillel agree about an uncovered basket; Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan dispute a covered basket.
Asks how the animal could have fallen into a covered basket.
For example, the basket is used by removing its cover, so the animal could fall in only at that point.
Asks again: is the basket not taught as similar to a woman, who is considered covered?
A woman is covered, but blood commonly flows from her, so she is treated as uncovered; the basket is similar when uncovered.
Alternatively, Shammai and Hillel agree about produce stored in the corner of a basket.
Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan dispute produce stored in the corner of a house.
Objects that the Gemara on 3b explicitly says the case concerns a basket.
The 3b case: produce in one corner of a basket is moved to another corner; Hizkiyya does not presume impurity moved, Rabbi Yohanan does.
Asks whether we presume that impurity moves from place to place.
Cites a mishna on a man touched at night who is later found dead: Rabbi Meir deems him pure, while the Rabbis deem him impure.
A baraita adds that impurity is presumed only in the state and place where the item was found.
Proposes: the place rule applies only to burning teruma, while uncertain impurity merely suspends teruma's status.
Asks whether teruma is really suspended in such a case, given the possibility of earlier death elsewhere.
Objects with a mishna on a rusty or broken needle over teruma, which shows the teruma is definitely pure without suspension.
Cites another mishna: a burned creeping animal or a zav's rag found on olives leaves them definitely pure, again without suspension.
Explains the proposed distinction: the presumption applies to lenient and stringent cases alike, but only in the place where items were found.
Objects with a mishna and baraita: a loaf on a shelf above an impure garment is pure, though it could only have touched it on falling.
The baraita continues: the loaf is pure unless one says it is clear that no person entered there.
Rabbi Elazar: this principle is needed only where the top surface is inclined, so the loaf is presumed pure.
No proof can be drawn from there, since the baraita itself states its reason.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's reason: a pure man entered, took the loaf off the shelf, and avoided the impure garment.
Objects: a raven, which often touches creeping animals, might have thrown the animal into the basket after it was emptied.
Replies that a person acts with intent, so one may assume he moved the loaf, but a raven does not act purposefully.
Objects: the loaf is an uncertain impurity in a private domain, which is deemed impure, so it should be impure.
Replies that an object lacking consciousness is deemed pure in cases of uncertainty, in public or private domain alike.
Alternatively, the baraita concerns rabbinic impurity, and its word madaf matches the light leaf in Leviticus.
The mishna: the Rabbis say the halakha follows neither this tanna nor that tanna.
A baraita: the Rabbis reject Shammai, who made no safeguard, and Hillel, who went beyond his bounds.
The Rabbis' rule: a twenty-four-hour period shortens examination-to-examination, and examination-to-examination shortens the twenty-four hours.
Asks how this rule works in practice.
Example: examined pure on Sunday, skipped two days, found impure on Wednesday; she is impure for only twenty-four hours.
Asks for a second example.
Second example: examined pure in the first hour, skipped two hours, found impure in the fourth; she is impure back only to her last examination.
Objects that this is obvious, since her earlier pure examination means she cannot be impure for twenty-four hours.
The baraita teaches the parallel rule even though it is obvious, because it mirrors the first rule.
Rabba suggests the Rabbis' reason is that a woman senses her own flow.
Abaye objects: if so, her time should be sufficient, since she would sense an earlier flow.
Rabba did not mean this seriously; he raised it only to sharpen Abaye's mind.
Asks: what then is the real reason for the Rabbis' view?
Shmuel's teaching: the Sages required women to examine themselves morning and evening, to render night and day items fit.
A woman who skipped the required examination loses the purity of items touched during the day or night period.
Asks what is meant by the period of a day or night, given twenty-four hours of retroactive impurity.
It means an additional day or night period, making twenty-four hours in total.
Rav Pappa objects that sometimes three day or night periods fall within twenty-four hours, so the rule is not exact.
The Sages made their measures uniform so that no cases are distinguished.
Alternatively, the set period prevents a sinner from profiting by her transgression.
Asks what difference lies between these two explanations.
The difference: a woman prevented by circumstances from examining is not a sinner under the second explanation.
The mishna: for a woman with a fixed cycle who examined at that time and found blood, her time is sufficient.
Asks whether the mishna follows Rabbi Dosa rather than the Rabbis, given Rabbi Eliezer's list of four women.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer lists four women whose time suffices, while Rabbi Dosa says every woman with a fixed cycle has sufficient time.
The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Dosa only for blood at an irregular time; at the fixed time they agree, so the mishna follows all.
Objects: by inference Rabbi Dosa holds time sufficient even off-cycle, so who taught the stain baraita that makes her impure retroactively?
Asks whether the stain baraita follows the Rabbis rather than Rabbi Dosa.
Rabbi Dosa may be the author too: he disagrees only for a flow at the fixed time, agreeing that off-cycle blood is retroactive.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asserts that the baraita's ruling on retroactive impurity of blood stains is universally agreed upon.
Challenges the reading by proposing the mishna be interpreted in the opposite way.
Explains the stringent reading is chosen because the alternative reading would permit leniency.
Baraita states a woman with a fixed cycle has retroactive impurity from stains; the Gemara infers the same for other women.
Asks whose opinion the baraita follows.
Identifies R. Hanina ben Antigonus's view via Shmuel: all stains are retroactively impure except a girl not yet at her time.
Asks whether R. Hanina ben Antigonus holds that blood stains impart impurity at all.
Cites a baraita declaring all women's stains impure, challenging the attribution of a no-stain view to R. Hanina.
The baraita's R. Hanina ben Antigonus says time-sufficient women have no stain impurity.
Asks whether this means such women have no blood-stain impurity at all.
No; it means no retroactive stain impurity, though impurity applies from that point onward.
Asks whether R. Hanina's view implies the first tanna holds stains are retroactively impure.
Yes; the first tanna follows Rabbi Meir, who is stringent about blood stains.
Cites a baraita, attributed to Rabbi Meir, in which all women's stains are retroactively impure.
R. Hanina ben Antigonus teaches time-sufficient women's stains follow sightings; young girls are impure only once their time to see has arrived.
Asks when a young girl reaches the time she can see menstrual blood.
Answers that this begins when the days of youth arrive.
Cites the mishna on a woman who has intercourse using examination cloths.
Shmuel holds a cloth used before intercourse does not reduce the twenty-four-hour period like a regular examination.
Asks the reason for Shmuel's opinion.
Rav Ketina says she is excited and hurried for intercourse, so the examination is not proper.
Asks why excitement for intercourse should invalidate the examination.
Excitement means she does not insert the cloth into her recesses and folds.
Objects that the mishna's plural examination cloths suggests one cloth before and one after intercourse.
Asks whether the plural means one cloth before and one after intercourse.
No; both cloths are used after intercourse, one for each partner.
Cites a mishna: Jewish women customarily use two examination cloths during intercourse, one for each partner.
Asks why the mishna needs both examinations if both cloths are used after intercourse.
Necessary to exclude doubt that a mustard-sized blood drop could be hidden by a drop of semen.
Alternatively, both examinations are obligatory, as the Sages required one before and one after intercourse.
Objects that the mishna's wording implies the examination is voluntary rather than mandated by the Sages.
Proposes emending the mishna so it reads that a woman must engage in intercourse with examination cloths.
Restates the mishna: intercourse with examination cloths reduces the twenty-four-hour period and the examination-to-examination interval.
Asks why the mishna also says the examination reduces examination-to-examination time, given it already reduces the period.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether it is necessary to teach that examinations reduce the time between examinations.
Explains the ruling is needed lest one think the Sages worry about losing pure items only over a full day.
Mishna: a woman with a fixed cycle who sat on a bed handling pure items and saw blood is impure, while the items remain pure.
Asks why the mishna mentions the bed, since that detail seems superfluous.
Teaches that a time-sufficient woman's bed is not impure, implying a retroactive-period bed is impure, supporting Ze'eiri.
Objects that a bed lacks consciousness to be asked, so an uncertain-status item there should be deemed pure.
Ze'eiri refers to a bed carried by her friends, which counts as their extended hand and so has consciousness.
Rabbi Yohanan's principle: uncertain impurity caused by a person's hand requires consulting a Sage, even for an item resting on the ground.
Rabbi Yohanan states that uncertain impurity caused by a person is impure, since even a vessel on the ground counts as having consciousness.
Cites a baraita where uncertain contact by a wrapping cloak leaves pure items pure, challenging Rabbi Yohanan's view.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel proposes repeating the action to test contact; the Rabbis reject repeated actions for purity determinations.
Asks why the items remain pure if the uncertainty arose through a person's hand, which Rabbi Yohanan treats as impure.
Rav Hoshaya's rule: uncertainty in the private domain is impure, in the public domain pure; the baraita concerns the public domain.
Ze'eiri holds that a menstruating woman's retroactive-period bed and chair transmit impurity onward to a person and his garments.
Asks whether this is so, since Avimi brought a baraita limiting bed impurity to the level caused by her touch.
Cites Avimi's baraita stating a menstruating woman's bed and chair during the retroactive period are impure at the level of her touch.
Asks whether the baraita means the bed transmits no impurity to a person, just as her touch does not.
Rava responds that the baraita cannot be read that way and offers an a fortiori argument.
A fortiori: a vessel moved during the retroactive period is impure, so beds and chairs are impure there too.
Objects that Avimi's baraita apparently does not accept Rava's a fortiori inference.
Proposes the baraita means her bed and chair are impure, not merely at the level of her touch.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori: her touch impurifies a person who then impurifies garments, so her bed and chair do the same.
Baraita, per Rava: a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity reaches beds, food, and sealed vessels, but not her count or her partner.
Rabbi Akiva says she does render her partner impure retroactively, though her count starts only from when she saw blood.
Baraita: a woman seeing a blood stain is impure retroactively to the last garment check, disrupting her zava count and impurifying her partner.
Baraita: teruma touched in either case is suspended; it is neither eaten nor burned.
Asks why Rava's a fortiori is needed if he heard the baraita, and if not, how he derived it.
Rava did hear the baraita, but it alone might mean beds impurify only touched items, so he derived the a fortiori argument.
Rav Huna: the retroactive period of a menstruating woman applies to sacrificial food but not to teruma.
Asks why the Hagiga mishna does not list this among higher purity levels applying to sacrificial food but not teruma.
The Hagiga mishna lists only impurities with a Torah-based connection, and rabbinic retroactive impurity is excluded.
Objects from the baraita that food impurity applies to both sacrificial food and teruma, challenging Rav Huna.
Brings a mishna: priestly women who partake of teruma must examine themselves even afterward, per Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks why the examination afterward matters, since whatever happened to the teruma already happened.
Rav Hisda: the examination protects the remaining teruma before her from impurity from later retroactive status.
Rav Huna reads the mishna as requiring burning of remaining teruma in her hands, if she examined herself promptly and found impurity.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled per Rabbi Eliezer that a woman who passed three cycles without bleeding is not retroactively impure.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi later remembered the disagreement but said Rabbi Eliezer is worthy of reliance.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how R. Yehuda HaNasi could rule like R. Eliezer in exigent cases if halakha was decided against him.
Halakha was not stated here; R. Yehuda HaNasi later saw many Sages disagreed, so R. Eliezer may be relied upon in exigent cases.
Explains the case must involve teruma, since sacred food did not exist in R. Yehuda HaNasi's day, so the Rabbis' view conflicts with Rav Huna.
Resolves via Ulla's report that some Galilean groups kept sacred-food purity standards, so it can be practiced in R. Yehuda HaNasi's time.
Baraita: Rabban Gamliel's maidservant, examining between each loaf, found impurity only in the last; Rabban Gamliel limits retroactive impurity to that last one.
The baraita teaches the case involved teruma loaves, which seems to conflict with Rav Huna.
Teruma here means the teruma of the thanks-offering loaves, four of forty loaves that are sacred food, not teruma.
Asks why she would bake the thanks-offering teruma loaves alone, since all forty are baked together first.
The case involved dough separated during kneading; Rav Tovi bar Rav Ketina holds four loaves fulfill the thanks-offering obligation.
Asks whether forty loaves are required for the thanks offering rather than four.
Asks how teruma can come from four loaves, since the verse specifies one whole loaf rather than a slice from each.
Dough was separated during kneading, as in the maidservant's case, so the teruma is taken before the loaves are formed.
Second baraita: Rabban Gamliel's maidservant, examining between each wine barrel, found impurity only in the last; Rabban Gamliel limits the impurity to it.
If both incidents involved sacred food, asks why she would need to return and ask the same question again.
Each incident involved sacred food, with two different maidservants.
Another version: Rav Huna holds retroactive impurity of a menstruating woman applies to both sacred food and teruma.
Asks the source of this, from the Hagiga mishna's omission of it among higher purity levels for sacred food only.
Rav Nahman objects that a baraita explicitly says retroactive impurity applies only to sacred food, not teruma.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak reports Rav Nahman's reading: the baraita concerns non-sacred food prepared to sacred purity standards, not teruma-standard food.
Mishna in Ḥalla: dough whose impurity uncertainty arose before kneading may be prepared impure; after kneading it must be prepared in purity.
Baraita explains: pre-kneading dough may be made impure since it is non-sacred; post-kneading dough, like ḥalla, may not, and a new baraita begins.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ḥalla of uncertain purity is suspended: neither eaten as pure nor burned as impure.
Asks what ḥalla of uncertain status means, since it seems to indicate uncertainty specific to ḥalla, not ordinary food.
Abaye and Rava reject reading this as equal proofs, like two paths, since ordinary non-sacred food also becomes impure there.
Mishna in Zavim: when a zav and a pure person handle a heavy load, the pure person may be impure by leaning, a less likely uncertainty.
Asks whether untithed non-sacred food is really like ḥalla, so that it is impurified even by leaning.
Baraita permits a woman who immersed that day to separate ḥalla from dough, since third-degree impurity is pure for non-sacred food.
The baraita's reason: the dough has third-degree impurity, and such impurity is considered pure for non-sacred food.
Objects that if untithed food were like ḥalla, her touch would impurify it, as it impurifies actual ḥalla.
Abaye: decrees extend uncertain impurity to untithed food only where definite impurity impurifies non-sacred food, excluding one who immersed that day.
Asks about a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity, which definitely impurifies non-sacred food, yet no decree applies to her uncertain impurity.
Source: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak reports Rav Nahman: retroactive impurity reaches sacred-standard food but not teruma-standard non-sacred food.
Teruma-standard food is less stringent since no teruma is mixed in; alternatively, retroactive impurity is rabbinic and so leniency is possible.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer lists four women whose impurity starts from the sighting; Rabbi Yehoshua restricts this to a virgin.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asserts the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, closing the prior dispute.
Defines the virgin, pregnant and nursing categories, and reports Rabbi Meir's view that a nursing woman impurifies retroactively.
Defines the elderly woman as one with three cycles without bleeding, and reports Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei's rulings on such sightings.
Clarifies that the time-sufficient rule applies only to the first sighting; a second sighting follows ordinary rules unless the first was forced.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer rebukes Rabbi Yehoshua for hearing only one case while he heard many, so his view is weightier.
Rabbi Eliezer's new-moon metaphor: only one who saw the moon testifies, and he heard more rulings than Rabbi Yehoshua.
Reports that during Rabbi Eliezer's life practice followed Rabbi Yehoshua, and after his death Rabbi Yehoshua restored Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Asks why Rabbi Eliezer was not followed in his lifetime.
He was a Shammuti, and fear that one ruling would spread to others, and honor for him, blocked protest until after his death.
Shmuel teaches that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases, the first being the four time-sufficient women.
Second case: a woman bleeding during labor pains counts as zava only if relief lasts twenty-four hours, per Rabbi Eliezer.
Mishna on a zav's seven clean days: Rabbi Eliezer deems them presumptively pure, while Rabbi Yehoshua says only two days count.
Rabbi Akiva requires counting only the seventh day; a baraita says Rabbi Eliezer's view is more correct, and halakha follows him.
Mishna on vessel exteriors: Rabbi Eliezer says they impurify liquids but do not disqualify foods, even teruma; Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees.
Rabbi Yehoshua's a fortiori: since one who immersed that day disqualifies teruma food, exteriors that impurify liquids should too.
Asks how Rabbi Eliezer refutes this inference.
Exterior impurity is rabbinic while immersion is Torah law, and a fortiori arguments cannot derive rabbinic law from Torah cases.
Sages decreed liquids, not foods, contract impurity from impure exteriors, since zav liquids are primary impurity and foods are less susceptible.
Asks what distinguishes vessel exteriors, which are treated more leniently, from the interior.
Exteriors are more lenient: if only the exterior is impure, the interior, handles, and rim stay pure, unlike when the interior is impure.
Asks what Shmuel teaches, since the mishnah already explicitly states the halakha in all four cases.
Shmuel teaches that a final ruling cannot be drawn directly from Talmudic statements without amoraic confirmation.
Asks whether another case belongs on the list, citing a Yevamot mishna in which Rabbi Eliezer gives a ruling on levirate marriage.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teaches that the minor may refuse her marriage, and reports Shmuel's principle that halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Explains Shmuel's four cases apply only to Seder Teharot, while other orders contain many such rulings.
Cites Rabbi Eliezer's basket-combining ruling in Ḥalla, outside Teharot, as an exception to Shmuel's four-case principle.
Asks why the ḥalla case is stronger proof than the levirate case, since neither appears in Seder Teharot.
The levirate case differs because Rabbi Elazar holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer there.
Mishna in Yevamot: Rabbi Elazar says the minor must refuse, annulling her marriage retroactively, matching Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Asks whether Rabbi Elazar really holds like Rabbi Eliezer, since Yevamot says both views are needed for different cases.
Suggests the levirate ruling is weaker proof, since Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava also holds like Rabbi Eliezer.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava testified on five matters, including minors refusing marriage, which the Gemara uses as evidence.
Asks why the baraita says minor girls in the plural, if it refers only to the two cases of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Eliezer.
Plural means minor girls generally, in all cases where Rabbi Elazar's ruling applies, not specifically Rabbi Eliezer's.
Objects: if plural means generally, the one-witness baraita should say women; the discrepancy shows the ruling concerns two specific minors.
Rabbi Elazar similarly says the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer in four cases.
Asks whether there are truly no more such cases, since a mishna supports Rabbi Eliezer on the minor.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says the court instructs a minor to refuse her husband, the case Rabbi Elazar upholds.
Repeats that Rabbi Elazar held the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Asks whether Rabbi Elazar's four cases are limited to Teharot, and if so whether other orders truly have such cases.
Mishna in Shevi'it: fragrant plants such as balsam carry Sabbatical sanctity, a ruling Rabbi Pedat attributes to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Pedat says the tanna who holds balsam is fruit, and so sanctified, is Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Zeira rebukes Pedat: following Rabbi Eliezer on balsam conflicts with his father's view that halakha follows him in only four cases.
Infers from Pedat's failure to reply that Rabbi Elazar's four cases are limited to Teharot, with no other such cases.
Asks why the minor-refusal case is difficult, since it conflicts with Rabbi Elazar's four-case limitation.
Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Eliezer in the minor case, since the mishna has him say the court instructs the minor to refuse.
Asks again whether Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Eliezer in the minor case, given Yevamot's teaching that both views are needed.
Asks whether there are other cases where Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Eliezer, citing a Berakhot mishna on the placement of havdala.
Rabbi Abba explains: the havdala case is not Rabbi Eliezer's own view, but was stated in the name of Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how R. Eliezer could be cited for R. Ḥanina ben Gamliel's view, since R. Eliezer was much older.
Answers that R. Elazar ruled like R. Eliezer because R. Ḥanina ben Gamliel held his view too.
Asks whether R. Ḥanina ben Gamliel really holds like R. Eliezer.
Baraita: Yom Kippur services use seven blessings and confession, with an abridged evening prayer, seemingly against R. Ḥanina.
R. Ḥanina ben Gamliel, citing his forefathers, says one recites the full eighteen blessings to include havdala in the fourth blessing.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak explains R. Ḥanina said this in his forefathers' name, but did not personally hold it.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Zeira: do you not hold that the balsam-as-fruit tanna is Rabbi Eliezer, given his orla ruling?
Mishna in Orla: Rabbi Eliezer holds cheese curdled in orla sap is prohibited, since the sap counts as fruit.
Rabbis dispute Rabbi Eliezer only over tree sap, agreeing on fruit sap, as Rabbi Yehoshua's Orla mishna shows.
Alternatively, Rabbis dispute Rabbi Eliezer only for fruit-bearing trees, agreeing that barren trees' sap counts as fruit.
Mishna in Shevi'it: Rabbi Shimon says sap is exempt from Sabbatical sanctity, while the Rabbis say it applies since sap is its fruit.
Asks whether the Rabbis in the mishna are those who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer, which would prove agreement on barren trees.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the Rabbis there are Rabbi Eliezer himself, who holds barren-tree sap is its fruit.
Asks why the case specifies barren trees, when Rabbi Eliezer holds fruit-bearing trees' sap is fruit too.
Rabbi Eliezer argued from their view; the Rabbis replied sap is not fruit whether from a fruit-bearing or barren tree.
Mishna and baraita define a virgin as one never having menstrual blood, even if married or gave birth and bled from hymen or birth.
Asks whether this is so, since Rav Kahana's teaching lists three types of virgins.
Rav Kahana's teaching: virgin human, ground, and sycamore; a virgin woman may marry a High Priest and has a higher marriage contract.
Virgin ground is unworked; relevant to the rough stream rite and to sales.
Virgin sycamore is unfelled; relevant to sales, and to the Sabbatical prohibition on felling it, per a mishna.
Asks: if a menstrual-blood virgin exists, why did the baraita not list it among the virgins?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the list includes only unmodified terms, and menstrual virginity needs a modifier.
Rav Sheshet: the list includes only items dependent on outside action, unlike menstrual flow.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Rav Ika: the list includes only items that will not revert, unlike menstrual flow that ceases at old age.
Ravina: the list includes only items buyers particularly care about, unlike menstrual blood.
Asks whether buyers are not particular about menstrual blood, citing baraitot on blood's fortuity and plentiful children.
Alternative: the list includes only items buyers eagerly purchase, not those they do not, such as a woman without menstrual blood.
Baraita defines virgin ground as soil with hard clumps and no loose dirt; a shard shows it was worked, and hard rock shows virgin ground.
Mishna: a pregnant woman's time is sufficient once her fetus is known; Sumakhos cites Rabbi Meir that this is three months.
Supports Rabbi Meir's three-month claim with Genesis 38:24, which mentions three months before Tamar's pregnancy was reported.
Asks why Rabbi Meir calls this only an allusion, since an explicit verse is written.
Some women deliver at seven months, so the verse may apply only to nine-month pregnancies, making it an allusion.
Baraita: a presumed-pregnant woman who bleeds and then miscarries non-viable matter keeps her pregnancy status, so impurity runs only from then.
Isaiah 26:18 alludes that one who miscarries wind counts as pregnant, though not explicit proof.
Asks why this is called only an allusion, since the verse is explicit proof.
The verse is written about males, so its childbirth imagery is symbolic and supports no halakhic inference.
Baraita: a woman in labor pains who miscarries non-viable matter bears as a zava, contradicting the view that such a miscarriage is a proper birth.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: the Torah deems blood near birth pure, which seems to contradict the rule that this woman is retroactively impure.
Rav Pappi replies: set aside that baraita, since the twenty-four-hour retroactive rule is only rabbinic.
Rav Pappa explains the leniency is because the pregnant woman's head and limbs feel heavy, and this applies here too.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether blood seen before the pregnancy became known makes her impure, given its proximity to that time.
Rabbi Zeira replies that the heaviness explanation fails here, since she did not feel heavy at the time, so she is impure.
An elder asks whether a pregnant woman who missed the examination on her fixed cycle must examine, since her blood has stopped.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Rabbi Meir's mishna: fear suspends bleeding, implying that without fear a missed examination makes her impure.
Mishna and baraita: a nursing woman's time suffices until weaning; per Rabbi Meir, four or five years of nursing keeps her exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon hold the nursing exemption lasts only twenty-four months, after which impurity applies again.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: for Rabbi Meir blood turns to milk; for the others her limbs dislocate until twenty-four months pass.
Why state Rabbi Meir's ruling and the other view separately, and does Rabbi Yosei hold two reasons at once?
The clause is needed to teach that Rabbi Yosei holds only the dislocation reason.
A baraita repeats the positions: Rabbi Meir says blood turns to milk; Rabbi Yosei says limbs dislocate until twenty-four months pass.
Rabbi Ilai asks what the reasoning of Rabbi Meir is.
Rabbi Ilai cites a verse from Job asking who can bring a pure thing out of an impure one, supporting Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara asks how the Sages interpret that same verse.
Rabbi Yohanan explains the verse refers to semen, which is impure, yet the person formed from it is pure.
Rabbi Elazar holds the verse refers to the red heifer water: the sprinkler is pure, while one who touches it is impure.
Objection from a verse: the sprinkler must wash his clothes, so the sprinkler cannot be pure.
The Gemara explains that sprinkling here means touching, which makes the toucher impure.
If sprinkling means touching, why does the verse mention both terms, and why must the sprinkler wash but the toucher need not?
Sprinkling must mean carrying the purification water, which is why the verse uses that term.
If it means carrying, why did the Torah not simply write carrier explicitly?
The term sprinkling teaches that one becomes impure only by carrying the measure of water needed for sprinkling.
This works if sprinkling requires a minimum measure, but if not, what can be said?
Even if no measure is needed for the body, the vessel holding the water requires a measure, as the Mishnah teaches.
Solomon's verse, saying he thought he would be wise but wisdom was far from him, supports this paradox of purification water.
Mishna: an elderly woman is one for whom three thirty-day cycles passed near old age without menstrual blood.
What is considered close to old age?
Rav Yehuda says anyone her friends call elderly qualifies; Rabbi Shimon gives his own view, continuing the discussion.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Defines an elderly woman as one people call mother, Mother, and who is not embarrassed by it.
Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak: one of them defines the category as a woman who does not take offense at being called that.
The other of the two defines the category instead as a woman who is not embarrassed by being called that.
What is the practical difference between the two definitions?
The difference arises when a woman is embarrassed but does not take offense at being called that.
How long is a typical menstrual cycle?
Reish Lakish, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, holds that the average cycle is thirty days long.
Rava, citing Rav Hisda, holds that the average cycle is twenty days long.
The views do not conflict: one counts days of impurity as part of the cycle, while the other does not.
A baraita: an elderly woman who sees blood after three cycles of thirty days is sufficient; after a third such instance she is like other women.
The baraita continues: it need not teach the case of even intervals; the rule applies even if her intervals shorten or lengthen.
Why would the baraita need to say this, since even intervals set a fixed cycle and her time should then suffice?
Objection: if the baraita followed the Rabbis who oppose Rabbi Dosa, it should have been worded differently to include even intervals.
Reply: read the baraita as altered, or as stating Rabbi Dosa's view that fixed even intervals make her time sufficient.
The mishna: Rabbi Eliezer holds that a woman with three cycles without blood who then bleeds has sufficient time; Rabbi Yosei disagrees.
Rabbi Eliezer cites a case from the village of Hitlo, where a girl who stopped menstruating for three cycles was ruled to have sufficient time.
The other Sages reply that a ruling made in exigent circumstances is no proof.
What were the exigent circumstances?
Some say there was a drought; others say the Sages feared losing many pure items if the girl were ruled retroactively impure.
A baraita reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled per Rabbi Eliezer, saying he may be relied upon in exigent circumstances.
What does after he remembered mean? If the halakha follows the Rabbis, how could he rule like Rabbi Eliezer even in exigent circumstances?
The halakha was never decided; several Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer, so he may be relied upon in exigent circumstances.
A baraita on a young girl and an adult woman: the pattern of sufficient time and retroactive impurity after three cycles, following Rabbi Eliezer.
The Master restates the baraita: after three cycles without blood, a girl who then bleeds returns to girlhood status and her time is sufficient.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the halakha if she again sees blood at regular thirty-day cycles?
Rav Giddel, citing Rav: the first and second sightings leave her time sufficient; after the third, she is retroactively impure, and the same holds after three cycles.
Restating the question: what is the halakha if she again sees blood at regular thirty-day cycles?
Rav Kahana, citing Rav Giddel and Rav: the first sighting leaves her time sufficient; after the second she becomes retroactively impure.
Who is the tanna of the baraita?
It is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that a presumptive cycle is established after two occasions.
Difficulty: the later clause follows Rabbi Eliezer, so the baraita cannot be Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who ruled only in exigent circumstances.
Rather, the tanna is Rabbi Eliezer, who holds the cycle rule of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, that two occasions establish a presumptive cycle.
A blood stain between the first and second sightings renders a young girl pure; one between the second and third is the disputed case.
Hizkiyya holds that a blood stain between the second and third sightings renders her impure.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that such a stain renders her pure.
Hizkiyya's reason: had she actually seen blood it would be impure, so her stain is also impure.
Rabbi Yohanan's reason: she is not yet presumptively a menstruant, so we do not render her stain impure.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Ilai objects: what is the difference between this young girl and a menstrual virgin, whose stains are deemed pure?
Rabbi Zeira replies: a virgin's secretion from her torn hymen is common, so her stains are presumed to be from the hymen; the young girl's is not.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: a young girl's saliva and garment, and her stains after two sightings, are pure.
What difference does it make who said the ruling?
It matters whether it is one Sage's view against two dissenting opinions, which would make Hizkiyya's view a minority.
When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted the ruling as Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak's, so Rabbi Yohanan's view echoed his teacher's majority opinion.
Rav Hilkiya bar Tovi: a young girl who bleeds continuously for seven days has only one sighting and needs two more before she is impure.
Why stress continuous discharge, since stopping and restarting would count as two sightings?
Rav Hilkiya meant that continuous discharge for seven days counts as one sighting; he did not say even.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya: a woman who constantly drips blood is not treated like one who has a full sighting.
Objection: but such a woman did see blood, so she should count as a sighting.
Reply: he meant she is treated like one who stops and restarts, not like one who discharges continuously, even when dripping.
Objection: the contrast implies that continuous discharge streams like a river for seven days, which is physically impossible.
Reply: the constant dripper's status is simply that of one who continuously discharges, so both count as one sighting.
A baraita: unmarried Jewish girls are presumed pure before maturity and impure afterward, and women must examine minors until they mature.
Rabbi Yehuda: examine them with oil applied inside and wiped off outside, not by hand, which would scratch them.
Rabbi Yosei: a pregnant or nursing woman with three cycles without blood is sufficient; a baraita recited before Rabbi Elazar repeats this.
Rabbi Elazar objects that the baraita opens with two categories but closes in the singular, so it is inconsistent.
Perhaps the baraita concerns a pregnant woman who is also nursing, and it teaches in passing that the two periods combine.
Citing a baraita: pregnancy days count toward nursing days, and nursing days toward pregnancy days, supporting the combined count.
The baraita continues with examples: missed cycles split between pregnancy and nursing combine to three, so her time is sufficient.
How can nursing days count toward pregnancy days, since birth brings bleeding that breaks the count of three cycles?
Three answers: a dry birth without bleeding; menstrual and birth blood are discrete; or the baraita teaches only one of the two cases.
The mishna: her time is sufficient only for the first sighting; after the second she is impure like other women.
Rav holds that this qualification applies to all four cases: menstrual virgin, elderly woman, pregnant woman and nursing woman.
Shmuel holds the qualification applies only to menstrual virgin and elderly woman; pregnant and nursing women are sufficient throughout.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish agrees with Rav that the qualification applies to all four cases.
Rabbi Yohanan agrees with Shmuel that only the virgin and elderly cases are qualified, while pregnancy and nursing are sufficient throughout.
The Gemara suggests the dispute parallels a tannaitic dispute about a pregnant and nursing woman.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds that a woman with continuous discharge is sufficient for all her days of pregnancy and of nursing.
Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon limit the sufficiency to the first sighting; from the second she is impure like other women.
Mishna: if she saw the first sighting through unnatural circumstances, her time is sufficient even for the second sighting.
Rav Huna: if she jumped and bled three times, she has established a fixed cycle.
Objection: if the cycle were of days alone, it would be impossible, since on non-jumping days she would not see blood.
Reply: the fixed cycle is caused by jumping, so three jump-triggered sightings establish a pattern.
Objection from a baraita: a pattern caused by recurring external accidents does not establish a cycle at all.
Reply: the baraita means no cycle of days alone or jumps alone, but one combining specific days with jumps.
Isn't it obvious that days alone do not establish a cycle?
Rav Ashi: the case is jumping on Sunday, then missing the next Shabbat jump but bleeding on Sunday, showing the day itself causes the flow.
Rav Huna's second version: three jumps establish a cycle for days, not for jumps.
What are the circumstances of that version?
Rav Ashi repeats the Sunday example: the matter is revealed retroactively that the day, not the jumping, causes the flow.
Mishna: women must examine daily, except a menstruating woman or one observing the blood of purity; examinations depend on timing and priestly status.
Rabbi Yehuda: priestly women must also examine after finishing eating teruma, to check for bleeding during that time.
Gemara explains the exemption: a menstruating woman does not need examination during her days of impurity.
If Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds days of impurity do not establish a cycle, the mishna works; but on Rabbi Yohanan's view she should examine.
Rabbi Yohanan clarifies: a cycle is established during menstruation only when the first two sightings came from a closed source, not an open one.
The Gemara interprets the mishna's blood-of-purity clause as referring to a woman finishing impurity after birth, ready to begin her days of purity.
This works for Rav, who holds post-birth and purity blood come from one source, so continued flow into purity days remains pure.
Objection: for Levi, who holds two distinct sources, she should examine at the end of the post-birth period, since the impure source may not have stopped.
Levi replies: in accordance with whose opinion is that ruling? It is not his view, so the objection does not apply.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the mishna's unattributed opinion as Beit Shammai's, followed by a dispute; an unattributed view then does not necessarily set the halakha.
Alternatively, the mishna teaches she is observing the blood of purity, not that she anticipates it.
If the mishna teaches she is observing purity, what is the point of stating it?
Lest you think she must examine since she may establish a cycle, the mishna teaches that a cycle is not formed from pure-source blood transferring to impure-source blood.
Objection: this works for Levi, who holds two sources, but for Rav, who holds one source, she should examine since she may establish a cycle.
Even for Rav, both bloods come from one source, yet she does not establish a cycle from purity days carrying over into impurity days.
The Gemara cites a mishna on a married young girl: Beit Shammai give her four nights of purity; Beit Hillel say until the wound heals.
Shmuel explains Beit Hillel: attribution to the hymen holds only if bleeding recurs with intercourse; a non-intercourse sighting or changed appearance renders her impure.
Objection from Rabbi Yona: the mishna says a virgin needs no examination before intercourse, yet her blood's appearance could have changed.
Rava: the first clause implies a virgin must examine, supporting Shmuel, but then the two clauses of the mishna contradict each other.
Resolution: the latter clause concerns a virgin who had intercourse, where examination is inconclusive, and the first clause concerns one who had not.
A baraita repeats Beit Hillel's rule with the same conditions: bleeding recurring with intercourse, sighting without intercourse, or changed appearance.
Mishna: she must examine twice daily, and at certain times before intercourse.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the twice-daily examination concerns only pure items; she is permitted to her husband without examination.
Isn't it obvious, since the mishna's first examination is in the morning, which concerns items and not intercourse?
Rather, Rav Yehuda's statement concerns the latter clause, and applies only to a woman handling pure items, who must also examine before intercourse.
What is Rav Yehuda teaching, since the mishna already establishes presumptive purity for husbands, and the case could be limited to women with a fixed cycle?
But the mishna deals with a woman who has a fixed cycle, so how is the halakha extended?
The mishna covers both those with and without fixed cycles, teaching that handling pure items requires examination even for a woman with a cycle before intercourse.
But didn't Shmuel already state, via Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya, that a woman without a fixed cycle may not have intercourse until she examines?
Shmuel stated one ruling explicitly; the other was an inference from it, reported by his students in his name.
A baraita confirms: examination is for pure items, not intercourse; if the husband left her presumptively impure, she remains impure until she says she is pure.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Yehuda whether a woman should examine herself before intercourse with her husband.
Rav Yehuda says no: a scrupulous husband might fear impurity and separate from his wife out of conscience.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether examining right after intercourse makes the husband liable for a sin offering.
Rav Huna objects: can a full examination be done within the time needed for menstruation to begin? Isn't that time too short?
A baraita defines that time as the moment an examination cloth enters as the male organ exits, which allows only an external wipe.
Rabbi Abba's real dilemma concerns whether she should wipe immediately, which can be done quickly; some say the dilemma is this.
Rabbi Abba asks whether examining right after intercourse makes the husband liable for a provisional guilt offering.
Rav Huna again says no, for the same reason: a scrupulous husband might separate from his wife out of fear of impurity.
Mishna: she must also examine herself when about to have intercourse with her husband.
Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Yannai: this pre-intercourse examination is the examination of virtuous women.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects: the tanna says women must examine, yet Rabbi Ami calls it optional for the virtuous.
Rabbi Ami replies that anyone who fulfills the Sages' rulings is virtuous, praising adherence to halakha rather than going beyond it.
Rava objects: if the virtuous are those who fulfill the Sages, the non-fulfilling are not called virtuous, yet they are not called wicked either.
Rava explains: virtuous women do not reuse an examination cloth; others reuse them and are careless about it.
Rabbi Zeira, citing Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya, Shmuel: a woman without a fixed cycle is forbidden to her husband until she examines herself.
Rabbi Zeira objects: if the fixed-cycle woman needs no examination, this contradicts the mishna requiring examination even for her.
Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya: a fixed-cycle woman must examine only if awake, not asleep, while a woman without a cycle must examine either way.
Rava suggests a better answer: Shmuel requires examination for intercourse only where she also handles pure items, and so holds it is not required for intercourse alone.
A baraita on donkey drivers, laborers and returnees: wives remain presumptively pure unless left impure, and then remain impure until they declare purity.
How does Shmuel explain this baraita, since either case seems contradicted by his own ruling?
The baraita concerns a woman with a fixed cycle whose husband asks after travelling, so she has time to recall any onset of bleeding.
Rav Pappa asks Rava what the halakha is for acting on this baraita, perhaps by waking her to ask whether she is pure.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava rejects the idea of waking her: it would embarrass her and force her to wonder whether she is pure.
Rav Kahana reports that the wives of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna said their husbands did not require examination before intercourse.
Why ask the wives rather than the Sages themselves?
Perhaps the Sages were lenient in rulings for others but stringent in their own conduct.
A baraita: a woman without a fixed cycle is forbidden to her husband and loses her marriage payments and benefits; he must divorce her and never remarry her. Rabbi Meir holds this.
Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus: she may be intercourse-permitted, examined with two cloths; Abba Hanan's view is that it is woe to her husband.
The Gemara explains each clause: she is forbidden lest she ruin him; her marriage payments and benefits lapse since she is unfit for intercourse; the divorce must be final.
Isn't this obvious?
Not obvious: it covers a woman who later establishes a cycle, so he must not remarry her; the first husband would not have divorced her if he knew, and the divorce would be void.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus.
To what case does Shmuel's ruling apply, given his other rulings on examination for handling pure items and for intercourse alone?
Rabbi Zeira, citing Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeya, Shmuel: a woman without a fixed cycle may not have intercourse until she examines herself.
We interpreted that ruling as applying to a woman who handles pure items; the two rulings were cited by different Sages.
Chapter-closing formula: Hadran alach, Shammai omer, marking the end of this chapter and the start of the next.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: examining for emissions is praiseworthy for women, but a man who examines frequently should have that hand severed.
Asks what distinguishes women from men, since men are sensitive to arousal and women are not.
Asks why the Mishna specifies frequent examination for men if even occasional examination is risky.
Replies that the restriction concerns semen, while a man checking for zav discharge is praised like a woman.
Baraita: even for semen, a man may examine himself with a hard rock or earthenware that does not warm the body.
Asks whether a man may not examine himself with a cloth at all.
Cites a baraita permitting self-examination with a cloth or any item the man wishes.
Abaye resolves it: the baraita means a coarse cloth, which does not warm the body, just as in the Mishna.
Asks where Abaye's ruling was originally stated.
Points to the Mishna about a priest who feels his limbs quake while eating teruma and holds his penis.
Challenges holding the penis: a baraita says whoever holds and urinates brings a flood upon the world.
Abaye answers that the Mishna permits holding only with a coarse cloth.
Rava says even a soft cloth is permitted, since the semen has already been uprooted and holding cannot increase it.
Abaye forbids even a soft cloth, fearing that contact might lead to further emission.
Rava is not concerned that contact might lead to further emission.
Challenges Rava: a baraita compares repeated examination to placing a finger in the eye.
The baraita's analogy: an eye keeps tearing while a finger remains in it.
Rava replies that the concern applies only to dripping emission, not to emission with quaking limbs.
Rabbi Eliezer repeats his ruling that holding the penis while urinating brings a flood upon the world.
The Sages object: a man who sprays urine on his legs looks like one with a severed penis, casting doubt on his children.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that people may cast doubt on his children rather than he sin even briefly before God.
Another baraita: Rabbi Eliezer tells the Sages one can urinate from a high place or into loose soil instead.
Asks which of Rabbi Eliezer's two replies came first, since a prohibition followed by a remedy seems inconsistent.
Rather, he first gave the practical solution, and only afterward the prohibition when the Sages objected.
The Sages ask what a man should do if he has neither a high place nor loose soil.
Rabbi Eliezer again says it is preferable for others to doubt his children than for him to sin before God.
Asks why one must refrain to such an extent from holding the penis.
Because holding may cause a man to emit semen for naught.
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that one who emits semen for naught is liable to death at Heaven's hand.
Supports Rabbi Yohanan from the story of Onan, who spilled his seed and was slain by God.
Rabbi Yitzhak and Rabbi Ami say emitting semen for naught is like shedding blood.
Supports this from Isaiah, reading the word as squeezing out seed rather than slaying children.
Explains that the word is read as squeezing, sohatei, rather than slaughtering, shohatei.
Rav Asi says one who emits semen for naught is as if he worships idols.
Supports Rav Asi by comparing the phrase under every leafy tree in two verses about idolatry.
Narrative: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel stood on the roof of the synagogue at Neharde'a.
Rav Yehuda asks Shmuel what he should do, since he needs to urinate.
Shmuel instructs him to hold his penis and urinate outward, away from the roof.
Asks how Rav Yehuda could do this given the prohibition.
Cites Rabbi Eliezer's baraita again as a challenge to Rav Yehuda's conduct.
Abaye explains that the sages treated the situation like a troop of marauders who are afraid.
Cites the mishna on marauders entering a town: in peacetime open casks are forbidden, in wartime permitted.
Infers from the mishna that fear prevents marauders from pouring libations, so their wine is permitted.
Applies the same reasoning here: since Rav Yehuda is afraid, he will not come to sexual thoughts.

Suggests the fear of the night and of the roof, that he might fall.
Suggests the awe of his teacher, and alternatively the awe of the Divine Presence in the synagogue.
Suggests the awe of his Master, God, and cites Shmuel's praise of Rav Yehuda as not born of woman.

ranges.en: Completes the ruling: touching from the corona upward, toward the body, is prohibited.

Rabbi Ami: one who brings himself to arousal is not admitted within the Holy One's sanctuary.
Supports this by contrasting Onan, who was slain for evil, with the verse that God does not favor wickedness.
Rabbi Elazar also speaks about the severity of this transgression.
Asks what is meant by the verse about hands full of blood.
Explains that the verse refers to those who commit adultery with the hand, by masturbating.
A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the adultery prohibition covers adultery by hand or by foot.
Sages teach that converts and those who play with children delay the coming of the Messiah.
Explains the converts clause through Rabbi Helbo, who compares converts to a scab harmful to Israel.
Asks what the category of those who play with children refers to.
Rejects the reading that it means homosexuality or emission by other limbs, since such acts merit stoning or the flood.
Proposes that it refers to men who marry minor girls, causing emission for naught.
Rabbi Yosei: the son of David will not come until all souls destined for bodies have been born.
Supports this with Isaiah 57:16, reading the spirit and souls as the unborn souls that delay the Messiah.
Raises a dilemma: is the severing rule a binding halakha or merely a curse?
Come and hear: Rabbi Tarfon says a hand reaching the penis should be severed upon the navel.
The Sages object: if a thorn lodged in one's belly, one would not remove it, which seems absurd.
Tarfon replies that he should not remove the thorn, preferring a split belly to descending to the pit.
Asks what the Rabbis meant by saying the belly would be split, given the halakha interpretation.
Rejects the reading that the rule is practical halakha, since the objection would not then make sense.
Resolves it: Tarfon means that one who inserts his hand below the navel has his hand severed.

Tarfon replies that he should not remove it.

Mishna: a deaf, imbecile, blind, or insane woman may be assisted by competent friends and then eat teruma.

Cites a mishna: a deaf person the Sages speak of everywhere neither hears nor speaks.
A blind woman examines herself and shows the cloth to her friend; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina says blind is not in the mishna.
An insane woman affected by illness is a separate category from the imbecile mentioned in the mishna.
Baraita on an imbecile priest: immerse him, feed him teruma in the evening, and keep him from sleeping.

Baraita in the name of Rabbi Elazar: prepare a metal pouch that does not warm the penis.
Abaye explains that metal means copper, which does not absorb liquid, so any drop would be visible.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda: hyssop stems are treated as copper because they absorb no water.
Rav Pappa concludes that trousers are prohibited too, since they warm the penis.
Objects: Exodus 28:42 commands linen trousers for priests, which seems to conflict with this.
Replies that priestly trousers differ: they are like horsemen's riding trousers, with no opening.

Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok asked the Sages at Usha about the period after time passed.

Rabbi Yohanan: Rabbi Meir follows Akavya and deems the woman impure if she sees green blood from her body
If so, why would Rabbi Meir mention the liquid status, since the explanation should refer to the woman seeing it

Asks how the Rabbis would respond, and then why Rabbi Meir deems green blood impure
Rabbi Meir's suggestion: green blood should count as liquid that makes seeds susceptible, but Rabbis require blood of death
If so the Rabbis answered well, so why does Rabbi Meir still disagree with them

Objection from a mishna: a louse from anywhere on the body would be the standard, not only the head
The halakha refers specifically to a louse on her head
Ami of Vardina in the name of Rabbi Abbahu: red like blood from a young man's finger, until age twenty
Objection from the mishna: the woman may attribute the stain to her husband, but how can he be unmarried

Rabba bar Rav Huna: the ḥeret in the mishna is ink, and a baraita says the same
Asks why the baraita mentions both heret and ink if it means ink alone
Had it said only ink, one would think the clear upper part of ink, so it adds the darker blackness of ink
Dilemma: does the black ḥeret mean moist or dry ink
Rabbi Ami broke up dried ink to examine blood, which resolves the dilemma in favor of dry ink
Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name and Rabbi Elazar: black as ink, wax, grape or olive defines the impure and pure shades
Ulla: black means like the very dark garments of Siva'a, and an Arab's garment was torn for a sample
Rabbi Yohanan: black blood is like the black cloths of bath attendants from overseas
Asks whether this means those cloths are black
Objection: Rabbi Yannai instructed not to be buried in black or white, yet these cloths are not black
The distinction: Rabbi Yannai's cloth is a garment, Rabbi Yohanan's is a cloth placed on furniture
Shmuel: examine all blood on white linen; Rav Yitzhak bar Avudimi: black blood on red linen
Rav Yirmeya of Difti: they do not disagree, since each addresses a different type of blood
Rav Ashi: if so Shmuel should have excepted black, so the question is only about black itself
Rav Ashi: Shmuel and Rav Yitzhak bar Avudimi disagree about black blood itself
Ulla: for all five types, deeper is impure and lighter is pure, as stated for black
Asks what distinguishes black, that the mishna states this rule only for that color
Rabbi Hanina's view that black is faded red could have made even lighter black impure, so the mishna clarifies
Rabbi Ami bar Abba: deeper is impure for all five, and lighter is also impure except for black
Asks what purpose the Sages' measures then serve
The measures exclude a color so faint that it does not qualify as impure blood
Rami bar Abba's version: deviation from the measures means pure, except black, which is impure if deeper
Bar Kappara's rulings on diluted-wine blood, tested by the Sages, and Rabbi Hanina's praise of his sensitivity
The Sages taught that the crocus shade refers to moist saffron, not dry
Four baraitot give conflicting placements of the crocus shade relative to its upper and lower parts
Abaye: the crocus has three layers of three leaves each, so the baraitot do not conflict
Abaye's method: grasp the middle leaf of the middle layer and compare it with the blood
Rabbi Abbahu: the mishna refers only to crocus flowers still in their clumps of earth
Baraita on red earth from Beit Kerem with the views of Meir, Akiva, Yosei and Shimon
Baraita on the red earth test: water amount, muddy versus clear, and muddying with a vessel
Dilemma: does one muddy the water by hand or only with a vessel
Baraita: the examination is done only in a cup, which suggests a vessel is required
The proof is rejected: it does not say whether muddying must be done by vessel alone; left unresolved
Rabba bar Avuh: the examination must be done at the place the earth came from
Rabbi Hanina crumbled earth without water, and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei cursed that method with diphtheria

ranges.en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei: only Rabbi Hanina may examine blood without water, as he alone is wise enough
Rabbi Yohanan: Rabbi Hanina's wisdom makes him avoid examining blood, since his rulings always contradict his
Rabbi Elazar: Rabbi Hanina's humility leads him to examine blood, so Elazar should as well
Rabbi Zeira: Babylonians' complex nature makes him unwilling to examine blood
Asks whether the appearance of blood depends on people's nature, given that Rabba knew Babylonians yet could not judge blood
Ulla refuses to examine blood in Pumbedita, reasoning from Rabbi Elazar's refusal at Rabbi Yehuda's locale
Asks why Rabbi Elazar was called the master of Eretz Yisrael in wisdom
Story: Rabbi Elazar identified a wife's blood as desire-blood, and Rabbi Ami learned it was from her husband's absence
Ifera Hurmiz sent blood to Rava, who identified it as desire-blood, and her son doubted it was not luck
Rava correctly identified sixty samples; the last, lice blood, was verified by a lice comb sent as a gift
Rav Yehuda: after his wife's remark on the first drop, he stopped examining blood except postpartum blood
Rav Yehuda: he still examines postpartum blood, which is clean and reliably determined by its color
Yalta's blood: Rabba bar bar Hana ruled it impure, and Rav Yitzhak bar Yehuda ruled it pure
Asks how Rav Yitzhak could overturn Rabba's ruling, given the baraita that forbids this
Rav Yitzhak first ruled impure, then changed after Yalta said Rabba always ruled her pure for such color
Asks whether people are credible to present claims like Yalta's
Yes; a baraita accepts a woman's claim that she saw blood of this color but lost it
Dilemma: is a woman credible when she reports a learned authority ruled her blood pure?
Proof from the baraita is rejected: there the blood is not before her, while here it can be examined
Challenge from the Yalta incident, where the ruling reversal seems to contradict the baraita
Resolution: Rav Yitzhak first ruled impure, then changed due to Yalta's report, so the incident is not a clear proof
Rav Yitzhak relied on his learning, reluctant at first in deference to Rabba bar bar Hana
Story: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled blood impure at night, pure by day, then impure again, doubting himself
Objection: he certainly erred, since a halakhic authority may not reason from what the blood would be if moist
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi examined three times, since a judge rules only on what his eyes see
Examination practices: candlelight, between pillars on a cloudy day, and only between sunlight and shade
Mishna on the diluted-wine shade, two parts water to one of Sharon wine, and a baraita follows

ranges.en: Sharon wine, new and undiluted, is the benchmark color for examining blood.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi requires examining all such blood only in a simple Tiberian cup.
The Gemara asks the reason for using a simple Tiberian cup.
Abaye explains that cup thickness tracks capacity, so a thin Tiberian cup shows the wine's redness more clearly.
Chapter-closing formula marking the end of the preceding chapter.
Mishnah rules that a discharged tissue piece makes a woman impure only if blood accompanies it.
Rabbi Yehuda rules she is impure whether or not blood accompanies the tissue.
Shell, hair, soil, or mosquito-like discharges are tested in water; if they dissolve, it is blood and she is impure.
Fish, grasshopper, or creeping-creature-like discharges make her impure only if blood accompanies them.
Animal-like tissue sets the impurity periods by the fetus's sex, following the Torah rules for male or female births.
If the fetus's sex is unknown, Rabbi Meir imposes the combined male and female periods.
The Rabbis say a non-human-form fetus counts for no periods, so she may resume intercourse absent uterine blood.
Shmuel, quoted by Rav Yehuda, limits Rabbi Yehuda's impurity ruling to tissue resembling the four impure blood colors.
Rabbi Yohanan offers an alternative: all agree on impurity for four-color tissue and purity for other colors.
The dispute concerns a woman who cannot recall what she discharged.
Rabbi Yehuda follows the majority of tissue pieces, while the Rabbis reject that majority reasoning here.
The Gemara objects to this position, asking whether it is really so.
Rav Hoshaya brings a baraita on red, black, green, and white tissue, with Rabbi Yehuda deeming impurity either way.
The baraita contradicts Shmuel, since the Rabbis deem green and white tissue pure, against his stated limit.
Proposed reconciliation: Rabbi Yehuda disputes only red and black tissue, not green and white.
That reconciliation fails, since the baraita would then teach nothing; it also poses a further problem for Rabbi Yohanan.
Proposed reconciliation for Rabbi Yohanan: the Rabbis dispute only green and white tissue.
That reconciliation fails, since teaching the red and black case would then be pointless.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzchak resolves the dispute: the sages differ on whether the womb can open without blood.
He cites a baraita about a woman in difficult labor whose discharge is uncertain, illustrating the same dispute.
