ranges.en: Uncertain birth or zava status means she brings an offering, but it may not be eaten.
Rabbi Yehoshua says she brings an offering that is eaten, since opening the womb requires blood.
Introduces an alternative version of the preceding discussion.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, limits Rabbi Yehuda's impurity ruling to tissue resembling the four impure blood colors.
The Gemara challenges this position, asking whether it is really so.
Rav Hoshaya brings a baraita on red, black, green, and white tissue, with Rabbi Yehuda deeming impurity either way.
The baraita teaches the Rabbis deem green and white tissue pure, yet Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, contradicting Shmuel.
Proposed reconciliation: Rabbi Yehuda disputes only red and black tissue, not green and white.
That reconciliation fails, since teaching the green and white case would then be pointless.
Rav Yehuda gives a different explanation: the sages dispute whether the womb can open without blood.
He cites a baraita about a woman in difficult labor whose discharge is uncertain, illustrating this dispute.
Rabbi Yehoshua's view within that baraita: she brings an offering that is eaten.
Sumakhos, citing Rabbi Meir, rules that tissue should be torn open and blood inside renders her impure.
The Gemara explains this ruling is stricter than the Rabbis' view, since Sumakhos counts internal blood.
Rabbi Aha rules that tissue is torn open and a red appearance inside renders her impure.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Aha's ruling follows Sumakhos but is more stringent.
Rabbi Binyamin rules that a bone inside torn tissue makes it a fetus, rendering the mother impure from childbirth.
Rav Hisda limits the bone ruling to white tissue.
Scholars from Hadyab bring a baraita on white tissue containing a bone, rendering the mother impure.
Rabbi Yohanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, requires accumulated blood inside torn tissue for impurity.
The Gemara notes this resembles Sumakhos but is more lenient than all earlier opinions.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether blood seen through a tube counts, given the verse's wording about her flesh.
Rabbi Zeira replies that the verse's wording teaches two things, including that blood inside counts and a tube is pure.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yohanan's ruling about tissue would not apply equally to blood seen through a tube.
The cases differ: it is typical for a woman to see blood in tissue, but not through a tube.
The Gemara asks whether the tube case is itself a dispute between tannaim.
A baraita rules that even tissue full of blood renders her impure only if blood emerges alongside it.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that only blood directly from her flesh impurifies, not blood in a sac or tissue.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's view is identical to the first tanna's view, making it redundant.
Proposed fix: the whole baraita is Rabbi Eliezer's view, so it differs from the first tanna.
The Rabbis rule that blood found in tissue is not menstrual blood, only tissue blood.
The Gemara asks whether the first tanna also deems her pure, so what is the difference between them.
The difference is the case of cracked tissue, where blood touches her body directly.
The first tanna holds that cracked tissue with direct blood contact makes her impure.
The Gemara asks the reason for this exception.
Blood touching her flesh fulfills the verse's requirement, so it is read as her flesh.
The Rabbis hold that even cracked tissue leaves her pure, since its blood is not menstrual, and menstrual blood would impurify even through a tube.
Abaye says all agree that blood seen through a tube renders her pure.

ranges.en: Explains the dispute: whether menstrual blood is typically found inside discharged tissue.
Rava offers another explanation: both sides agree such blood is not menstrual, so it does not impurify.
Rabbi Eliezer holds the woman is pure while the blood's source is impure, whereas the Rabbis hold both are pure.
Rabba asks Rav Huna whether a man who sees semen extracted with a sliver of wood becomes impure.
Rav Huna answers that the man is pure, since semen impurifies only when it blocks the tip of the penis.
Rabba objects: if emission alone impurifies, a zav's count should not be halted by touching impurity.
Rabba asks why a baraita says a seminal emission negates the seven-day count if it impurifies only by contact.
Rav Huna explains the negation arises because a zav's emission always contains bits of ziva.
Rabba objects that a seminal emission should then negate the whole count, as ziva does.
The baraita continues, using the verse's wording to limit a seminal emission's negation to one day.
Rav Huna replies that pure ziva negates the whole count, while ziva mixed with semen negates only one day.
Rabbi Yosei asks whether dry blood impurifies a woman, given the verse's wording about flow.
Rabbi Elazar cites a mishna stating menstrual blood and corpse flesh impurify whether wet or dry.
Rabbi Yosei clarifies his dilemma concerns blood that was dry from the outset.

ranges.en: If dissolving shows blood, why would the item not be impure even when it fails to dissolve?
Rabba explains that an item that does not dissolve is not blood but a distinct entity.
Asks whether such cases actually occur in practice.
A baraita reports Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok's account of two incidents raised before the Sages in Yavne.
The first incident: a woman discharging red shell-like items, whose doctors traced them to a wound in the womb.
The second incident: a woman discharging red hair-like items, traced by the doctors to a mole in the womb.
Reish Lakish says the test uses lukewarm water, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prescribes mashing the item with saliva.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two opinions.
Ravina explains the difference is whether the item counts as blood when it can be mashed by pressure or only when it dissolves by itself.
Cites a mishna on soaking dried carcasses for twenty-four hours, and asks whether discharged items need the same soaking.
Explains the dilemma: carcasses are hard when dry, while blood is soft, so the soaking period may differ; the question is left unresolved.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda, who deems tissue impure either way, would not also disagree with the Rabbis about fish-like discharges.
Reish Lakish says this is also disputed, while Rabbi Yohanan says the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, since blood does not take the form of a creature.
Challenges Rabbi Yohanan's view by noting that Rabbi Yehuda would then also dispute the Rabbis in the fish-like case.
Answers that the version of the teaching is reformulated: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish both say the case is disputed, with the mishna following the Rabbis.
Cites the mishna on tissue shaped like a domesticated animal, undomesticated animal, or bird, setting periods by sex, with Rabbi Meir's view on unknown sex.
Shmuel gives the reason for Rabbi Meir: the Torah uses formation language for animals as for man.
Argues by reductio that a sea-monster-shaped discharge should then make the mother impure as after childbirth.
The Sages reply that halakhot may be derived from formation to formation, but not from creation to formation.
Asks what the difference between formation and creation is, illustrating verbal analogy with a case of house leprosy.
Argues that the sea-monster case can be derived by a different verbal analogy from man, since creation is stated for both.
The Sages reply that the verse on creation teaches the matter itself, while the formation verse is superfluous and serves the analogy.
Objects that the roles could be reversed, so the sea monster analogy with man is equally valid.
Explains that formation is free on both sides for man and animals, while creation is free only for man, not for sea monsters.
Asks why the formation term for animals is free, citing parallel verses about animals and creeping things.
Answers that the creeping animal in that verse refers to land creatures, so the creation term for sea monsters is not superfluous.
Asks what the practical difference is between a verbal analogy free on one side and one free on both sides.
Shmuel, citing Rabbi Yishmael, explains that analogies free on one side can be refuted logically according to the Rabbis, but not according to Rabbi Yishmael.
Asks what difference there is for Rabbi Yishmael, since he derives from both kinds of analogy equally.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that when two conflicting analogies arise, the one free on one side is disregarded in favor of the one free on both sides.

ranges.en: Explains why the Torah renders the animal-man analogy free on both sides, so the sea-monster analogy is not used.

Asks what practical difference the Rabbis see between an analogy free on one side and one not free at all.
Explains the difference arises when two conflicting analogies exist: the one free on one side is then preferred.
Asks what logical refutation exists against the man and sea-monster analogy, which is free on only one side.
Rabbi Yohanan explains Rabbi Meir's view: formation is stated for these animals as it is for man.
Rabbi Ami objects that by the same logic a mountain-shaped discharge would make the mother impure as after childbirth.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba replies that a woman cannot discharge a mountain, only a clod-like stone.
Rabbi Ami asks whether an amorphous discharge is impure as after childbirth, since the verse uses creation for wind.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba replies that Torah matters may be derived only from other Torah verses, not from the Prophets.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan's reason for Rabbi Meir: such animals have eyes like a human.
Objects that a snake-shaped discharge, with round pupils like a human, should likewise impurify, and asks why the mishna omits it.
Explains that Rabbis may dispute Rabbi Meir only for snakes, which lack formation language, while animals have it.
Raises a difficulty from a mishna saying an animal with a round pupil is blemished, implying animal eyes differ from human eyes.
Resolves the difficulty: one statement concerns the pupil and the other the whole eyeball in its socket.
Rabbi Yannai explains Rabbi Meir's view: animals have forward-facing eyes like a human, unlike birds and snakes.
Raises a difficulty: Rabbi Meir deems a bird-shaped discharge impure, contrary to Rabbi Yannai's explanation.
Abaye replies that Rabbi Meir refers only to the little owl and great owl, whose eyes face forward.
Objects with a baraita of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus, who accepts Rabbi Meir only for animals and the Rabbis for birds.
Asks which birds Rabbi Hanina means, since owls' forward eyes should bring them under Rabbi Meir's view too.
Explains the baraita is incomplete: Rabbi Meir concedes to the Rabbis on other birds, disputing only owls.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok supporting Abaye: Rabbi Meir distinguishes birds, requiring examination.
Asks whether the examination instruction in that baraita refers to Rabbi Meir or to the Rabbis.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika rejects the proof, since the examination instruction may reflect the Rabbis' view.
Asks why the Rabbis would deem an owl-shaped discharge impure, but not a land animal-shaped one.
Answers that owls have cheeks like a human, which makes their form count as formation.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a female fetus accepted in betrothal by her father makes her sister forbidden to the husband.
Objects that the impurity applies only if the creature's kind survives, citing Rav Yehuda's quotation of Rav on Rabbi Meir.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov remarks that Rabbi Yirmeya tried to make Rabbi Zeira laugh with this question, without success.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, states the principle that Rabbi Meir's ruling depends on the discharge's kind continuing, and Rav Yirmeya adds a further view.

ranges.en: Mishna teaches that a discharged animal-like fetus is not a full-fledged offspring, per Rabbi Meir, while the Rabbis require human form.

Argues from the mishna that if animal-shaped fetuses survived, the son following them would be a firstborn for inheritance.
Rava rejects the proof: animal-shaped fetuses may survive, but the inheritance verse excludes sons whose fathers would not mourn.
Rav Adda bar Ahava asks Abaye whether a human fetus found in a slaughtered animal is permitted to be eaten.
Suggests resolving the question from Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that a pigeon-shaped fetus found in a slaughtered animal is forbidden.
Rejects the comparison: a pigeon fetus lacks hooves entirely, whereas a human-shaped one has solid feet, so the question remains open.
Mishna says non-human-formed discharges are not impure; Rav teaches that a goat-bodied fetus with a human face is human, but not the reverse.
Explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir counts a face with one human-like eye as human, while the Rabbis require a full human face.
Objects that a baraita says the opposite, with Rabbi Meir requiring only part of a human face.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba replies that if the baraita is taught, he cannot dispute it and follows his tradition from Rav.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yohanan, requires the entire face, including forehead, eyebrows, eyes, cheeks, and chin, to be human.
Rava, citing Hasa, requires only one side of the face to appear human, with each paired feature counting once.
Explains that Rabbi Yohanan and Hasa both follow the Rabbis, differing only on whether the full form or part of it is required.
Objects with a baraita listing facial features, apart from the ear, that render the fetus human, against Hasa's reading.
Abaye resolves the baraita: it requires each feature, excluding the ear, and the one-feature view counts one of each paired feature.
Rava rules that a single eye or thigh counts as human only if placed where it normally appears on the face or hip.
Rava rules that a fetus with a punctured esophagus renders its mother impure, while a sealed one does not.
A baraita says a fetus with a sealed body does not render its mother impure as after childbirth.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi defines a sealed body as one lacking a limb whose removal from a living person would cause death.
Asks how much of the lower body, when removed from a living person, would cause death.
Rabbi Zakkai begins to answer the question on how much must be removed.

ranges.en: Three amoraic views set the limit of a fetus's missing body: above the knee, the orifices, or the navel, per Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yohanan, and others.
Explains the dispute between Rabbi Zakkai and Rabbi Yannai: whether a tereifa can survive beyond twelve months.
Explains the Yannai and Yohanan dispute through Rabbi Elazar's ruling that a limb removed from a living animal makes it a carcass.
Rav Pappa limits the dispute to missing lower body parts, and Rav Giddel quotes Rabbi Yohanan that a sealed-skull fetus leaves the mother pure.
Rav Giddel quotes Rabbi Yohanan that a fetus shaped like a palm branch, with a formless lower body, leaves the mother pure.
Rabbi Yohanan rules a fetus with a mashed but not flat face renders its mother impure, while Reish Lakish rules her pure.
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from a baraita on a shaped hand or foot, which implies a mashed face would count.
Rav Pappi limits the dispute to a completely flat face, reversing the earlier version of who holds which view.
Asks why Reish Lakish did not raise the same objection from the baraita against Rabbi Yohanan.
Explains Reish Lakish did not object, since Rabbi Yohanan would reply that a sealed body equals a flat face.
Rabbi Hiyya's sons rule a flat-faced fetus impure, and their father asks whether any case was brought before them.
Rabbi Hiyya tells them to reverse the ruling, since they wrongly applied a stringency that leads to leniency.
Rav holds a fetus with two backs and two spines is not an offspring, while Shmuel holds it is, with different dietary rules for animals.
Asks what Rav and Shmuel actually dispute.
Cites Rav Hanin bar Abba's reading of a verse about a split-hoofed animal with two backs as the source of the dispute.
Explains Rav and Shmuel differ on whether such a living animal exists or only a fetus with that form.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya objects to Rav from a baraita disqualifying a priest with two backs, implying such a creature survives.
Rav replies the baraita refers to a crooked spine, and a true two-backed creature cannot survive.
Objects with a baraita listing animal fetuses forbidden as unslaughtered carcasses, excluding one with two backs and two spines.
Asks whether the exclusion means such fetuses are forbidden even inside the womb, contradicting Shmuel.
Explains each Sage reads the baraita through his own reasoning, with Rav's reading covering animals born in the air.
Concludes the prohibition applies only once the animal emerges into the air, and a two-backed fetus is forbidden even inside the womb.

ranges.en: Shmuel explains the baraita: gestation-period limits apply only to incomplete pregnancies, while a two-backed fetus is forbidden only once outside the womb.
A baraita taught before Rav: a shapeless fetus does not impurify, since the verses on circumcision apply only to a child fit for the eighth day.
Explains the verses exclude non-viable offspring, and Rav amends the baraita to also exclude a two-backed, two-spined fetus.
Rav Huna objects to Rabbi Yirmeya's plan to rule per Shmuel, noting this stringency leads to leniency and the halakha follows Rav.
Rava asks whether large livestock, like humans, can give viable birth after seven months of pregnancy.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak cites a baraita: an animal discharging at that stage is forbidden as an unslaughtered carcass.
Asks whether the baraita must then refer to large livestock, which would show they cannot survive at seven months.
Answers that the baraita refers to small domesticated animals, which are not viable before five months.
Objects that if the baraita refers to large livestock, its ruling would be unnecessary, and if to small animals, the point is obvious.
Explains the baraita is needed for small animals, since otherwise one might think a sheep born two months early would survive.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, rules a lilith-shaped fetus with wings renders its mother impure as after childbirth.
Cites a baraita on Rabbi Yosei's account of a Simoni case, where the Sages ruled the winged fetus a viable offspring.
Recounts a case of a snake-shaped discharge: Hanina ruled impurity, and Rabban Gamliel summoned Rabbi Yehoshua to rebuke him.
Hanina's daughter-in-law reports Rabbi Yehoshua's earlier ruling, which he then recalls and acknowledges as his own.
Abaye draws the lesson that a scholar should state the reason for his ruling so that it can be remembered later.
Mishna: a gestational sac full of fluid, blood, or colors is not concerning, but one containing tissue sets the periods of a woman who gave birth.
Objects that a sac of mixed colors might have held an embryo that liquefied, so the mishna seems wrong.
Abaye replies that undiluted wine would be needed to liquefy an embryo, so the concern is not realistic.
Rava explains the sac would show a missing portion of mass if an embryo had liquefied.
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that a liquefied embryo would leave the sac uniform in color, unlike the mishna's description.
Abba Shaul, a former gravedigger, reports that bones of heavy drinkers burn, black, or are fat, depending on the amount of wine and food.
Abba Shaul recounts chasing a deer into a corpse's thighbone for three parasangs, which the Sages identify as Og's thighbone.
Abba Shaul relates standing in a corpse's eye socket up to his nose, which the Sages identify as Absalom's eye.
Objects that Abba Shaul could not have been a midget, and notes he was the tallest of his generation, as were later sages.
Continues the chain of tall sages: each reached only the shoulder of the one before, down to Rav Yehuda and Adda the attendant.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Preface anecdote comparing the height of the Pumbedita governor with others, not a halakhic position.
Students ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the halakha for a sac full of flesh.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that he has not heard the ruling from his teachers.
Rabbi Yishmael transmits his father's ruling: a blood-filled sac causes menstrual impurity, a flesh-filled one postpartum impurity.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects that two separate halakhot in one statement cannot be accepted as a tradition.
Gemara reasons that the blood ruling follows an individual Sage, so the flesh ruling may follow Rabbi Yehoshua, whose view is not halakha.
Baraita: a sac without developed tissue is an offspring according to Rabbi Yehoshua, but not according to the Rabbis.
Resh Lakish, citing Rabbi Oshaya: the dispute applies only when the amniotic fluid is turbid; with clear fluid all agree.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the opposite: the dispute applies only when the amniotic fluid is clear.
Dilemma: does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limit the dispute to clear fluid, or apply it to both cases?
Objection: a baraita is cited that appears to contradict the turbid-fluid reading.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya derives from Genesis 3:21 that God makes skin only for an already formed person, so a sac with skin is an offspring.
Conclusion: the question depends on skin, regardless of whether the fluid is turbid or clear.
If the dispute concerned turbid fluid, the verse would be unnecessary, so the dispute must concern clear fluid.
Rav Naḥman cites Rabba bar Avuh: the dispute is about turbid fluid, and with clear fluid all agree there is no offspring.
Rava raises an objection against Rav Naḥman's view.
Mishna on firstborn animals: signs of an offspring differ for small animals, large animals and women.
Rava argues that if the dispute concerns clear fluid, the mishna's distinction between women and animals is explained by the verse.
If the dispute concerns turbid fluid, the same logic should apply to women and animals alike, so the dispute must concern clear fluid.
Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua is uncertain about the status of a turbid sac, so he rules stringently in both cases.
Regarding monetary matters such as redeeming a firstborn, doubt is treated leniently, so later births are exempt.
Regarding ritual matters for animals, doubt is treated stringently, and likewise the woman's impurity is stringent.
Gemara asks: is Rabbi Yehoshua really uncertain, since he cites a verse as proof for the woman's impurity?
Rabbi Yehoshua holds the impurity is rabbinic, and the verse is only a supporting allusion, not the real source.
Rav Ḥanina bar Shelamya summarizes the positions attributed to each Sage discussed so far.
Rav Ḥanina asks Rav which of these positions he holds.
Rav replies that in both cases the woman need not be concerned about the status of a birth.
Shmuel rules that in both cases the woman must be concerned, and the Gemara notes he is consistent with his approach.
Rav Dimi's tradition: in Neharde'a the Sages never deemed such a woman pure, except for one sac that came before Shmuel.
Shmuel's test: a hair placed on one side of that sac was visible on the other, so it contained no offspring, supporting his ruling.
Mishna: if tissue developed in the sac, the woman has the status of one who gave birth, with both male and female strictures.
Baraita asks for the definition of a sac in which tissue developed.
Abba Shaul: formation begins with the head, and the two eyes look like two fly droplets.
Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches that the eyes are distant from each other and the nostrils look like fly droplets.
Rabbi Ḥiyya adds that the eyes are close together, the mouth is a hair-like line, and the body is lentil-sized; a female shows a line.
At this stage the embryo has no arms or legs.
Job 10:10–12 is cited as scriptural support for the description of the embryo at this stage.
The sex of the embryo is not examined with water, because water is too strong.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuation of the baraita: the embryo is examined with oil and viewed only in sunlight.
Gemara asks how one examines the embryo in the baraita.
Gemara answers that the obvious method is as already stated, so the real question is how to determine sex.
The real question: how does one determine whether the embryo is male or female?
Abba Shaul bar Nash uses a smooth sliver: if it catches, the embryo is male; if not, female.
Rav Naḥman cites Rabba bar Avuh: the sliver test indicates male only when moved from below upward, not from the sides.
Rav Adda bar Ahava gives the full wording: a female shows a cracked-barley-like line along the body.
Rav Naḥman objects that the line may instead be the thread between the testes.
Abaye replies that the testes are not yet discernible at this stage, so the line must be the vagina.
Rabbi Amram: at the stage of developing limbs the thighs look like crimson threads, thicker like woof.
Baraita on the arms: two crimson strings; Rabbi Amram says they resemble warp threads.
Shmuel instructs Rav Yehuda Shinnana not to issue a ruling on such an embryo until hair grows.
Gemara asks whether Shmuel really said this, since he elsewhere required concern in both cases.
Rav Ami explains Shmuel: concern about impurity stands, but purity days are withheld until hair grows.
Gemara asks whether Shmuel is therefore uncertain about the status of a gestational sac.
An incident shows Shmuel's expertise: he dated a fetus to forty-one days by counting from immersion, and a husband confessed.
Shmuel is exceptional in his proficiency; his ruling of uncertainty applies to less expert people.
Mishna: a woman who discharges a sandal fetus or an afterbirth observes the strictures of one who bore male and female.
Baraita: a sandal fetus resembles a sea sandal fish; it is an offspring from the outset but was crushed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a sandal fetus resembles the tongue of a large bull.
Students testified in the name of their teachers that a sandal fetus must have the shape of a face to count as an offspring.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: the halakha is that a sandal fetus requires the shape of a face.
Rav Adda, Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzḥak: the face need not be in its proper place; even on the back of the head it counts.
Parable of a man slapped whose face was pushed backward, illustrating how external pressure can displace a face.
In Rabbi Yannai's days the Sages wished to deem pure a woman who discharged a sandal fetus without a face.
Rabbi Yannai objects: you would be declaring pure women who have discharged offspring.
Objection: a baraita teaches that a sandal fetus requires the shape of a face, contrary to Rabbi Yannai.
Rav Beivai, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: this ruling comes from Rabbi Neḥunya's testimony, an individual view not accepted as halakha.
Rabbi Zeira: Rav Beivai was credited with the ruling because he stated it first before the Sages.
Why does the mishna mention the sandal fetus, since a sandal fetus always has a twin?
If a female twin was born, mentioning the sandal fetus is unnecessary; the case here is a male twin.
Lest one infer from Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami that the twin's sex determines the sex of the sandal fetus by the order of emission.
The mishna teaches that the sandal fetus may be female even with a male twin, since both may have emitted seed simultaneously.
Alternatively, the ruling covers a female twin born before sunset and the sandal fetus after, which affects the count of days.
If the sandal fetus is male the count starts from the first birth; if female, from the last birth.
Gemara begins asking why the sandal fetus case appears in other mishnayot, given that it always has a twin.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reference to the Bekhorot ruling on a son born after a sandal fetus.
Gemara asks what practical matter this halakha of the later son affects, given the twin born with the sandal fetus.
The later son is a firstborn for inheritance but not for priestly redemption.
Mishna in Karetot: a woman who discharges a sandal fetus brings a birth offering.
Gemara asks what practical matter this halakha is relevant to.
If a woman bears a full-fledged child by caesarean and a sandal fetus through the womb, she brings an offering for the sandal fetus.
Gemara asks why the mishna is needed if Rabbi Shimon counts caesarean births as full offspring who already require an offering.
Rabbi Yirmeya: a gentile who bore a full-fledged child and then converted before bearing a sandal fetus still brings an offering for it.
Objection: are these answers correct, given a baraita that twins exit the womb wrapped around one another?
Rav Pappa defends the answers: the twins lie offset, so the head position determines which one exits first in each mishna.
Rav Huna bar Taḥlifa, citing Rava, offers an alternative: the twins lie side by side and the cases are reversed, depending on which part emerges first.
Mishna: an afterbirth in a house renders the house impure, because there is no afterbirth without an offspring.
Rabbi Shimon dissents: the offspring turned to blood before emerging, so the house is not a tent over a corpse.
Baraita describing the afterbirth: thin like woof thread at first, wider later, hollow, and never less than a handbreadth long.
Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya: five items have a minimum measure of one handbreadth.
The five items listed: the afterbirth, the shofar, the lulav spine, the sukka wall, and the hyssop.
The afterbirth halakha is as stated, and the shofar is addressed by a baraita.
Gemara asks how long a shofar must be.
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel: long enough to hold in one hand with four fingers and still show a handbreadth on each side.
Gemara asks what the halakha is regarding the spine of a lulav.
Rabbi Parnakh citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the lulav spine must protrude at least a handbreadth beyond the myrtle.
Baraita on the sukka wall: two full walls and a third wall of at least a handbreadth.
Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches that the hyssop must measure at least a handbreadth.
Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa cites a mnemonic of the five items, noting two amoraic rulings among them.
Abaye: revise the wording so Rabbi Ḥiyya states the hyssop rule himself rather than as a baraita.
Gemara asks whether there are other cases of a one-handbreadth minimum, such as the mishna on a one-handbreadth cube transmitting impurity.
The five items were stated only for a one-handbreadth length, not for a one-handbreadth cube.
Gemara asks about a mishna on a stone protruding from an oven by a handbreadth, which counts as part of the oven.
The five-item rule covers cases where a shorter measure is unfit; here, a stone under a handbreadth is a fortiori part of the oven.
Gemara begins to ask whether there are yet other such cases.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara asks whether toy ovens for girls also have a one-handbreadth minimum.
Rabbi Meir: an oven begun at four handbreadths keeps impurity when broken if its remains are four handbreadths tall.
The Rabbis: this applies to large ovens; for small toy ovens any size suffices, and the majority of the remains counts.
Gemara asks how small the any-size measure is.
Rabbi Yannai: one handbreadth, the size of toy ovens; Rabbi Oshaya does not address disputed matters.
Since disputed matters are excluded, the protruding-stone case is also a dispute and so Rabbi Oshaya omitted it.
Rabbi Yehuda: a protruding stone counts as an oven handle only at one handbreadth, and only when it protrudes toward the wall.
Objection: the Table frame in the Temple is one handbreadth wide, as stated in the Torah.
Rabbi Oshaya does not deal with matters written in the Torah.
Objection: the Ark cover is one handbreadth thick, and its measure is not stated in the Torah.
Rabbi Oshaya does not deal with consecrated items.
Objection: a cross beam over an alleyway needs only one handbreadth width, a rabbinic matter.
Rabbi Oshaya deals only with matters written in the Torah whose measure is not explicit there.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta cites Rav: for the first three days the afterbirth is attributed to the offspring; afterward there is concern for another.
Rav Kahana objects: did Rav say this, when Rav also said a second offspring does not remain after a viable one?
Rav Kahana reconciles: the first offspring is nonviable in one case and viable in the other.
Rav Yitzḥak rejects this reconciliation: Rav stated the explanation explicitly.
Rav's explicit ruling: after a nonviable newborn, the afterbirth is attributed to the offspring for three days, then concern arises.
Rav's ruling for a viable birth: no concern for another offspring until ten days have passed.
Narrative: Shmuel's circle sees Rav Yosef approaching, and Shmuel remarks he can easily be refuted.
Shmuel asks Rav Yosef what Rav said about the afterbirth.
Rav Yosef: one attributes the afterbirth only to a viable item.
Shmuel confirms with Rav's students, who affirm the ruling; Rav Yehuda had not transmitted it to him.
Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about a crow-shaped discharge accompanied by an afterbirth.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the afterbirth is attributed only to an item of a species that has an afterbirth.
Rabbi Yosei asks the halakha if the afterbirth is tied to the crow-shaped item.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: you asked about a matter that does not exist.
Objection from a baraita: an afterbirth tied to domestic animals, wild animals or birds gives no concern for another offspring, but an untied one does.
Concluding ruling of the baraita, imposed on the cases described.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara explains that two offspring account for the stricter ruling, presenting its own reasoning.
Hypothesis that both the sac and the afterbirth disintegrated, implying two offspring were born.
Calls the hypothesis a refutation of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's claim.
Tradition from Shmuel: the Sages attributed an afterbirth to an offspring born up to ten days earlier.
Rabbi Yochanan's case: an afterbirth attributed to an offspring born up to twenty-three days earlier.
Rav Yosef objects that the teaching was stated as twenty-four days, which conflicts with the account.
Rav Yitzchak's case: a fetus delayed thirty-three days after its twin is recounted.
Rav Yosef objects that the teaching should instead say thirty-four days.
Rav Yosef asks how this works for one who holds a woman gives birth at nine months, not in pieces.
Answers that it is possible for one fetus to be complete at seven months and another at the start of nine.
Asks what can be said for one who holds a woman at nine months does not give birth in pieces.
Proposes reversing the tradition: thirty-three days for the afterbirth and twenty-three for the offspring.
Rav Menachem's case of twins born three months apart, whose names were Yehuda and Chizkiya.
Points out the Master said a woman cannot conceive and conceive again, which contradicts the case.
Abaye answers that one drop split into two, one completed early in the seventh month and one late in the ninth.
Baraita teaching that an afterbirth inside a house renders the house impure.
Baraita clarifies the point is that no afterbirth exists without an offspring, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold the house is pure.
Asks Rabbi Meir whether he agrees a bowl removed to the outer house is pure.
Rabbi Meir replies with his reasoning about why the outer-house case differs.
Argues that just as it is not in the outer house, it is not in the inner house either.
Rabbi Meir replies the cases differ: rot that occurred once versus rot that occurred twice.
Narrative: Rav Pappa sat behind Rav Bibi before Rav Hamnuna and began to speak.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon?
Rabbi Shimon holds that any impurity mixed with a different kind of material is nullified.
Rav Pappa says this is also the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi.
Narrative: they laughed at Rav Pappa's remark.
Dismisses the remark as obvious and asks what is new in it.
Rav Pappa responds that one should speak up even about such a matter, not stay silent before one's teacher.
Cites the verse from Proverbs as support for speaking up.
Continues the verse from Proverbs, urging a person to put a hand to the mouth.
Narrative: Rabbi Shimon proceeds in line with his own reasoning.
Baraita: a full vessel of rotting produce into which any amount of dust fell is impure.
Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, declares it pure.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon?
Rabba recounts finding the Rabbis of Rav's school sitting and speaking on the matter.
The Rabbis argue that two portions of dust could collect on one portion of rot, leaving it lacking.
Rabba answers them on the contrary: two portions of rot cannot fail to accumulate on one portion.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabba's counter continues: one portion of dust would fall on the rot, so the reasoning fails.
Rabba explains that this is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon: its end is like its beginning.
Analogy: just as its beginning becomes a different thing, a gangilon, so does its end.
Asks what the analogy refers to, and introduces a baraita as the source.
Baraita: a corpse that has rot is one buried naked in a stone coffin or on a stone floor.
Baraita: a corpse lacking rot is one buried in its clothing, a wooden coffin, or on a brick floor.
Explains the rot rule applies only to a corpse, excluding a slain person whose body is not intact.
Baraita: a full vessel of rot into which any amount of dust fell is impure.
Rabbi Shimon declares it pure.
Baraita: a full vessel of rot scattered within a house renders the house impure.
Rabbi Shimon declares it pure in that case.
Explains both teachings are needed: the first case alone might be read as gathering, which the Rabbis cite.
Suggests the Rabbis might concede to Rabbi Shimon in the scattered case.
Argues that if the first case were taught alone, the scattered case would be read the same way.
Rabbi Shimon's view that impurity does not return and reattach; the Rabbis might concede in this case.
Baraita: a full vessel of rot with dust in a cemetery is impure, so both cases are taught.
Rabbi Shimon declares it pure.
What is the reasoning of the Rabbis?
Because one cannot fill a vessel with rot and dust in a cemetery lacking a full vessel of rot.
Now that you say Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is its end like its beginning, the cemetery case conflicts.
What is the reason in the case of the afterbirth?
Rabbi Yochanan explains it is due to nullification by majority, and he followed his reasoning.
Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov said one matter, the one we have just described.
Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: an animal with a bloody discharge is buried and exempt from firstborn status.
Rabbi Chiya taught that such a fetus does not impart impurity by touch or carrying.
If it does not impart impurity, why is it buried?
It is buried to publicize that it is exempt from firstborn, so it is apparently a viable offspring.
Why did Rabbi Chiya teach that it does not impart impurity by touch or carrying?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: it is due to nullification by majority.
Rabbi Ami reports Rabbi Yochanan saying Rabbi Shimon agrees his mother is impure for childbirth.
An old man offers to explain Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning to Rabbi Ami.
Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning derives from the verse in Leviticus about a woman who conceives and bears a male.
The verse applies even if she bore nothing but a form like the seed, so she is impure for childbirth.
Resh Lakish holds that a fetus torn apart in its waters becomes like a corpse whose form is confused.
Rabbi Yochanan asks Resh Lakish from where it is known that a corpse with a confused form is pure.
Proposes a source: a teaching of Rabbi Shabbtai citing Rabbi Yitzchak of Magdala about a burned corpse whose skeleton remains, which is impure.
Narrative: an incident occurred in which large openings were declared impure.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara infers from the earlier case that the skeleton remaining is the reason the openings were declared pure.
On the contrary, the same inference can be drawn the other way: small openings declared pure only because the skeleton remained.
Small openings are also impure, since each one is fit to remove a single limb.
Ravina tells Rav Ashi that Rabbi Yochanan holds a particular view.
According to whose view is Rabbi Yochanan's position?
According to Rabbi Eliezer, as we learned in a mishnah.
Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer says the measure of ashes of a burned corpse is...
How is the case of a burned corpse whose skeleton remains to be understood?
Abaye: it is a case where the corpse was burned on a kettle.
Rava: it is a case where the corpse was burned on a bench.
Ravina: it is a case where the burning left it so the body was charred.
Baraita: a woman who miscarries a severed hand or leg is impure for childbirth, and one does not worry about a sealed womb.
Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna both hold that one does not grant her days of purity.
What is the reason?
Say that she removed her birth, distancing it from the time of the miscarriage.
Rav Yosef objects from a baraita: if it is unknown what she miscarried, she sits for both cases, so such cases should say she distanced her birth.
Abaye: if the teaching concerned a niddah, one might think she brings an offering that is not eaten, so it teaches that it is eaten.
Rav Huna: if a fetus put out its hand and withdrew it, the mother is impure for childbirth.
Supports Rav Huna from the verse in Genesis about the time of birth when a hand was put forth.
Rav Yehuda objects: if a fetus put out its hand, the mother is not concerned for anything.
Rav Nachman says Rav Huna explained to him that she is concerned.
We do not give her days of purity until most of the fetus emerges.
But the teaching says she is not concerned for anything at all.
Abaye: she is not concerned by Torah law for anything, but by rabbinic law she is concerned.
But the verse itself says it.
It is rabbinic, and the verse is merely a support.
Mishnah: a woman who miscarries a tumtum or androgynos sits for male and female, depending on the case.
Mishnah: a fetus that is severed or castrated becomes like a newborn once most of its body has emerged.
Mishnah: it counts as born when most of its head emerges, defined as once the forehead emerges.
Why does the mishnah mention a tumtum alone and an androgynos alone?
Restates the mishnah's cases: tumtum and male, and androgynos and male.
Is this needed, and what is the question here?
Explains why it is taught: since R. Yitzchak holds that a woman who seeds first bears male, one might derive the case of a male.
Suggests both seeded at the same moment, one producing a male and the other a female.
Rav Nachman, citing Rav: a tumtum and an androgynos who saw whiteness or redness.
If they saw whiteness or redness they are not liable for entering the sanctuary, but terumah is not burned for them.
If they saw whiteness and redness together they are not liable for entering the sanctuary, but terumah is burned for them.
Cites the verse in Numbers about the purity test applying from male to female.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse as quoted: send out a certain male and a certain female, not a tumtum or androgynos.
Asks whether the following mishnah can be brought as support for the view.
Cites the mishnah about tumtum and androgynos who saw whiteness or redness as support.
What is the reason for the rule?
It is because of the verse: from male to female.
Repeats the verse on sending out certain male and female, excluding tumtum and androgynos.
Ulla: no, this is the view of Rabbi Eliezer, as we learned.
Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer: liable for concealing impurity from a creeping thing, but not for concealing sanctuary impurity.
Mishnah of Rabbi Akiva: liable for concealing impurity but not for concealing sanctuary impurity, the verse being read differently.
What is the difference between their views?
Hizkiyah: the difference is between a creeping thing and a carcass; Rabbi Eliezer requires knowing which one caused impurity.
Rabbi Akiva holds that such knowledge is not required.
Objects: Rabbi Eliezer himself required knowing whether the impurity was from a creeping thing or a carcass, so here too one must know whether it was whiteness or redness.
For Rabbi Akiva, who holds liability is for impurity, here too liability is for impurity.
Asks Rav what distinguishes entering the sanctuary, given the verse about male and female.
If so, terumah too should not be burned, since the verse on a zav's discharge says for male and female.
Repeats the verse wording: certain male, certain female, not tumtum or androgynos.
That verse is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's view: the male term includes a leper for his springs, and the female term includes a leprous woman.
This verse is also needed for one who has purification in a mikveh, excluding clay vessels, according to Rabbi Yossi.
Objects: if so the Torah should have written adam, and if it had, one would think metal vessels are excluded from impurity.
Why is male and female needed if the other reading covers it?
It is needed for Rav's view; the whole passage belongs to Rav's view.
If so, the Torah should have written male and female instead.
What does from male to female mean?
If anything with mikveh purification is included, then when impure from other impurities they should not be sent out.
The verse says from male, from impurity of one who separates from a male, and where it says male to female it excludes tumtum and androgynos.
But in the case of valuations the verse says the male, which seems to conflict.
Baraita: the male includes only a man for valuations, not a tumtum or androgynos, while the woman's valuation is included by another verse.
The baraita's reason: the verse says the male and if female, so tumtum and androgynos are excluded.
Here in from male and female nothing is excluded; that case needs its own explanation.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara states the aim: to distinguish between the valuation of a man and that of a woman.
Quotes the teaching: a fetus that emerged cut or castrated, and so on.
Rabbi Elazar says even the head is counted with them.
Rabbi Yochanan says this applies only when the head is not with them; if the head is with them, the head exempts.
Shall we say the dispute is about Shmuel's view?
Shmuel holds the head does not exempt in miscarriages; for a complete fetus, everyone agrees.
They disagree about a cut fetus: one holds the complete fetus is counted, and a cut one is not.
The other holds a cut one is also counted, stated in a different formulation.
The reason for the teaching of cut or castrated is that if it is as it should be, the head exempts.
Both views hold that the head exempts.
Neither holds Shmuel's view, though some teach this teaching separately.
Rabbi Elazar: the head is not like the majority of the limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan: the head is like the majority of the limbs.
They disagree about Shmuel's view, and we learned in a mishnah.
Mishnah: a fetus that emerged cut or castrated, once most of it emerged, is like a newborn.
By inference, since the mishnah says castrated, a cut one is as it should be.
Mishnah: once most of it has emerged, it is like a newborn.
This is difficult for Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan replies: say cut and castrated, but the mishnah says or, so the mishnah means this.
Restated: cut or whole, and castrated, once most emerged it is like a newborn.
Rav Pappa: this is a dispute between tannaim, cut or castrated, once most emerged is like a newborn.
Rabbi Yossi says it counts from when the fetus is as it should be.
What is he saying?
Rav Pappa explains: this is what he is saying.
Restated: cut and castrated, once most emerged, is like a newborn.
Concludes that as it should be, the head exempts.
Rabbi Yossi says: once most emerged, it is as it should be.
Rav Zevid objects: by inference, for a castrated one even most does not exempt.
We hold that most is like the whole, so the objection does not stand.
Rav Zevid explains that this is what the teaching says.
Rav Zevid's reading: cut and castrated, once most emerged is like a newborn; as it should be, the head exempts.
Rabbi Yossi says: once most emerged, it is as it should be for life.
A baraita teaches the same: cut or castrated, once most emerged, is like a newborn; as it should be, the head exempts.
Rabbi Yossi says: once most emerged, as it should be for life.
What is as it should be for life, and what is most of the head?
Rabbi Yossi says: once the temples emerge; Abba Chanan reports this in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rabbi Yehoshua says: once the forehead emerges.
Others say: once the horns of the head are seen.
Mishnah: a woman who miscarried and it is unknown whether it was a fetus or not sits for male, female, and niddah.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one who crossed a river and miscarried brings an offering that is eaten, following the majority of women who bear viable offspring; we learned this.
Asks why she should sit as a niddah, and suggests following the majority of women instead.
The mishnah refers to a woman whose pregnancy was not established; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi spoke of an established pregnancy.
Brings a baraita on animals: one that went out full and came back empty, the next firstborn is doubtful, following the majority of animals.
Dismisses this as obvious.
Ravina explains: the majority of animals bear what exempts from firstborn, the minority bear what does not.
If all birthing women are soiled, the fact that she was not soiled means the firstborn is viable.
Rather, say most births soil; this one, not being soiled, spoils the majority for her.
Ravin came and said that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina raises an objection.
Ravin says he does not know what the objection is, as it was taught.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A woman who went out full and came back empty and brought the blood before us: three weeks pure and ten weeks one impure, one pure.
She may have intercourse at thirty-five, and they immerse her ninety-five immersions.
This is the view of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, who say thirty-five.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it suffices that the immersion be done at the last.
Explains the first weeks: the first is no intercourse, perhaps a male was born; the second and third follow the same reasoning of birth sex and the flow.
In the fourth week, though she sees blood, she may have intercourse because that blood is pure, not because majority is disregarded.
Asks what the refutation is, since the matter is not because majority is not followed.
Perhaps she distanced her birth, so the timing is explained.
The fifth week is pure, so she may have intercourse; in the fourth week each day is in doubt at the end of birth and start of niddah.
Perhaps it is the beginning of niddah, and she must sit seven for niddah from the twenty-first day.
Rabbi Shimon, who forbids this lest she come to doubt, holds she may have intercourse when she saw blood in the evening.
In the evening they immerse her ninety-five immersions; the first week they immerse her.
They immerse her at night, since perhaps she gave birth to a male.
The second week they immerse her at night, perhaps a female was born, and by day as well.
Perhaps she gave birth to a male with a flow, which explains the immersion.
The third week they immerse her by day.
Perhaps she gave birth to a female with a flow, so immersion is at night.
Beit Shammai hold to their reasoning: one who immersed by day needs a long immersion.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how the Beit Shammai immersion total of ninety-five can be explained if extra immersions are removed.
Rav Yirmeya explains the extra immersion as covering a woman who arrives at twilight, when the day-or-night status is uncertain.
Asks what purpose the thirty-five immersions serve for Beit Hillel, who say no immersion is needed after a long day of purity.
Explains the immersions as covering the end of impurity, the end of the zava's seven clean days, and nightly immersion in the fifth week.
Asks why the baraita needs to mention ten weeks when eight and a half weeks would suffice.
Says the baraita completes the half week to a full week and mirrors the pattern of impure and pure weeks.
Objects that Beit Hillel's count omits immersions required because the woman may be a zava.
Replies that Beit Hillel count only immersions required before intercourse, not those after it.
Objects that Beit Shammai, who count post-intercourse immersions, should also count zava immersions.
Replies that Beit Shammai's count concerns childbirth immersions, not immersions due to zava alone.
Objects that Beit Shammai do count immersions due to a woman who gave birth as a zava.
Replies that such immersions are tied to childbirth, since they are delayed until the post-birth zava status ends.
Restates the baraita's instruction that the woman immerses each night of the first week.
Asks why she should not also immerse in daytime, since each day might complete her clean days.
Explains the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires the seven clean days to be counted in the court's presence.
Asks whether she should also immerse at the end of the first week, after counting seven clean days.
Replies that the baraita is not addressing immersions required once a week.
Asks whether she should immerse on the first day, in case she is a lesser zava who counts clean days day by day.
Replies that the baraita deals only with a greater zava, who must count seven clean days.
Concludes that the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires the seven clean days to be counted in the court's presence.
Concludes that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who forbids a zava intercourse on her seventh day to avoid uncertainty.
Concludes that immersion at its proper time is a mitzva, so she immerses daily.
Gives Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda's view that one final immersion suffices and immersion at its time is not a mitzva.
Mishnah rules that a woman who discharges on day forty-one after immersion keeps the impurity of both male and female births.
Rabbi Yishmael gives separate periods for male and female births, with the female formation completing on day eighty-one.
The Sages say the male and female formations both conclude on day forty-one.
Asks why the mishna mentions the strictures of a male birth at all.
Objects that the mishna would otherwise teach the female strictures, so the male mention must concern other days.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the mishna would then treat the woman as always menstruating, with no period of purity at all.
Explains the male-birth strictures: bleeding on day thirty-four and again on day forty-one keeps her impure until day forty-eight.
Applies the same logic to a female birth: bleeding on day seventy-four and again on day eighty-one keeps her impure until day eighty-eight.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that on day forty-one she observes male-birth and menstrual strictures but not female-birth strictures.
Baraita reports Rabbi Yishmael's verse-based reasoning, that male and female births each yield impurity and purity in a set pattern.
Yishmael infers that embryo formation time parallels the length of the impurity and purity periods for each sex.
The Rabbis reply that one cannot derive embryo formation time from the length of postpartum impurity.
The Rabbis cite Cleopatra's experiment on her maidservants, which showed both sexes fully formed by day forty-one.
Yishmael answers that he brings proof from the Torah while they bring proof from fools.
Asks what Torah proof Yishmael actually brings for his position.
Proposes Yishmael's derivation from the double impurity and purity periods as his Torah proof.
Objects that the Rabbis already rejected deriving embryo formation from the lengths of impurity periods.
Answers that the verse adds a second childbirth mention for a female, implying her embryo takes twice as long.
Asks why Yishmael calls the Cleopatra proof a proof from fools.
Suggests the female-embryo maidservant conceived forty days earlier, so her embryo needed eighty days.
Asks how the Rabbis would respond to this suggestion about the purgative given to the maidservants.
Yishmael replies that some pregnancies are not terminated by the purgative, so an earlier conception is possible.
Baraita version: Yishmael cites Cleopatra's experiment, finding a male fully formed at forty-one days and a female at eighty-one.
The Rabbis reply that one does not bring proof from fools.
Asks why the Rabbis regard this as a proof from fools.
Explains they suspect the female-embryo woman conceived forty days later, so formation took only forty days.
Yishmael answers that the maidservants were entrusted to a steward who prevented intercourse during the experiment.
The Rabbis reply there is no guardian against licentiousness, so the steward himself may have had intercourse with her.
Objects that if the womb were opened on day forty-one, the female embryo would already show male-like development.
Abaye responds that the two embryos showed identical signs of age, so the female developed in eighty days.
Mishna: the Rabbis hold that both male and female formation conclude on day forty-one.
Asks why the mishna repeats the Rabbis' view, since it matches the first tanna.
Proposes that the unattributed view agrees with the Rabbis, so the majority opinion should govern.
Replies that it is obvious the halakha follows the unattributed view as a general principle.
Explains the mishna settles that the majority opinion governs, lest Yishmael's verse-supported reasoning be adopted.
Rabbi Samlai compares the fetus in the womb to a folded notebook and describes its posture.
Describes the fetus eating and drinking like its mother, and its orifices switching once it enters the air of the world.
A lamp is lit above the fetus's head, so it sees from one end of the world to the other.
Cites Job 29:3 about God's lamp shining above my head and lighting my path through darkness.
Explains the wonder: a person asleep can dream of a distant place, so seeing across the world is plausible.
No days are more blissful for a person than the days spent as a fetus in the womb.
Cites Job 29:2 about wishing to be as in the months of old.
Explains that the days with months but no years are the months of gestation.
A fetus is taught the entire Torah while in the womb.
Cites Proverbs 4:4, where a teacher instructs the speaker to hold fast to his words.
Cites Job 29:4 about God's counsel being upon my tent as further support.
Asks why Job 29:4 is needed, since Proverbs might refer only to a prophet.
Replies that Job's verse shows ordinary people, not only prophets, were taught the Torah in the womb.
When the fetus emerges, an angel slaps its mouth, making it forget the entire Torah.
Cites Genesis 4:7 that sin crouches at the entrance, showing the newborn is immediately liable to sin.
The fetus does not leave the womb until the angels administer an oath to it.
Cites Isaiah 45:23 that to Me every knee shall bow and every tongue shall swear.
Interprets the bowing of every knee as referring to the day of one's death.
Cites Psalms 22:30 that all who go down to the dust shall kneel before Him.
Interprets the swearing of every tongue as referring to the day of one's birth.
Cites Psalms 24:4 about the clean-handed one who kept the oath he took before birth.
Asks what the oath is that the angels administer to the fetus.
The oath is to remain righteous even if the world praises you, since the soul given is pure and must be kept pure.
School of Rabbi Yishmael: a priest gives teruma to an am ha'aretz and threatens to burn it if he does not keep it pure.
Rabbi Elazar's statement begins here and continues onto the next daf.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks which verse teaches that the fetus is put under an oath at birth.
Cites Psalms 71:6, where the speaker says God took him out of his mother's womb, with the word gozi.
Asks how one knows that the word gozi is a term for administering an oath.
Cites Jeremiah 7:29, cut off your hair, read as the nazirite's vow, to show gozi means taking a vow.
Rabbi Elazar compares the fetus in the womb to a nut floating on water that sinks in one direction or the other.
A baraita says the fetus lies in the lower compartment for three months, the middle for three, and the upper for the last three, then turns to emerge.
Ties the turning of the fetus to the mishna's teaching that female labor pains are greater than male labor pains.
Asks which verse shows that the fetus initially lies in the lower part of the womb.
Cites Psalms 139:15, I was woven together in the lowest parts of the earth, as proof of the lower position.
Asks why female birth labor is greater than male birth labor.
A male fetus is born face down as it engaged in intercourse, while a female turns its face around before birth.
A baraita states intercourse is harmful in the first trimester, tolerable in the second, and beneficial in the third.
A baraita says intercourse on the ninetieth day of pregnancy is as if one spills blood.
Asks how a man could know that it is the ninetieth day of pregnancy.
Abaye says one should have intercourse anyway and rely on God to protect the simple, citing Psalms 116:6.
A baraita states God, father, and mother are partners: the father supplies bones and brain, the mother skin and flesh.
God supplies the spirit, soul, face, senses, speech, movement, understanding and wisdom to the person.
When a person dies, God takes His part and the parents' parts are left behind.
Rav Pappa explains this with the adage of removing the salt from meat and then tossing the meat to a dog.
Rav Hinnana bar Pappa introduces his teaching on divine and human creative work.
Cites Job 9:10 about God doing great and countless wonders.
Explains that flesh and blood cannot secure an open flask opening downward, while God keeps the fetus safe in an open womb.
Another contrast: a heavier item on a scale sinks, while a heavier fetus rises higher in the womb under God's design.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili introduces a teaching on the wonder of human creation.
Cites Psalms 139:14 about being fearfully and wonderfully made.
Explains that human planting of mixed seeds yields distinct plants, whereas God forms a child from both seeds in one womb.
Offers a second illustration: a dyer's herbs in one cauldron yield one color, while God gives each seed its own distinct features.
Rav Yosef introduces a teaching on Isaiah 12:1.
Cites Isaiah 12:1, I will give thanks to You, for You were angry with me.
Asks what matter the verse is actually speaking about.
Gives a story of two travelers: one was held back by a thorn and later thanked God when his companion's ship sank.
Rabbi Elazar's teaching on the same theme is introduced.
Cites Psalms 72:18-19, God alone does wondrous things, as the basis for Rabbi Elazar's teaching.
Explains that even the person who experienced the miracle does not recognize it as a miracle.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa introduces his teaching on creation from the clear part of the semen.
Cites Psalms 139:3, You measure my going about and lying down, as the basis for the teaching.
Explains that a person is created not from the entire drop but from its clear, procreative part.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael gives the parable of a man winnowing grain in a granary, taking the food and leaving the waste.
Rabbi Abbahu raises a contradiction between two psalms of David.
Cites II Samuel 22:40 and Psalms 18:33, the two verses with girds me spelled differently.
David says God selected him, separating the procreative part of the semen, and girded him with strength.
Rabbi Abbahu introduces his teaching on Balaam's blessing.
Cites Numbers 23:10, who has counted the dust of Jacob or numbered the stock of Israel.
Explains that God counts the times Israel engage in intercourse, awaiting the drop from which a righteous person will form.
Balaam's eye went blind after he presumed God would not look at this matter, as Rabbi Yohanan's teaching adds.
Cites Numbers 24:3, the saying of the man whose eye is shut, as proof of Balaam's blindness.
Rabbi Yohanan's teaching on the same theme is introduced.
Asks about Genesis 30:16 and cites it, and he lay with her that night, concerning Leah conceiving Issachar.
Explains that the verse teaches God contributed to that act.
Cites Genesis 49:14, Issachar is a large-boned donkey, to show God guided Jacob's donkey to Leah's tent.
Rabbi Yitzhak, quoting Rabbi Ami, states the fetus's sex is determined by who emits seed first at conception.
Cites Leviticus 12:2 about a woman who bears seed and gives birth to a male.
A baraita reports the earlier view on who emits seed first, which the Sages did not explain until Rabbi Tzadok did.
Cites Genesis 46:15, the sons of Leah with his daughter Dinah, to show who emits seed first determines the sex.
Cites I Chronicles 8:40 about the sons of Ulam with many sons and sons' sons.
Asks whether a person has the power to have many sons and sons' sons.
Explains that the verse shows such abundance comes from God, to be drawn from a specified source.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some men delay emission so their wives emit seed first, and the verse credits them as if they had many sons.
Rav Ketina and Rava give methods for ensuring that all of one's children are male.
Rabbi Ami holds that conception happens only close to the onset of the menstrual cycle.
Cites Psalms 51:7, behold I was brought forth in iniquity, to support the menstrual-proximity view.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that conception happens only near the time of the woman's immersion.
Cites the next clause of Psalms 51:7, in sin did my mother conceive me, to support the immersion view.
Asks how one knows that the root for sin here means purification.
Cites Leviticus 14:52 where the house is purified, and Psalms 51:9, purge me with hyssop, to show het means purifying.
Rabbi Yitzhak, quoting Rabbi Ami, says a male birth brings peace to the world.
Cites Isaiah 16:1, send lambs for the ruler of the land, where the word for lambs is similar to male.
Explains that the word male is read homiletically as this is a kar, a gift that brings stability.
A male comes into the world with his loaf of bread, meaning he can provide for himself.
Cites II Kings 6:23, he prepared great provision, to show kar means sustenance.
A female comes into the world with nothing, since she comes clean and empty.
Explains that people do not give a girl sustenance until she asks for it.
Cites Genesis 30:28, appoint me your wages, where Laban's word resembles the word for female.
Students of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai ask why the Torah requires a woman after childbirth to bring an offering.
Explains that in pain she swears never to resume relations, so the offering atones for her later violation.
Rav Yosef objects that she violates the oath knowingly, and the offering would be a sheep or goat for an oath.
Students ask why a male birth makes a woman impure seven days and a female birth fourteen.
Rabbi Shimon explains that she regrets her oath sooner after a joyful male birth than after a sorrowful female birth.
Students ask why circumcision is performed specifically on the eighth day.
So that the parents are not left unhappy at a joyful ceremony while still barred from intercourse.
A baraita introduces Rabbi Meir's view on the reason for the seven-day separation.
Asks why the Torah makes a menstruating woman impure for seven days.
So that the husband does not grow accustomed and repulsed, but she remains dear to him as on her wedding day.
Students of Rabbi Dostai ask why men pursue women for marriage rather than the reverse.
Rabbi Dostai offers the parable of a lost item: the owner seeks it, and man seeks what he lost from his own body.
Asks why a man engages in intercourse facing down while the woman faces up.
Each faces the place from which they were created, the man from earth and the woman from man.
Asks why an angry man is more readily appeased than a woman.
The man is like the earth that yields to pressure, while the woman is like bone that resists molding.
Asks why a woman's voice is pleasant while a man's is not.
The man is like earth, which makes no sound when struck, while the woman is like bone, which resonates.
Cites Song of Songs 2:14, for sweet is your voice, to support the claim that a woman's voice is pleasant.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter, which begins with the mishna on Samaritan girls.
Mishna: Samaritan girls are menstruating from the cradle, and Samaritan men impart impurity to lower bedding like upper bedding.
Samaritan men are treated as those who have intercourse with menstruating women, since Samaritan women count seven days for every blood emission.
Entering the Temple in such garments incurs no liability, and their teruma is not burned, because the impurity is uncertain.
Asks what the mishna's case is: if girls already see blood, Jewish girls too are menstruating, and if not, Samaritan girls are not.
Rav Sheshet's explanation: the case is unspecified, and since a minority of girls see blood, we are concerned for each girl.
Asks which tanna holds that one must be concerned for the minority.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Identifies the anonymous view as Rabbi Meir's, who forbids minors from halitza and levirate marriage.
The Rabbis accept that minors cannot perform halitza, and ask why they still cannot enter levirate marriage.
Rabbi Meir replies that a minor may turn out to be a sexually underdeveloped spouse, causing forbidden intercourse without purpose.
The Rabbis object that most minors are not underdeveloped, so one follows the majority rather than the rare case.
Objects that Rabbi Meir may be concerned only for a common minority, not for the rare case of menstruating young girls.
Replies that menstruating young girls are also a common minority, as the Gemara goes on to show.
Cites a baraita with three incidents in which baby girls were immersed before their mothers, showing early menstruation occurred.
Asks why Rav Yosef's Babylonian case requires immersion, since Shmuel says impure touch does not disqualify teruma outside Eretz Yisrael.
Mar Zutra says the immersion was needed because smearing teruma oil counts as eating.
Cites Leviticus 22:15 in a baraita, read to include one who smears and one who drinks in the teruma prohibition.
Asks why a verse is needed to cover drinking, since drinking is already included under eating.
Explains the verse includes smearing, teaching that smearing is treated like drinking.
Offers a second derivation from Psalms 109:18 that liquid entering the body is like oil into the bones.
If Rabbi Meir's view holds, the Gemara asks, we should also be concerned for minority young girls among Jews.
Jewish girls are subject to menstrual law only when they see blood, while Samaritans do not separate, so only they were decreed.
Asks what the interpretation of the difference between a woman and and if a woman is.
A baraita derives from and if a woman that a one-day-old girl has the status of a menstruating woman.
Asks how the verses conflict with another baraita about intercourse involving a three-year-old girl.
The contrary baraita derives from the word woman that intercourse by a girl aged three years and a day renders impure.
Rava says these are halakhot from Sinai, which the Sages supported with verses.
Asks which halakha is derived from a verse and which is from Sinai, and why the verse wording would not distinguish them.
Concludes that the three-year-old intercourse rule is from Sinai, and the one-day menstruation rule is derived from a verse.
Asks why a verse is needed at all once the three-year-old intercourse rule is established as halakha.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse excludes a man from becoming impure through red semen.
Objects that a ten-day-old girl's ziva status should be derived from the menstruation rule, so the verse is unnecessary.
Replies that without the verse one might think menstrual law for a one-day-old girl is stringent, so ziva law needs its own inclusion.
Objects that the Torah could write ziva for ten-day-old girls directly, so the and if a woman verse must be for something else.
Objects that the Torah already excluded red semen elsewhere.
One verse excludes red semen and another excludes a man who is rendered a zav by blood from his penis.
A baraita cites Leviticus 15:2, any man, to include a one-day-old boy in zav impurity, following Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds the verse is unnecessary, since male and female already include minors.
Asks whether the verse including a minor boy also includes a one-day-old, given a contrary baraita.
The contrary baraita cites Leviticus 15:16, and a man, to show a boy aged nine years and a day is included.
Rava says these halakhot are from Sinai and the Sages supported them with verses.
Asks which halakha is from Sinai and which is from a verse, noting the unspecified wording would include a one-day-old.
Concludes the nine-year-old rule is from Sinai, while inclusion of a one-day-old boy is derived from a verse.
Asks why a verse is needed at all once the rule is established as halakha.
The verse excludes a woman who has a white discharge from zava impurity.
Asks why the Torah needs to write the one-day-old boy rule and the one-day-old and ten-day-old girl rules separately.
Both verses are needed: a male-only verse would not show girls are included, since girls are not made impure by three sightings in one day.
A female-only verse would not show boys are included, since boys are not impure from sightings beyond their control.
Asks what the mishna means by the lower bedding is like the upper bedding, since pressure makes the lowest mattress impure anyway.
The lower bedding of a man with a menstruating woman is like the upper bedding of a zav, imparting impurity only to food and drink.
Asks from where it is derived that the bedding above a zav imparts impurity only to food and drink.
Cites Leviticus 15:10, whoever touches any thing that was under him shall be impure.
Asks what the expression under him means.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the bedding-beneath-zav rule is already derived from whoever touches his bed, so the verse must teach something else.
Explains the verse teaches that any item under which a zav is sitting, the bedding above him, imparts impurity.
Cites Leviticus 15:10 on the one who bears these things, to show the bearer of a zav's item also becomes impure.
The verse moved the bedding above a zav from severe to lesser impurity, so it imparts impurity only to food and drink.
Objects that the verse may only lower the impurity of the bedding to not pass to garments, leaving impurity to people and garments.
Replies that the verse says he shall be impure, indicating lesser impurity.
Asks from where we derive that the bedding beneath a man who has relations with a menstruating woman is impure.
A baraita cites Leviticus 15:24 and draws on the phrase her impurity be upon him to teach the seven-day impurity.
The baraita derives from her impurity be upon him that such a man imparts impurity like the menstruating woman to people and vessels.
Derives that his bedding and seat are impure like hers, citing Leviticus 15:24, every bed upon which he lies.
Asks what the separate phrase every bed adds if the impurity was already stated.
The verse lowers his impurity to lesser status, so he imparts impurity only to food and drink.
Rav Ahai objects that the verse may only lower impurity so that the man's bedding does not pass to garments.
Rav Asi replies that the verse states every bed shall be impure, which indicates lesser impurity.
Objects that the verse is a generalization followed by a detail, so only the items specified are impure.
Abaye says the seven-day phrase separates the general and detailed clauses, so the principle does not apply.
Rava holds that the principle does apply even to distant clauses, and the term every is only an amplification here.
Rabbi Yaakov objects that the man should be treated like the woman, with both touch and bedding stringent or both lenient.
Rava replies that the verse says her impurity be upon him, meaning the impurity is imposed stringently on him.
Asks whether all Samaritan men are considered men who have relations with menstruating women, since some are unmarried.
Rabbi Yitzhak of Migdal says the halakha applies only to men who are married.
The mishna states Samaritan women keep the seven-day period for each blood emission, and Rabbi Meir says this would be a great remedy if they did.
Explains Samaritan women see green blood, count seven days from it, and then complete the days from it, so they immerse while still impure.
Rami bar Hama objects that Samaritan women could count that day, and Jewish women would also count it, since part of a day counts as a whole.
Rava objects that if part of a day counts as a whole for zava, a seminal emission in a zav's count could not nullify a day.
Replies the case is a seminal emission adjacent to sunset, when no remainder of the day remains to count.
Objects that the verse on the zav's seminal emission should not be read as limited to emissions adjacent to sunset.
Replies that the verse must be read that way, because the principle that part of a day counts as a whole forces it.
Rami bar Hama asks whether a woman who discharges semen after relations negates her count of clean days for ziva.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes that the woman was merely touching semen and so did not negate her count.
Rava says Rami bar Hama's dilemma is baseless, since a zava negating a single day is not a coherent option.
Cites Leviticus 15:28, and after that she shall be pure, to show no impurity may separate the seven clean days.
Objects that a zav himself negates only one day from his count for a seminal emission, so Rava's reasoning fails.
Replies that the verse only forbids a ziva impurity from separating the days, leaving semen emission open.
Cites part of the mishna on Samaritan garments, which do not require a sin offering or burning of teruma.
Recounts Rav Pappa's visit to Tavakh, where an elderly woman points him to Rav Shmuel as a Torah scholar.
Rav Pappa infers Rav Shmuel is God-fearing, and Rav Shmuel hosts him with a bull while raising a difficulty.
Raises a contradiction: the mishna on Samaritan garments implies teruma is not burned for uncertain impurity.
Cites another mishna listing six uncertain impurities, including am ha'aretz garments, where teruma is burned.
Rav Pappa replies the case concerns a Samaritan ḥaver who is meticulous about purity, so the mishna lessens concern.
Rav Shmuel rejects this, since the mishna concerns men who have relations with menstruating women, not a ḥaver.
Rav Pappa leaves in embarrassment and relates the exchange to Rav Shimi bar Ashi.
