Rav Shimi asks why Rav Pappa did not answer that the Samaritan had immersed and then the garments touched teruma.
Explains the case: the Samaritan immersed, then trod on the ḥaver's garments, which then touched teruma, so it is not burned.
If the concern were am ha'aretz impurity he has immersed, and if it were relations with a menstruating woman, that is uncertain.
Even if he had relations, two uncertainties remain about her count, which forms a compound uncertainty, so teruma is not burned.
Rav Pappa objects that the impurity could be derived from am ha'aretz garments, which impart impurity to people and garments.
Rav Shimi replies that the mishna refers to a naked Samaritan, so none of his garments touch the ḥaver's garments.
Mishna: Sadducee girls who follow their ancestors' ways are like Samaritan women, while those who follow Jewish ways are like Jewish women.
Asks what the halakha is when a Sadducee woman's custom is unknown.
Suggests inferring from the first clause of the mishna that unspecified Sadducee girls are like Jewish women.
Rejects this, since the latter clause could equally imply unspecified Sadducee women are like Samaritan women, so no inference follows.
Cites Rabbi Yosei's opinion in the mishna to conclude that the first tanna holds unspecified cases are like Samaritan women.
A baraita tells of a Sadducee who spat on the High Priest's garments in the marketplace, and the High Priest went to ask his wife.
The Sadducee's wife says Sadducee women fear the Pharisees and show their blood to the Sages, so the garments are pure.
Rabbi Yosei testifies that the Sadducee women in his neighborhood showed their blood to the Sages, except one who died as punishment.
Objects that the High Priest could have been concerned about am ha'aretz saliva, and Abaye and Rava respond about Sadducee ḥaverim.
Rava's teaching that follows is introduced, continuing onto the next daf.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: On a festival the Sages treated am ha'aretz impurity as pure, so the High Priest's concern was about relations with a menstruating woman.
Cites Judges 20:11, all the men of Israel gathered as one man, which makes all of them ḥaverim during the festival.
Mishna: Beit Shammai deem gentile menstrual blood and a leper's pure-period blood pure, while Beit Hillel say it is like moist saliva and urine.
Mishna: Beit Shammai say a woman's blood before immersion is like saliva and urine, impure only while moist, while Beit Hillel say it is impure moist or dry.
Beit Shammai concede that a woman who gives birth as a zava has blood impure whether moist or dry.
Objects that Beit Shammai should accept the Torah's zav verse, which would make gentile ziva only rabbinically impure.
Cites Leviticus 15:2 and infers that gentile ziva is not impure by Torah law, but is treated as a zav by rabbinic decree.
The Sages decreed that gentiles be treated as zavin in all their matters of ritual purity.
Beit Shammai reply that the rule applies only to males, since applying it to females would make Torah-impure blood treated as moist or dry.
Objects that moist-only impurity for gentile saliva and urine should be ruled as no impurity, to distinguish them from a Jewish zava.
Replies that a conspicuous marker is needed for the saliva and urine, which are common, but not for the less common blood.
Rava holds a gentile male's ziva is impure even by Beit Shammai, while a gentile's semen is pure even by Beit Hillel.
Rava explains a marker is possible for gentile ziva, but a gentile's semen needs one too, so its impurity is only rabbinic.
The Sages decreed impurity for a gentile's ziva that is not dependent on action, but not for emissions that depend on action.
Asks whether the case of gentile and Jewish emissions supports the view that gentile semen is pure, or only impure rabbinically.
A baraita states that the semen of a Jew is impure everywhere.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: the semen of a gentile is pure anywhere, even in a Jewish woman's womb, except for urine mixed into it.
Objects that the baraita may mean gentile semen is pure only by Torah law, impure by rabbinic law, as with urine.
Concludes from the baraita that gentile semen is pure even by rabbinic law.
Cites the baraita that a Jew's semen is impure everywhere, even in a gentile woman's womb.
Asks whether this baraita resolves Rav Pappa's dilemma about a Jew's semen inside a gentile woman.
Rav Pappa's dilemma concerns semen more than three days after intercourse, since within three days it is impure.
Frames the dilemma: whether gentile women's wombs make semen foul within three days, and it remains unresolved.
Mishna: Beit Shammai deem a female leper's blood during her purity days pure, while Beit Hillel deem it impure when moist.
Asks what the reasoning of Beit Hillel is.
Rabbi Yitzhak derives from Leviticus 15:33, male or female, that a leper's emissions, including a female leper's, impart impurity.
Asks what the sources of a female leper's emissions are.
Explains that the verse must mean her blood during her purity days, since other sources could be derived from the male case.
Asks how Beit Shammai answer, since a male leper's case cannot be transferred to a female, who is not bound by the same restrictions.
Asks how Beit Hillel respond, and why the Merciful One would write the rule only for females.
A kal vachomer argument: if a female is not bound by the male's requirements, the verse's inclusion should apply to her emissions, not males.
Beit Hillel conclude that since the emission does not apply to the male, it applies to the female's blood during her purity days.
Beit Shammai object that a female's case is not comparable, since she is impure through rape, so the male case is not derivable from hers.
Beit Shammai's alternative: the verse covers any male, adult or minor, which Beit Hillel derive from the law of the zav.
Beit Hillel cite the law of the zav, which applies to adult or minor, as proof that minors are included.
Rav Yosef reports Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's position on the zav.
Asks whether a minor zav's first sighting imparts impurity through touch.
Cites Leviticus 15:32, this is the law of the zav and of him from whom seminal emission goes out.
The verse makes whoever has a seminal emission impure, and his first sighting imparts impurity; the minor's first sighting may not.
Rav Yosef asks whether the first sighting of a minor combines with his emission to impart impurity.
Rava says: come and hear a baraita.
A baraita: as an adult's first sighting imparts impurity, so does a minor's first sighting.
Rav Yosef asks whether a leper's first sighting imparts impurity through carrying, since it is like the source of a zav.
Rava says: come and hear another baraita.
Cites Leviticus 15:2, its discharge is impure, to show the discharge is impure in some respect.
Asks whether this refers to a zav alone.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the verse is unnecessary, since a drop causing impurity to others should a fortiori cause impurity to itself.
Rava concludes that the verse's inclusion of a second sighting shows a place of ziva is not itself a source of impurity.
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta says to Rava that the verse may refer to a zav who is not a leper.
Asks from where Rava knows the verse refers to a zav who is a leper, and suggests it may refer to a plain zav.
Counters the a fortiori argument: the scapegoat causes impurity to others while itself remaining pure, so the inference fails.
Abaye asks what purpose Rav Yosef's dilemma about a leper's first sighting serves.
Explains that Rav Yosef's own teaching already derives zav law for minors, leaving the leper inclusion for the sources of emission.
The Merciful One compares a leper to a full zav, so a leper's first sighting imparts impurity through carrying, as a zav does.
Rav Huna says the first sighting of a zav imparts impurity even if it occurred beyond his control.
Derives Rav Huna's view from Leviticus 15:32, comparing the first sighting to a seminal emission that occurs beyond control.
Brings a mishna on examining a man with a first sighting and asks whether the examination concerns impurity or the offering.
Suggests the latter clause of the mishna, examining at the second sighting, shows the examination concerns impurity.
Concludes that since the latter clause concerns impurity, the first clause does too.
Rejects the comparison, since each examination may serve a different purpose.
Cites Rabbi Eliezer's view that the third sighting is examined because of the offering, and infers the first tanna means impurity.
Replies that all agree the examination concerns the offering, and the dispute is over reading the word et.
The Rabbis do not interpret et, so the third sighting of a male is like that of a female, and no examination follows the third sighting.
Rabbi Eliezer interprets et, so the third sighting still requires examination and the fourth counts as a sighting even beyond control.
Cites Rabbi Yitzhak's question: a zav is already included among those with seminal emission, so why is he treated separately.
The separate passage makes a zav lenient, since he is not impure through emission beyond control, and stringent in other respects.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling that a zav imparts impurity to the bedding and seat he sits on, as a primary source.
Asks which sighting of ziva Rabbi Yitzhak means, since the second sighting cannot be the minor case and the first contradicts Rav Huna.
Objects that the first sighting cannot render bedding or seat impure, so the stringency must refer to a later sighting.
Clarifies Rabbi Yitzhak's view: a zav's separate passage is lenient on the first sighting and stringent on the bedding and seat.
Rav Huna compares ziva to barley dough water, noting its source, consistency, and appearance compared to semen.
Mishna: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the blood of a woman who gave birth but has not immersed.
A baraita: Beit Hillel argue that a woman who has not immersed should be treated as menstruating, as is a menstruating woman who did not immerse.
Beit Shammai reject the comparison, since a menstruating woman who immersed and then bled is still impure, unlike a woman who gave birth.
Beit Hillel counter with the woman who gives birth as a zava, showing that failure to immerse after seven clean days makes blood impure.
Beit Shammai maintain their refutation: a zava who gave birth still imparts impurity only while the blood is moist.
Asks whether the dispute extends to a zava who counted seven clean days but did not immerse, given the mishna's agreement.
Resolves it: the baraita concerns a woman who counted seven clean days, while the mishna concerns one who has not yet counted them.
A baraita states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel follow their respective views for a woman who gave birth as a zava and did not immerse.
Rav holds pure and impure blood come from one source, while Levi holds two sources that open and close alternately.
Asks what the practical difference is between the views of Rav and Levi.
Lists the cases: continuous bleeding from the impure period into the pure period, and from the pure period past its end.
Explains that for Rav the first clause is lenient and the second stringent, while for Levi it is the reverse.
Objects from the mishna that Beit Shammai say the blood is moist-only, which seems inconsistent with Levi's view.
Asks why Beit Hillel rule that the blood is impure whether moist or dry on Levi's view, since pure-period blood comes from the pure source.
Levi says the mishna concerns continuous flow from the impure period, and Beit Shammai hold there is one source.
Asks what the difference between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is on Rav's view, since Levi's view explains it.
On Rav's view the dispute is whether the days alone or the days plus immersion determine purity of blood.
Comes to prove from the mishna that Beit Shammai concede blood from a zava who gave birth is impure, whether moist or dry.
Asks why, on Levi's view, the blood would be impure whether moist or dry, rather than moist-only like a zava's saliva.
Levi explains the case as continuous flow from the impure source, which indicates impure blood.
Asks what purpose the mishna's teaching serves if the blood is obviously impure.
Beit Shammai's teaching is needed for a woman who gave birth as a zava, where the day-based purity applies only to a woman who gave birth.
A baraita on Leviticus 12:2 derives that a man, nights, and a zava who gave birth are included in the impurity rules.
Asks why the case of a woman who gave birth as a zava requires seven clean days, if purity follows Rav's single source.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why Levi needs a woman to wait seven clean days if any cessation of bleeding at the end of impurity suffices.
Explains the baraita requires only that the bleeding stop for any amount of time, so the following seven days count as clean days.
A baraita states that the days of pregnancy and nursing count toward each other for a woman who had no bleeding during them.
Gives examples of how the pregnancy and nursing periods combine to make three periods of no bleeding.
Asks why, on Rav's single-source view, three periods are needed, while Levi's view would only need a brief cessation.
Explains the baraita requires only a brief stop at the end of impurity so that clean days count toward three periods.
A baraita states Shammai and Hillel agree that a woman who bleeds again during her clean days is impure from the moment she sees blood.
Asks why, on Rav's view, the blood is impure only from when seen, since the impurity cannot reach back a full day.
Replies that there is no time between the end of the clean days and the blood, so retroactive impurity does not apply.
Asks why she is not impure from examination to examination, rather than only from when the blood is seen.
Replies that since retroactive impurity is not possible for her, the Sages did not decree impurity from the last examination.
A baraita on a woman who gives birth as a zava and did not immerse gives the Shammai and Hillel positions, as above.
Asks why, on Levi's view, Beit Hillel hold the blood is impure whether moist or dry, since it comes from the pure source.
Levi replies that the baraita follows the view that Shammai and Hillel agree, or it concerns continuous flow from the impure source.
Objects that the baraita speaks of a woman who counted seven clean days, so the continuous-flow reading does not fit.
Explains the case is a woman who gave birth to a female as a zava, where the first week's bleeding stopped and the second did not.
Mar Zutra taught that the halakha follows Rav as a stringency and Levi as a stringency, as reported by Rav Shemen.
Rav Ashi and Mareimar rule that the halakha follows Rav, whether as a leniency or as a stringency.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a woman with labor-type bleeding that stops for a full day before birth is a zava, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Yehoshua requires that the pangs stop for a full day and night, and the test concerns the pangs rather than the blood.
Asks how long before birth labor pains are still considered the cause of the blood.
Rabbi Meir says the labor-related rule applies even forty or fifty days before birth.
Rabbi Yehuda says the rule applies only within one month of the due date.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say labor pains do not occur more than two weeks before birth.
Asks whether every woman who bleeds with labor pains is considered a menstruating woman.
Rav says she is menstruating for one day, Shmuel says she must observe a clean day, and Rabbi Yitzhak says she is entirely pure.
Objects that the mishna teaches a woman bleeding during the days of menstruation is impure, while the days of ziva make her pure.
Cites a baraita with the same contrast between menstrual days and ziva days as the mishna.
Gives examples where a woman who rested from labor pains, and bled throughout, is considered one who gives birth as a zava.
Gives examples where labor pains did not stop long enough, so the woman is not a zava.
Sums up: bleeding close to birth with labor pains is not zava status, while bleeding with rest close to birth is.
Hananya ben Achi of Rabbi Yehoshua says that if labor falls on the third day, she is not a zava even if the day is mostly rest.
Asks what the purpose of the general principle is, if Hananya's ruling already covers the case.
A baraita derives from Leviticus 15:25, her blood, that blood from labor pains during zava days is excluded.
Explains the reasoning: blood from childbirth can be pure because purity follows it, while blood from circumstances beyond control is impure.
Objects that for a male zav, blood from circumstances beyond control is pure, so the reasoning could be reversed.
Replies that the case concerns a woman, and in her case no circumstance beyond control is found to be pure.
Offers a second answer: the verse excludes blood from childbirth from impurity and includes blood from circumstances beyond control.
Asks why the same reasoning would not apply to a menstruating woman's blood caused by childbirth.
Cites Leviticus 15:19 for the menstruating woman and derives that blood from circumstances beyond control is excluded from her status.
Reish Lakish cites Leviticus 12:5, the blood of purity, to show another case where blood does not make her impure.
Asks whether this case may instead be a menstrual case.
Shmuel's father derives from Leviticus 12:5 that blood during ziva days is pure in the case of labor pains.
Asks which case is meant by the ziva days proof.
Asks why the verse's wording as in her menstruation is needed, if the menstrual analogy is already clear.
Explains the verse teaches that even in comfortable circumstances the blood during childbirth's days is pure.
Recounts that Sheila bar Avina ruled per Rav, and Rav asked Rav Asi to retract the ruling, which Rav Asi misunderstood as excommunication.
Sheila objects that if Rav had retracted, he would have told him directly, and rejects Rav Asi's excommunication.
Asks whether Rav Asi is not afraid of the fire, meaning punishment for offending a scholar.
Rav Asi answers with a wordplay on the names of tanna'im, comparing his own name to a copper mortar that rot cannot harm.
Sheila replies with his own wordplay, comparing his father's name to an iron pestle that breaks a copper mortar.
Recounts that Rav Asi fell ill with alternating fever and cold, and then died.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates Sheila bar Avina preparing his shrounds, and the biers of Sheila and Rav Asi, whose myrtle flies between them as a sign of peace.
Rava raises a dilemma: does a zava's blood from labor pains negate her count of clean days?
Asks whether any impure substance negates the count, or only a substance that causes one to become a zav.
Abaye argues that impurity from circumstances beyond control does not make one a zav, yet it negates the count.
Rava rejects this, since such an emission is also a cause of zav status, as the mishna on examining sightings shows.
Abaye asks whether, on Rabbi Eliezer's view that the third sighting is examined, an uncontrolled emission does not negate the count.
Rava says yes, that is so according to Rabbi Eliezer.
Gemara tries to refute Rava from a baraita on Rabbi Eliezer's examinations after the fourth discharge.
Cites a second baraita: Rabbi Eliezer examines at the third, not the fourth, because the examination concerns the offering.
Replies that this is not about negating the count, but about Rabbi Eliezer's view alone.
Asks what the halakha is according to the Rabbis.
Cites a baraita of the father of Rabbi Avin: a zav's discharge negates seven days because it causes seven days of impurity.
Asks what it means that ziva causes seven days of impurity, and whether the cause is the point.
Concludes that a substance causing zav status negates the count, while one that does not cause it, such as labor blood, does not.
Abaye states the tradition that labor blood does not negate the count of clean days, following the Rabbis.
A baraita reports Rabbi Marinus that a birth in the middle of counting does not negate a zava's count.
Asks whether the birth days of impurity count toward the seven clean days.
Abaye holds the birth does not negate but does not count, while Rava holds it negates nothing and counts.
Rava derives from Leviticus 15:28, and after that she shall be pure, that no impurity may separate the seven days.
Rava argues that if the birth does not count, it separates the days, and Abaye replies that the verse concerns zav impurity only.
Rava cites a baraita: she counts from her ziva and not from her leprosy, and likewise not from her birth.
Abaye says the baraita should teach only the leprosy exclusion, not the birth one.
Rava replies that if the baraita teaches birth, leprosy follows by analogy, and otherwise it is covered by another verse.
Abaye says two verses are needed, one for a zav and one for a zava, since each case must be written separately.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse is needed to teach that a zava counts clean days even if she is a leper, since a zava might otherwise be excluded from this rule.
Likewise a zav must be taught to count clean days even if he is a leper, since a zav might otherwise be excluded.
Abaye states that birth days do not count toward the seven clean days of a zava.
Cites Leviticus 12:2, the superfluous phrase her menstrual sickness, which includes the man, the nights, and a zava who gave birth.
Asks whether the baraita requires only clean days free of birth impurity, and the Gemara replies that they must be free of blood.
Abaye derives from the comparison of birth days to menstrual days that birth days do not count toward the seven clean days.
Rava says the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that birth negates the days already counted.
Asks how one can derive the possible from the impossible, since a zava cannot also be a menstruating woman.
Rav Ahadevoi bar Ami holds the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who derives the possible from the impossible.
Rav Sheshet explains that the verse juxtaposes birth days and menstrual days, so the comparison must be made despite the impossibility.
Gives the alternative attribution of these answers, with Rav Pappa holding that the verse juxtaposes the two sets of days.
Introduces the mishna case of a woman with labor pains and bleeding who has both rested from labor and ceased bleeding.
Raises the dilemma: if she rested from both pangs and blood, is she impure or pure?
Rav Hisda holds she is impure, since the cessation of pangs shows the earlier blood was not from labor.
Rabbi Hanina holds she is pure, since the cessation of blood shows the bleeding was from the approaching birth.
Rabbi Hanina's parable: a king's soldiers leave before him, so the soldiers are known to be his even though the king follows.
Rav Hisda reverses the parable: soldiers arriving before the king show they are not his, so the earlier blood was not from labor.
Objects from the mishna of Rabbi Yehoshua that a woman who rested from both pangs and blood is pure, refuting Rav Hisda.
Rav Hisda replies that the mishna teaches the case of resting from pangs alone, since full cessation would be clearly impure.
Cites the mishna of a woman who had three days of labor pains with bleeding and then gave birth, as a zava.
Asks what the mishna's case is: if it is as taught, the extra days of pain are unnecessary, so it must mean otherwise.
Gives the alternative reading of the mishna: three days of pangs and bleeding, then resting from both, or two days of pangs and a day of rest.
Objects that the alternative reading refutes Rabbi Hanina.
Rabbi Hanina replies that the mishna is taught as stated, where she rests from pangs but continues bleeding.
Explains the mishna teaches that even resting from pangs at the start of the third day makes her impure, excluding Rabbi Hanina's view.
Asks why the mishna needs to state forty days before birth once fifty has been stated.
Rav Hisda resolves that fifty days applies to a sick woman and forty days to a healthy woman.
Rabbi Levi holds that birth purifies from ziva only on the days fit for zava count, while other bleeding remains menstrual.
Rav holds she remains pure even during the days fit for the zava count of seven days.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says that Rav's view follows from his own reasoning, and draws out its consequence.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah teaching that bleeding during labor pains in the zava-counting days does not render the woman impure.
Objection: Levi's position cannot explain the mishnah, since fifty days of pure labor bleeding are impossible for him.
Levi replies the mishnah does not say all days are pure; menstrual-day bleeding is impure, zava-day bleeding pure.
A different version attributes to Levi that birth purifies only if the days could make her a greater zava.
Asks for the reason behind Levi's limitation to days that could make her a greater zava.
Verse Leviticus 15:25 says many days, which supports limiting the rule to greater zava.
Abba Shaul in Rav's name: birth purifies even when the days could make her only a lesser zava.
Asks the reason for this ruling.
Answer: the verse uses days and all days, and those words are written in the lesser zava context.
Mishnah cited again as a difficulty for both opinions, since all agree only ziva-day bleeding is pure.
Reply: the mishnah is not saying all fifty days are pure, only split by menstrual and ziva days.
A baraita teaches Rabbi Meir's scenario in which a woman bleeds for a hundred and fifty days without greater zava.
Explains the scenario day by day: two days, seven menstrual days, fifty days of labor, eighty days of birth.
Rabbis object that by the same logic a woman could bleed all her life without becoming a greater zava.
Meir replies that the rule about labor blood does not apply to non-viable newborns, so the objection fails.
Baraita: a woman may see blood for one hundred days without the greater zava impurity applying.
Explains the hundred-day scenario in detail, with two days, seven menstrual days, eighty days, then seven and two.
Asks what this baraita is teaching us.
It excludes the view that the womb cannot open without blood, teaching that birth without bleeding is possible.
Rabbi Yehuda says one month suffices, citing Rabbi Tarfon; the matter has both leniency and stringency.
Gives examples: two days at end of eighth month plus one at ninth makes her a zava, while the reverse does not.
Rav Adda bar Ahava infers Rabbi Yehuda holds the ninth month's shofar blast makes blood pure.
Objection: Shmuel says birth occurs only at 271, 272 or 273 days, so the ninth month cannot be a birth month.
Reply: Shmuel spoke according to the early pious men, who had intercourse only on certain days.
Baraita describes the early pious men who had intercourse only on Wednesday, so their wives would not come to be pregnant.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the pious men chose only Wednesday for intercourse if avoiding Shabbat desecration was the concern.
Reply: the baraita means they had intercourse each week only from Wednesday onward.
Mar Zutra asks what the reasoning of the early pious men was.
Cites Ruth 4:13 where the word herayon, conception, has numerical value 271 days.
Mar Zutra holds that a seven-month birth can occur at an incomplete count, though nine-month births cannot.
Cites I Samuel 1:20 seasons and days, deriving that Samuel was born in the seventh month.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say labor pains do not occur more than two weeks before birth.
Shmuel asks the reasoning behind the Rabbis' position.
Cites Leviticus 12:5, impure as in menstruation but not as in ziva, inferring ziva blood is pure for two weeks.
Baraita: a scenario in which labor-pain bleeding for twenty-five days does not include greater ziva impurity.
Explains the twenty-five day scenario: two ziva days, seven menstrual days, two more, then fourteen pure days.
Baraita: twenty-six days of labor bleeding without a child cannot avoid making her a greater zava.
Objection: without a child, three consecutive days already suffice, so the baraita's claim fails.
Rav Sheshet reads the baraita as referring to a case where there is a child.
Rava objects that the baraita explicitly says without a child, so Rav Sheshet's reading cannot stand.
Rava reconciles: with a child twenty-six days is impossible, but with only a non-viable newborn three days suffice.
Asks the reason for the distinction regarding non-viable newborns.
Labor-pain blood does not apply to non-viable newborns, so the rule of twenty-six days does not hold there.
Mishna: all blood seen within eighty days of a female birth is pure until the child emerges; Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure.
Rabbis argue by a fortiori: if blood is lenient in purity days, it should be lenient in labor-pain days too.
Eliezer replies an a fortiori conclusion must match its source, so labor blood makes her impure only as menstrual.
Baraita cites the verse she shall observe, read as including the woman who bleeds within eighty days of birth.
Baraita restates the mishna: all blood within eighty days of a female birth is pure; Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure.
Rabbis reason a fortiori against Eliezer, using the before-birth and after-birth contrast for labor blood.
Eliezer again answers that the a fortiori conclusion must be no stricter than its source.
Rabbis offer another a fortiori version, with labor blood that accompanies the birth.
Eliezer replies that even many such a fortiori arguments yield the same limit, since the source is ziva.
Rava says Rabbi Eliezer won the argument against the Rabbis with this response.
Rava's proof: the verses speaking of her blood and her fountain of blood refer only to her own blood, not the child's.
Objection against Eliezer: one could say menstrual-day labor blood is impure and ziva-day blood is pure.
The verse she shall observe one observance for all, so all her purity-day blood is either pure or impure.
Mishna: for all eleven ziva days after the seven menstrual days, a woman has a presumptive status of purity.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a woman who did not check herself is pure during her clean days, but impure if her menstrual time came unchecked.
Rabbi Meir: a woman hiding from danger who missed her menstrual check is pure, since fear drives blood away.
Zav, zava and the woman counting a day for a day are presumed impure, since they have already had discharges.
Asks what halakha the first clause of the mishna is teaching.
Rav Yehuda: it teaches that she does not need to examine herself during the eleven ziva days.
Objection: the latter clause implies she must examine herself ab initio, so the first clause cannot mean that.
Reply: the latter clause concerns menstrual days; on ziva days she is presumed pure and needs no check.
Rav Hisda's alternative: the first clause follows Rabbi Meir, who forbids a woman with no fixed cycle only on menstrual days.
Why did Rabbi Meir require divorce, if intercourse would be permitted on ziva days?
Objection: the latter clause implies a woman with a fixed cycle, so the mishna must be read as incomplete.
Explains: this applies to a woman with no fixed cycle; a woman with a fixed cycle must examine herself.
Objection: the last clause follows Rabbi Meir, so the first clause must not; reply that the whole mishna follows him.
Rava: the mishna says that she does not impart impurity retroactively for a twenty-four hour period.
A baraita refutes Rava: even a woman observing a day for a day imparts retroactive impurity.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya in Shmuel's name: ziva days cannot combine to fix a menstrual cycle for her.
Rav Yosef says he never heard this halakha from Shmuel, challenging the statement.
Abaye cites a mishna on the fifteenth and twentieth day deviations, showing a woman may fix a cycle by deviating three times.
Shmuel via Rav Yehuda: the rule applies only to a woman whose ziva days would be fifteen days, not menstrual days.
Rav Pappa asks whether a woman must avoid intercourse on a usual ziva-day bleeding day out of concern.
Rav Pappa attempts to resolve it from the mishna's deviation to the twentieth day, which makes both days forbidden.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel's rule: the fifteen-day case, and Rav Pappa's reckoning of the twenty-two days from her actual bleeding.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects: the twenty-two days may instead be counted from the twenty-seventh day, so no proof follows.
Rav Huna supports counting from actual bleeding with an analogy to a hen whose laying routine is disturbed.
The hen's routine resumes the order established before the deviation, so the woman counts from her bleeding.

ranges.en: Attributes a baraita teaching to Rabbi Meir.

Leprous marks are not viewed by a blind priest, so blind judges are excluded, citing Leviticus.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan's view: produce needs intent once detached, and intent while attached does not count.

Zeira replies that the chicken was a wild one, never present while alive.

Abaye rebukes the mockers and explains Zeira's chicken as one that rebelled against its owner.
Explains that the word for wild means a chicken created from a rebellious one.

Cites the Ammonite verse as a mnemonic for permitted and prohibited animals, supporting Rav Pappa.

Baraita: a kosher bird fallen into a winepress is impure if meant for a Samaritan, pure if meant for a dog; Yohanan ben Nuri disagrees.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds he himself ruins her ziva halakhot, since the stain is attributed to the sighting.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether stains require an examination marking the end of the impurity counting.
Rabbi Asi was silent and said nothing in reply.
Later Rabbi Asi is found teaching the stain is attributed to the sighting within twenty-four hours, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Reish Lakish requires examination on the seventh day; Rabbi Yohanan attributes the stain regardless.
Zeira asks whether this implies stains require the end-of-impurity examination.
Asi confirms that this is the halakha.
Zeira reproaches Asi for not answering him earlier, asking whether he had forgotten.
Asi replies that the halakha came back to him while studying.
Mishna: a woman who sees blood at twilight on the eleventh day is uncertain between menstrual and ziva counts.
Mishna: similar uncertainty for a birth-related twilight emission, so these women err and bring an offering not eaten.
Rabbi Yehoshua: instead of remedying the misguided, remedy the uncertainty of the competent women.
The Gemara raises difficulty: the concern is only that twilight is night or day, and the flow is ziva.
Rav Hisda explains the mishna: uncertainty on the eleventh day, and on the seventh day of menstruation the reverse.
Asks whether these women who bleed at twilight are the misguided or the competent ones.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves that the women are not misguided but mistaken, so the Yehoshua teaching should read mistaken.
Baraita: a woman alternating impure and pure days may have intercourse on the eighth night, and on the eighteen-day cycle, per the schedule.
Baraita continues: with two impure and two pure days, intercourse is permitted on the eighth, twelfth, sixteenth and twentieth days.
Objects that she should also be permitted on the nineteenth day, since the zava days have ended.
Rav Sheshet explains the mishna's glutton clause means intercourse on that day is actually prohibited.
Rav Ashi says it is not prohibited, since she still must observe a clean tenth day, so the nineteenth must be clean.
Example: three impure and three pure days allow intercourse on two days, then never again.
Example: four impure and four pure days allow intercourse on one day, then never again.
Examples: five and five permit three days, and six and six permit five days, then never again.
Example: seven and seven permits seven of every twenty-eight days, after which the count restarts.
Example: eight and eight permits fifteen of every forty-eight days, with the cycle explained step by step.
Objects that the permitted days are only fourteen, not fifteen, because days fit for menstruation cannot count as clean days.
Rav Adda bar Yitzhak rejects the premise: menstrual days without visible blood still count toward the seven clean days.
A dilemma is raised before the Sages on whether such days count toward the seven clean days.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether days of childbirth without visible blood count toward the seven clean days of ziva.
Rav Kahana brings a baraita on a woman who miscarried after two days of blood, uncertain whether birth or ziva, and her days count.
Rav Pappa replies the dilemma is not resolved, because a birth of a male explains the extra days, unlike a certain female birth.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects to Rav Pappa that both possibilities count, so such days are reckoned.
Baraita examples: nine and nine permits eight of eighteen days; ten and ten permits as many days as ziva, up to one thousand.
Chapter-end marker: the chapter opens with blood of a menstruant and corpse flesh.
Mishna: menstrual blood and corpse flesh impure when moist and dry; ziva, semen and other fluids impure only when moist, unless soaked back.
Mishna continues: soaking takes a day in lukewarm water; Rabbi Yosei says dry corpse flesh is pure below an olive, impure by a ladleful.
Asks from where we derive that menstrual blood transmits impurity by contact and carrying.
Hizkiyya derives it from Leviticus 15 comparing the menstrual flow to the woman herself.
Asks the source that dry menstrual blood also transmits impurity.
Rabbi Yitzhak derives it from the phrase shall be in its impurity, meaning impurity persists even when dry.
Objects that this applies only to blood moist first, and asks the source for blood dry from the start, as in the mishna on red discharges.
The phrase shall be is amplification, teaching that menstrual blood in all these forms is impure.
Objects by analogy that her blood should also render couches and seats impure, as she does.
Asks whether the lying and sitting rule applies to a leprous stone, given the earlier reasoning.
Baraita: one might think a leprous stone renders lying or sitting items impure, so a verse excludes it.
Baraita a fortiori: a zav who does not impart by entering a house still imparts lying-sitting impurity, so a leprous stone should too.
Baraita concludes: the verse says the zav, excluding the leprous stone from lying-sitting impurity.
Gemara infers that without the exclusion, the stone would impart lying-sitting impurity though the concept does not apply to it.
Same derivation excludes menstrual blood: the verse says she herself, not her blood, imparts lying-sitting impurity.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: a menstruant transmits impurity to items under a heavy stone, so her blood should too, by the earlier analogy.
Rav Ashi replies that the verse's them excludes menstrual blood, since lying and sitting items do transmit impurity under a stone.
Asks from where we derive that a corpse's flesh is impure whether moist or dry.
Reish Lakish derives it from the verse on any impurity, read as amplification covering moist and dry.
Rabbi Yohanan derives it from the verse on a bone or grave, comparing the corpse to a dry bone.
Asks what practical difference lies between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan.
Baraita objection: crumbled corpse flesh is pure, which Reish Lakish's view contradicts; answered that it is dust.
Mishna objection: all of a corpse impart impurity except teeth, hair and nails, which challenges both views.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: only items created with a person at birth impart impurity, like bone.
Objects that hair and nails were also created at birth and are pure, so the explanation fails.
Restates the rule: items created with a person whose root does not renew, excluding teeth, hair and nails.
Objects that skin renews its root, per the tereifa mishna on a hide removed, so the rule fails.
Cites the mishna listing the skins whose status matches their flesh, including a dead person's skin.
Ulla holds a dead person's skin is pure by Torah law; the rabbinic impurity is a decree lest one make donkey rugs.
Alternative version: the skin does not renew, so Rabbi Meir's view is limited; Ulla still says Torah pure.
Ulla's ruling refers to the latter clause, where tanned skins are pure except a dead person's, decreed for rugs.
Asks whether flesh that renews its root should be impure, since then the same objection applies.
Mar bar Rav Ashi: flesh does not truly renew, as a scar forms in its place.
Asks from where we derive that ziva transmits impurity.
Baraita derives ziva impurity from Leviticus 15:2, its issue is impure.
Proposes an a fortiori inference that ziva should be impure because it imparts impurity to others.
Rejects the inference via the scapegoat, which imparts impurity yet is itself pure.
Verse his issue, it is impure, is needed to teach that ziva itself is impure.
Objects that this applies only to contact, not carrying, like a creeping animal's carcass.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye: no verse is needed for contact, since ziva is no less stringent than semen.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: if ziva transmits impurity by carrying, perhaps by contact it should not reach the garments, as with a carcass.
Baraita of the Aherim: the verse equates the zav's issue with the zav, so contact and carrying impart equally to person and garments.
Asks why the verse his issue it is impure is needed, once the zav's issue is already derived.
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta: the verse teaches the number of emissions, and the impurity is derived from its redundancy.
Asks from where we derive that a zav's saliva is impure.
Baraita: the verse on spitting on the pure person teaches that saliva imparts impurity only on contact.
Baraita: the superfluous and in the verse extends the impurity to phlegm, mucus and nasal fluids.
Asks from where one would think saliva imparts impurity without contact, requiring exclusion.
Verbal analogy with the yevama spitting in halitza is rejected: the verse teaches contact is needed.
Objects that this holds only for contact, not carrying, as with a creeping animal carcass.
Reish Lakish cites the school of Yishmael: on the pure person means that carrying saliva also imparts impurity.
Objects that carrying imparts impurity to garments, while contact does not, as with a carcass.
Reish Lakish again, citing the school of Yishmael: on the pure person contrasts with a pure case, saliva contact imparts to garments.
Objects that the verse could instead mean carrying a creeping animal, and asks why the verse specifies on the pure person.
Asks what nasal fluids are, as the baraita lists them among impure zav fluids.
Rav: nasal fluids are impure only when they flow through the mouth, since they carry saliva.
Rabbi Yohanan: even nasal fluids flowing through the nose are impure, as they are a bodily fluid included by the verse.
Asks why, on Rav's reasoning, the eye's tears are not counted, given Rav's view on likhol and poison.
Rav Hiyya bar Gurya: poison can be spat through the mouth, but tears do not exit the body that way.
Baraita lists nine zav fluids and their impurity grades, and notes nasal fluids are not included.
Objects that if Rabbi Yohanan is right the tanna should have listed nasal fluids, since he could not list them under Rav.
The tanna lists saliva, and all its derivations such as phlegm and mucus, so nasal fluids are covered by the same amplification.
Sources for liquid status: tears from Psalms, zav's blood from Numbers, milk from Judges, each cited as a liquid.
Baraita derives that a zav's urine is impure from the verse, and a fortiori from saliva coming from a pure source.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita replies: blood from the penis comes from an impure place yet is pure, so urine of a zav may be pure too; and this shall be includes urine.
Asks from where we derive that blood issuing from the penis is pure.
Baraita on the zav: his issue is impure excludes blood from mouth or penis, which is pure.
Suggests reversing, then Rabbi Yohanan in Shimon ben Yohai's name: urine, not blood, is impure, like saliva.
Objects with milk, which gathers and exits the body yet is only liquid-impure, undermining the saliva analogy.
Rabbi Yohanan refines: a severe impurity fluid must be like saliva, reabsorbed if not expelled, which excludes blood and milk.
Objects: derive from ziva that all fluids of a zav are impure even without gathering first.
Rava: ziva cannot be the model, since it uniquely imparts impurity to others.
Reish Lakish: a dried creeping animal whose skeleton is intact remains impure.
Objects that the mishna says dried creeping animals are pure.
Rabbi Zeira: no conflict, as one refers to fully intact bones and the other to partial bones.
Baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's school: the verse on creeping animals, reconciling moist and dry cases.
Rava: lizards of Mehoza with intact skeletons are impure, the dab being a creeping animal.
Reish Lakish: a burned creeping animal with intact skeleton is impure.
Objects with a mishna holding a burned creeping animal on olives is pure, since it is burned.
Rabbi Zeira: no conflict, the mishna refers to partial bones, Reish Lakish to intact bones.
Baraita on the verse: a complete creeping animal imparts, a partial one imparts in the moist case; burned distinguishes.
Sources for moist-only impurity: ziva, saliva, creeping animal, semen and carcass each tied to a verse about moisture.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether lukewarm soaking must hold the whole twenty-four hours or only at the start.
Baraita: Yehuda ben Nekosa requires lukewarm only at the start, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel for the whole period.
Mishna and baraita: dried corpse flesh is pure below an olive, and impure as decayed flesh by a ladle, per Rabbi Yosei and Shmuel.
Mishna: a creeping animal found in an alleyway makes items impure retroactively unless one examined it or the sweeping time is known.
Mishna: a blood stain found on a robe makes items impure retroactively, back to examination or laundering.
Mishna: dry creeping animals and stains impure retroactively; Rabbi Shimon says only moist ones reach back to when they could be moist.
A dilemma is raised: is a swept alleyway presumed examined, or presumed fully swept?
Asks what practical difference the dilemma makes.
Difference arises if the sweeper said he swept without examining; the two presumptions give different results.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternative difference: if the stain was found in a hole, examination of the robe covers its holes only under the examined presumption.
Introduces the mishna on blood stains found on a woman's robe.
Asks whether the laundering presumption means examined or thoroughly laundered, and its practical difference.
Difference arises if she laundered without examining: examined presumption excludes it, laundered presumption includes it.
Alternative difference for a stain on the side of the robe, where folds and stitches prevent thorough laundering.
Asks what the halakha is, and turns to a baraita.
Baraita of Rabbi Meir: the alleyway rule rests on the presumption that Jews examine alleyways when they sweep.
Baraita: the robe rule rests on the presumption that Jewish women examine robes when laundering them.
Rabbi Aha: relaunder the robe; if the stain's appearance changes, it arose after the earlier laundering.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: a stain from before laundering crusts and scrapes off, unlike a stain penetrating after; this supports the examined presumption.
Rabbi Elazar: the stated rule applies only to creeping animals, while a moist stain also imparts retroactively, since water could have wetted it.
Objects that the moist creeping animal too could have been dried and wetted, so it should impart retroactively, and answers it would be sundered.
Mishna: stains from Rekem are pure per the majority of gentiles; Rabbi Yehuda deems them impure, and the converts and Samaritans follow Meir and the Rabbis.
Gemara: the mishna's categorical gentile purity covers even Tarmod, so Rabbi Yohanan accepts converts from Tarmod.
Asks: but Rabbi Yohanan and the Elders both reject converts from Tarmod, due to intermingling of the lost tribes.
Objects: if Rabbi Yohanan agreed with the mishna, he would contradict his own principle that the halakha follows an unattributed mishna.
Amoraim disagree on Rabbi Yohanan's view: one says he rejects Tarmod converts, another that he accepts them by the unattributed mishna.
Asks: if the Rabbis purify Jewish women's stains, whose stains do they deem impure?
The mishna is incomplete: all agree Jewish stains are impure; the Rabbis hold Samaritans are converts under the threat of lions, hence gentiles.
Asks why the mishna would then say Samaritans are pure due to lack of suspicion, rather than simply as converts under lions.
Rewritten: stains among Jews and Samaritans are impure; stains in Jewish towns are pure; stains in Samaritan towns are a dispute.
Continues the paraphrase: Samaritan-town stains, Meir impure from suspicion, the Rabbis pure since they are not suspected.
Mishna: stains found anywhere are pure, except in inner rooms or near the house of impurity.
Mishna: the Samaritan house of impurity imparts tent impurity because they bury stillborns there; Rabbi Yehuda says they only cast them out.
Mishna: Samaritans are credible on burial places and animals' firstborn status, but not on marking graves regarding other matters.
Mishna: Samaritans are not credible on boughs, protrusions, or a beit haperas; the principle is that they are not credible where suspected. Gemara begins.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what verse the Samaritans expounded to exclude burial of stillborn children.
Samaritans read the boundary verse: only one with an inheritance has a boundary, so a stillborn child lacks one.
Objects that Samaritans reject the stumbling-block verse, so why is their testimony accepted about a burial place.
Rabbi Abbahu: the mishna refers to a Samaritan priest standing there, showing he holds it pure.
Objects that the priest may be impure, then that the teruma may be impure, and resolves each by its context.
Asks what the ruling adds if the testimony is already obviously credible.
Lest one think Samaritans lack knowledge of embryo stages, so they might bury a forty-day fetus as unformed.
Mishna: Samaritans are credible that an animal previously gave birth, so its offspring is not firstborn.
Objects again that Samaritans reject the stumbling-block verse, so why are they credible on the firstborn question.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba for Rabbi Yohanan: the Samaritan shears and works the offspring, showing it is not firstborn.
Asks what the ruling adds if the Samaritans already know this from the work.
Lest one think Samaritans lack knowledge of murky uterine discharge, which exempts firstborn status.
Mishna: Samaritans are credible on grave markings, so unmarked ground is pure.
Gemara: though marking is rabbinic, Samaritans observe it since Ezekiel 39:15 commands it.
Mishna: Samaritans are not credible on overhanging boughs or protrusions of a stone fence where the grave is unknown.
Explains the terms: overhanging boughs per the Oholot mishna, protrusions per the Tosefta.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: a beit haperas is impure from plowed bones, and one may blow dust to avoid them.
Rav Yehuda bar Ami, citing Rav Yehuda: a beit haperas trodden by many people is pure.
Baraita: one who plows a graveyard makes a beit haperas of a furrow, four or five seah; Samaritans are not credible on it.
Asks: but a baraita says a Samaritan is credible to say there is no grave in a lost-grave field?
The baraita speaks of testifying about the grave itself, a Torah matter, so Samaritans are credible on boughs too.
Rabbi Yohanan: the baraita refers to a Samaritan walking the whole area, whereas the mishna does not.
Asks what the baraita adds, if his testimony is obviously credible.
Lest a narrow strip of land with the same name extend into the nearby field, so he might be presuming the strip.
Mishna: Samaritans are not credible on any halakha they are suspected of not fulfilling.
Asks what the phrase this is the principle adds.
It adds Shabbat boundaries, which are rabbinic, and wine used for libation, which Samaritans do not avoid if gentile-touched.
Chapter-end marker: the chapter opens with the blood of a menstruant.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna lists blood stains on the body and clothing that make a woman impure or pure depending on where they are found.
A stain on a robe worn at night is impure because the robe moves while she sleeps.
The kerchief follows the same rule as the robe.
Shmuel rules that a woman who checks the ground, sits on it, and then finds blood is pure.
Shmuel cites the verse in her flesh to show she is impure only if she senses the emission.
Why does the verse say flesh, if it also teaches that blood inside the body counts like blood outside?
If so, it should say flesh alone; the extra word teaches that she must sense it in her flesh.
Still, why is the word in her flesh needed?
The verse teaches two lessons: blood must be in the flesh, not in a gestational sac or an amorphous lump.
Brings a mishna where Rabbi Meir says a standing woman is impure and a sitting woman is pure, against Shmuel.
How can the mishna work if she sensed while sitting, and why is she then pure?
If she did not sense, the mishna's ruling that standing is impure contradicts Shmuel.
She sensed, but the sensation was of urine; standing urination can push blood back into the uterus, while sitting cannot.
Brings a baraita on a cloth under a pillow: round stains are pure and elongated stains impure, against Shmuel.
If she sensed, why is a round stain pure? Does the baraita mean she did not sense?
If she did not sense, the baraita's ruling that an elongated stain is impure contradicts Shmuel.
She did sense, but the stain's shape decides: an elongated stain came from her body, a round one did not.
Brings a mishna on a husband's cloth after intercourse, with impure, liable and doubtful cases, against Shmuel.
If she sensed, why is a stain found after time only doubtful and exempt from a sin offering? Does it mean she did not sense?
If she did not sense, the mishna's ruling that an immediate stain is impure and liable contradicts Shmuel.
She sensed, but the sensation was of intercourse, so the stain came from her body.
Brings a baraita on three doubts about flesh and robe stains and on following the majority, as an objection to Shmuel.
The baraita continues: for touching and moving, the majority rule applies.
What does following the majority mean? Does it mean she is impure without any sensation?
It means the majority of her days involve a sensation; she may have sensed without noticing.
Re-quotes the baraita's doubts: a doubt about a flesh stain is impure, a doubt about a robe stain is pure.
How can a doubtful stain on the robe below the belt be pure?
The mishna teaches that a stain on the robe below the belt is impure, contradicting that.
If a stain on the flesh is above the belt, why is it impure?
The mishna teaches that a stain on the flesh not adjacent to the vagina is pure, contradicting the view.
Several resolutions: the stain may come from her body or from the outside world, depending on the location and the case, such as a butchers' market or a backward jump.
Brings the teaching that doubt about flesh is impure, and the mishna on flesh by the vagina, though she did not sense; again against Shmuel.
Rav Yirmeya of Difti says Shmuel concedes that in these cases she is impure even without sensation; his rule holds only by Torah law.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi says Shmuel's view follows the position of R. Nehemya.
The mishna quotes R. Nehemya: whatever cannot receive impurity cannot receive stains.
For Rav Ashi the principle fits the case of the ground.
For Rav Yirmeya, why does the case specify the ground and not also a robe?
A robe may not have been checked carefully and could have picked up blood from outside, so the case concerns examined ground.
Rav Yirmeya's view: even on carefully examined ground, the stain may come from her body, so she is pure.
The mishna rules that a stain on the heel or the top of the big toe makes her impure.
Why is the heel case clear, while the big toe needs a separate explanation?
Perhaps she sometimes touched the heel; the Gemara asks whether impurity may be presumed to move from one place to another.
Brings a baraita on a neck wound and hanging, arguing that impurity is not presumed to have been moved, against this reasoning.
The big toe is different, because it arises from stepping; impurity is not presumed to move from place to place there.
A baraita rules a stain on finger joints impure because women's hands are busy, which implies transfer, against the principle.
What is the reason for this ruling? Is it not because we say she examined with one hand and touched with the other?
The hand case differs, since her whole hand is made for touching, so she could touch the leg or the feet.
The mishna quoted: a stain on the leg and feet, on the inner side impure and the outer side pure.
Where does the boundary lie? The House of R. Yannai says up to the embrace area, and it is unclear whether the embrace is inside or outside.
Rav Katina's baraita says up to the embrace area, and the embrace itself counts as inside, which resolves the question against the other reading.
Rav Chiya bar Rav Avya taught the House of R. Yannai's rule explicitly, supporting the inside reading of the embrace.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about the status of a straight stain, drops, and a stain running across the thigh.
Comes a baraita on a stain of doubtful status on flesh and on the robe, objecting from the teaching.
Is this not the same kind of case, which would make the teaching a matter of the flesh alone?
No, perhaps this stain was shaped like a strap, which is a different case.
A story: a woman with blood on a cloth came before R. Yannai, who told her to go and return, which he then ruled.
A baraita: one does not teach leniency in purity matters but may teach stringency, which contradicts R. Yannai's lenient ruling.
A baraita reports R. Eliezer b. R. Yosei's ruling of prohibition in Rome, which the sages in the south confirmed as correct.
A baraita on a long robe worn over a short one, and whether both are impure when the upper reaches the vagina.
Another baraita: a woman who examined a cloth and lent it to a friend is pure, while the friend remains impure.
Rav Sheshet says the mishna's ruling applies to monetary law, while for impurity she is pure and her friend is impure.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how the case of two women and one bird differs from the case of a stain found on the robe of a woman who sold or lent it.
There the case differs because one of the stains is larger, leaving an extra sela of blood beyond the bird's share.
A baraita: a woman wearing three robes may attribute a stain to an external source only if she could plausibly have gotten it there.
Explains the baraita: passing a butchers' market makes an external source plausible, but otherwise the stain is hers.
The Mishna lists sources she may blame, such as slaughter or killing a louse, and how large a stain can be; it includes R. Akiva's ruling on a woman with a healed wound.
R. Akiva explains to his students that the Sages instituted the impurity of stains to be lenient, not stringent.
Brings the verse about a woman's issue being blood in the flesh, not a stain, to show that only blood is impure by Torah law.
Baraita on a cloth beneath the pillow: round stains are pure, elongated stains impure, as the view of R. Eliezer ben R. Tzadok.
The Gemara notes that this is taught in a baraita, supporting the Mishna's rule.
An incident where R. Meir and Rabbi attributed a stain to different sources, and a baraita on whether she sat or did not sit.
Cites a baraita that also teaches the rule about a stain from passing a butchers' market.
The baraita rules that after passing a butchers' market a doubtful stain is attributed to them, and it also covers killing a louse.
Whose view is the Mishna's rule that a woman may attribute a stain to a louse?
It is the view of R. Shimon ben Gamliel, who says she may attribute the stain either way, against the Sages' view.
R. Shimon ben Gamliel argues that on the other view no woman could ever be pure, because any bed could have a few drops of blood.
The Gemara concludes that R. Chanina ben Antigonus's bean-sized limit is accepted as the correct view.
R. Nachman bar Yitzchak says the Sages set the limit as a lupin bean, attributing the stain to a bedbug.
A baraita defines a bedbug: its length equals its width, and its taste equals its smell, which matters for stains and terumah.
Cites a Mishna on terumah: one who tastes a bedbug in his mouth must spit it out, since its taste resembles its smell.
How can one know the taste matches the smell, when the bedbug is an invisible creature?
The answer: a bedbug's smell is reliable because a bond has been made for anyone who crushes it.
Rav Ashi says that in a town with pigs, one does not attend to stains, since the stain could come from them.
R. Nachman bar Yitzchak says the case of a thorn-prick is like a town with pigs, and asks how large a stain may be attributed.
Rav Huna rules that she may not attribute a stain smaller than a bean, but may attribute one of a bean's size.
Rav Chisda rules that she may attribute a bean-sized stain, but not one larger than a bean.
The Gemara explains the dispute: whether the word up to includes or excludes the bean-sized stain itself.
Rav Huna replies that both kinds of cases exist, and here the stringent view applies in both.
Rav Chisda replies that the rule is generally stringent but not lenient, and here he follows R. Abahu's principle.
R. Abahu's principle: all measures set by the Sages are stringent, except the bean-sized measure for stains, which is lenient.
Some say this halakha stands on its own and is a separate teaching.
Rav Huna's view: a stain of a bean's size or more is attributed, and a larger one is not.
Rav Chisda's view: a stain of a bean's size or less is attributed, and the two disagree about a bean-sized stain.
Raises an objection from a baraita against the reading of the dispute just described.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teaching: if there are small drops below and large drops above, she may attribute the upper drops to an outside source up to a bean's size.
Asks whether a drop exactly a bean's size counts as small, which would contradict Rav Huna.
Stated case: a bean-sized stain with slightly more, where a louse is squashed in the area, and the question of its status.
Rabbi Hanina rules that such a woman is impure, since the stain is not attributed to a louse.
Rabbi Yannai rules that she is pure.
Explains Rabbi Hanina's view: she may attribute only a bean-sized stain to a louse, and the rule does not cover more.
Rabbi Yannai's view: she is pure.
Explains Rabbi Yannai: the leniency holds only where a louse is squashed on the stain, and then the blood is visibly from the louse.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma about a woman occupied with a bean-sized item and a stain just over a bean, under both rabbis' views.
Two possibilities: Rabbi Hanina's impurity applies only without an occupation, and even Rabbi Yannai's leniency needs a squashed louse.
Brings a baraita on red and black stains and on small and large stains, as an objection to the dilemma.
What is the case of the baraita? Is it not like the dilemma of a bean and slightly more?
The baraita refers to two bean-sized stains; the ruling is needed so one cannot place the bird's blood in the middle of the stain.
Rava rules that if one type of stain is found, she may attribute other stains of several types to that source.
Objects with the baraita: she may not attribute a black stain to a red item, which contradicts Rava.
Answers that the case of an occupation is different from Rava's case.
Another version: Rava rules that if she was occupied with one type, she may attribute stains of several types to it.
Objects again to Rava's version with the baraita on a red item and black stains.
Rava's ruling refers to a slaughtered chicken, which has several types of blood, so it is consistent.
Cites the incident in the Mishna where Rabbi Akiva ruled a woman pure.
A baraita: the Sages did not institute the rule of impurity from stains for leniency but for stringency, which conflicts with Rabbi Akiva's view.
Ravina says there is no contradiction: the Sages' rule is stringent for Torah matters, while the stains themselves are rabbinic.
Do the Sages dispute R. Eliezer ben R. Tzadok's view that the stain must be elongated, or not?
Baraita: an elongated stain joins drops, but separate drops do not join; this objects to the question.
Whose view is this? If it is R. Eliezer ben R. Tzadok, why does the joining rule matter if he deems any elongated stain impure?
Concludes that the Sages dispute, and R. Eliezer ben R. Tzadok says it only for a bed-stain, not for a stain on a garment.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the halakha follows R. Eliezer ben R. Tzadok, which implies that the Sages disagree.
Chapter-ending formula introducing the next chapter, which begins with a stain found on a woman.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: R. Meir rules that a woman who urinates standing is impure with blood in the urine, and sitting she is pure.
R. Yosei rules that she is pure in either position.
Mishna: a man and a woman urinate into a basin and blood is found on the water; R. Yosei deems her pure, R. Shimon deems her impure.
R. Shimon's reason: a man does not normally discharge blood with urine, so the blood is presumed to be the woman's.
Asks why the standing woman differs: the urine returns to the uterus, but the sitting woman's urine could do the same.
Shmuel answers that the mishna speaks of a steady stream, which does not bring blood back from the uterus.
Objects: even with a steady stream, blood could come after the water has finished.
R. Abba answers that the blood was found inside the basin, not on its edge, so it came with the urine.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows R. Yosei, and R. Abba ruled the same for a sage named Kala.
Raises a dilemma: a standing man and woman urinate into the same basin, and blood is found. Does R. Meir still deem her impure?
Reish Lakish holds that R. Meir rules the same in both cases.
From where does Reish Lakish know this? Does the mishna not say that both R. Meir and R. Yosei deem her pure?
The mishna mentions only R. Yosei's ruling, which indicates that R. Meir does not deem her pure in that case.
Objects: if R. Meir's view were so, why does the mishna teach one uncertainty at all? It should show R. Yosei's strength.
The mishna teaches a single uncertainty to show the strength of R. Yosei's lenient view, since a lenient rule is preferred.
R. Yochanan disagrees: R. Meir's ruling of impurity applies only to a single uncertainty, not a compound one.
Objects: if so, the mishna should say that R. Meir and R. Yosei both deem her pure in a compound uncertainty.
Yes, that is so; the mishna mentions R. Yosei first because it is his lenient view that it wants to convey.
A baraita is taught in accordance with R. Yochanan, quoting the basin case where R. Meir and R. Yosei deem her pure, R. Shimon impure.
Raises a dilemma: a sitting woman in the basin case, does R. Shimon's view apply only to a standing woman, or not?
Brings a baraita: a sitting woman is pure, a standing woman impure according to R. Meir, and R. Shimon says either way impure.
Raises a dilemma: a man and woman sitting together, does R. Shimon's presumption apply to them, or not?
Brings R. Shimon's principle that the presumption is that blood is the woman's, which makes no difference between standing and sitting.
Mishna: a woman who lends a robe to a gentile or a menstruating woman is responsible; three women sharing a robe or bench are all impure.
R. Nehemya rules the stain is pure in the case of a bench of stone, and states that what cannot receive impurity cannot receive stains.
Rav rules about the case of a gentile woman.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: From where does Rav know the mishna means a gentile woman who has once bled, like a menstruating woman?
Rav Sheshet says Rav said this halakha while dozing, so it was an error.
Cites a baraita on lending a garment to a gentile: the first tanna is lenient, while R. Meir requires a gentile fit to see blood.
Rava asks how R. Meir could be the stringent one, since he is the lenient one in the baraita.
Cites a baraita where the first tanna forbids attributing the stain to a gentile and R. Meir permits it, showing R. Meir is lenient.
Resolves the baraita: the first tanna requires a gentile who has bled, while R. Meir permits one fit to bleed even without bleeding.
Baraita: a woman who lends her garment to a zava in her day count may attribute the stain to the borrower, as R. Shimon ben Gamliel rules.
R. Yehuda HaNasi disagrees: neither woman may be blamed, so both are impure.
The tanna agrees that the stain may be attributed in cases where the borrower's status is not affected, such as a woman after childbirth or a virgin.
Why does the baraita need the clause about R. Shimon ben Gamliel, since only one woman's status is ruined?
The clause is needed so one does not think the status of the woman with the garment should be ruined, while the other's is not.
Rav Chisda says the dispute is like two people who walked on a pure path and an impure one and handled teruma.
Rav Adda objects that the two cases differ, since a woman can immerse at any time.
Rav Chisda replies that in the end she still needs immersion, so the cases are alike.
R. Yosei bar R. Chanina rules on two people who walked on two paths; the impure is attributed to the impure one, and this is agreed.
R. Yochanan asks R. Yehuda bar Leviy whether a stain may be attributed to another stain, in R. Meir's view.
R. Yehuda answers that this question need not be asked now, according to R. Meir.
Raises an a fortiori question: if a woman who sees from the body cannot attribute, is an outside stain even less attributable, or is there no difference?
Replies that they may attribute, and asks what the reason is, since they do not attribute.
Objects with a mishna: she may not attribute a stain on a stain, yet a loaned garment to a gentile or a woman sitting on the stain is attributed.
Asks whether the first clause, which says they may not attribute, and the last, which says they may, are not contradictory.
Answers that one is R. Yehuda HaNasi and the other is R. Shimon ben Gamliel.
Some say both are R. Yehuda, and the difference is between her first and second days.
Rav Ashi says both are R. Shimon ben Gamliel's view, so there is no contradiction.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the distinction between retroactive and prospective cases still leaves a difficulty for R. Shimon ben Gamliel.
Ravina says it is not difficult: the baraita means that the lender is defined as a woman who saw blood, so the attribution is to a gentile.
Baraita: a woman who lends a garment to a gentile woman who saw blood may attribute a stain to her.
Objects that the baraita also says she may attribute the stain to a woman observing her days of purity, which seems to conflict.
Mishna: three women who wore one garment; if they sat on a stone bench or a bathhouse bench, R. Nehemya deems them pure.
Rav Mattana cites the verse about the daughter of Zion sitting clean on the ground as the reason for R. Nehemya's view.
Rav Huna says R. Hanina rules that R. Nehemya deems her pure even on the exterior of an inverted earthenware vessel.
Answers why this needs stating: lest one decree impurity for the outside of a vessel because of its inside.
Abaye says R. Nehemya deems her pure for small rags that are not three by three fingerbreadths, since they serve neither the poor nor the rich.
Rav Chiya bar Rav Mattana teaches in Rav's name that the halakha follows R. Nehemya.
Rav Nachman objects that his father taught a case where the Sages ruled against R. Nehemya, which conflicts with that ruling.
What is the case the baraita refers to?
Baraita: two women grinding at a hand mill with a stain found beneath, and a bathtub and olive leaf case, where the Sages ruled both impure.
Rav Chiya bar Rav Mattana answers that the tannaim dispute the matter, and the Sages ruled in accordance with R. Nehemya.
Mishna: three women sleeping in one bed, where blood is found under one of them; they are judged as ready to see, and attribute the stain to one another.
Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, rules on a woman who examined herself at her regular time, following R. Peda's view on sin and guilt offerings.
R. Oshaya says that even if her husband was liable for a sin offering, her purity status is dependent.
If blood was found, who held it? Asks how the sun is responsible for holding back blood in that case.
R. Yirmiyah's parable: a child and an elder walking on a road, where the child hurries to arrive, explains R. Oshaya's view.
Abaye gives another parable of R. Oshaya: a finger in an eye that holds back a tear, which hurries once the finger is removed.
Baraita: how women may attribute stains to one another, by pregnancy, nursing, age and virginity, in different combinations.
Cites the Mishna we learned: women who were not fit to see are regarded as seeing.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna on three women in one bed: where blood is found under the middle or an outer woman, and how examinations affect each; compared to piles of stones, with R. Meir's view.
R. Meir's principle: an item presumed impure stays impure until one knows exactly where the impurity is.
The Rabbis hold that one searches down to bedrock or virgin soil, after which the impurity is presumed moved by an animal.
Asks what distinguishes the first clause, which makes all three impure, from the latter clause, which distinguishes by location.
R. Ami says the first mishna refers to women lying intertwined, so one cannot tell the inside woman from the outside one.
Why does the tanna need the analogy to piles of stones, since the ruling is clear without it?
R. Meir says to the Rabbis: why do you disagree with me about stones but concede in the case of blood?
The Rabbis reply that the cases differ: a raven could have carried away the corpse-bulk, but the blood must have come from one of the women.
Baraita: R. Meir's account of a fig tree in Kfar Sava where a skull was later found, showing that an examination not fully thorough is no proof.
Baraita: R. Yosei's account of a cave of channels where workers later found a mortar full of bones, again showing an incomplete examination.
Baraita: R. Abba Shaul's account of a rock at Beit Chorin where sheets were laid on dry ground and a pit full of bones was found, identified as Yishmael ben Netanyah's pit.
Cites the verse in Jeremiah about the pit into which Yishmael cast the slain men as proof that the pit held corpses.
Asks: did Gedaliah kill them, when Yishmael killed them?
Yishmael killed them, but since Gedaliah should have heeded Yochanan ben Karach and did not, Scripture counts it as if he had killed them.
Rava says that an evil report should be heeded even if one does not accept it; the Galilean youths came before R. Tarfon after a report of murder.
R. Tarfon replies that he will hide them, and tells them to hide themselves, since the Sages say an evil report must be heeded.
Cites the verse where God tells Moses not to fear Og, king of Bashan, as a source for the scriptural basis of the story.
Why did Moses fear Og and not Sihon, if both were brothers, sons of Achiyah, the son of Shamchazai?
R. Yochanan says in R. Shimon bar Yochai's name that Moses knew Og would be spared through Abraham's merit, and Og escaped from the flood.
Baraita: for a garment in which a stain was lost, one rubs it with seven substances; R. Shimon ben Elazar disagrees.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Shimon ben Elazar's method: examine a lost stain section by section; a needle for new cloth, the sun for worn cloth, at least three fingerbreadths.
Baraita: a garment of forbidden mixed kinds that was lost may not be sold to a gentile or made a saddlecloth, but may be made a shroud.
Rav Yosef explains that this implies the commandments will be nullified in the future, since the dead would otherwise benefit from the mixed garment.
Abaye objects with R. Yannai's teaching that a corpse may be buried in mixed kinds only for eulogy, not burial.
Rav Yosef replies that R. Yochanan permits even burial in such a shroud.
R. Yochanan's reasoning is supported by the verse in Psalms about being set apart among the dead, which he reads as freedom from the commandments.
Rafram bar Pappa says Rav Chisda rules that a garment of mixed kinds that was lost may be dyed and worn.
Rava asks Rafram where the Elder, Rav Chisda, derives this halakha from.
Rafram answers from the Mishna about searching piles of stones for impurity, where a raven could have taken it, so the thread fell out.
Rav Acha son of Rav Yeiva says in Mar Zutra's name that one may wear a cloak where a flax thread fell out and it is unknown whether all of it did.
What is the reason for the leniency? The Torah prohibition needs all three of combing, spinning and weaving, and the rabbis' decree does not apply.
Rav Ashi objects: the Torah prohibition may apply to any one of the three activities, so the leniency is not established.
Baraita: a colored garment does not render a woman impure from a blood stain, according to R. Natan bar Yosef, because the Sages permitted colored garments to ease her stains.
What enactment did the Sages make? Does the word permitted imply that colored garments were previously prohibited?
Yes, as taught in a Mishna on Vespasian's war: the Sages sought to decree against colored garments but preferred to permit them to ease blood stains.
