Mishna: seven substances are applied to a stain to tell blood from dye, including tasteless saliva, split bean liquid, urine, natron and borit.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna on the seven substances for a lost stain: how each is applied, and that a stain that does not vanish shows it is dye, while one that vanishes is blood.
Baraita: the natron in the mishna is Alexandrian, not the lower-quality natron of Anpantrin.
Rav Yehuda says borit is ice plant.
Objects: a baraita lists borit and ice plant separately, so they are two different substances.
If borit is not ice plant, what is it?
Objects from a baraita on Sabbatical Year plants, which lists borit separately, and argues that borit cannot be sulfur, against both identifications.
Rav Yehuda identifies Cimolian earth as the earth called pull out and stick in.
Shmuel identifies eshlag from seafarers, who say it is called ashlega, found in the pearl shell and removed with an iron skewer.
Baraita: if seven substances fail to remove the stain, and it is then removed after the garment is dyed, the items handled with the garment are impure.
Objects that soap also removes dye, so the baraita must mean six substances were applied first, since the garment may then be impure from uncertainty.
Another baraita: if the seven substances are applied again and the stain vanishes, the items handled earlier remain pure.
R. Zeira explains: the items handled between the first and second washing remain pure, but items handled after the second washing are impure, since he showed concern that it was blood.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Abba asks whether purity depends on whether the owner is particular about the stain, since the first washing's items are pure.
Rav Ashi says yes, citing R. Hiyya's baraita on a menstrual stain nullified by the seven substances; the outcome depends on particularity.
Mishna in Kelim: a chamber pot that absorbed a zav's impure liquid, which fell into an oven, makes the oven impure once heated.
Reish Lakish says the oven is impure only for lesser liquids once heated, while greater liquids make it impure even unheated.
R. Yochanan says that for both kinds of liquid, the oven is impure only if it was heated.
R. Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish from the mishna on the seven substances: absorbed blood that does not emerge does not impart impurity, so the oven should be the same.
Reish Lakish replies: leave aside blood stains, which are impure only by rabbinic law, so the rule differs for Torah-impure liquids.
R. Yochanan raises a further objection from R. Hiyya's baraita on nullifying a menstrual stain with the seven substances.
Reish Lakish replies that R. Hiyya learned it from R. Yehuda HaNasi, so the baraita must be wrong and the objection fails.
R. Yochanan objects from the Oholot mishna: a quarter-log of corpse blood absorbed in a house's floor makes vessels there impure only when present at the outset.
The continuation of the Oholot mishna: blood absorbed in a garment is examined, and it is impure only if a quarter-log emerges when washed.
Rav Kahana replies that this is a leniency about the quarter-log measure, since it is corpse blood impure only by rabbinic law.
Reish Lakish objects from the Oholot mishna: absorbed liquid that cannot emerge is pure, so if it can emerge it is impure even before emerging.
Rav Pappa defends R. Yochanan: when the liquid cannot emerge and the owner is not particular, all agree the garment is pure, and when it can emerge and he is particular, all agree it is impure.
The dispute is when the liquid can emerge but the owner is not particular: Reish Lakish holds the garment impure, R. Yochanan holds it pure.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that the liquid makes the garment impure only if the owner is particular about it, and otherwise it does not.
Baraita: tasteless saliva is saliva of a person who has tasted nothing since the evening.
Rav Pappa suggests the baraita follows the view that one ate nothing all night.
Rava objects that the baraita says from the evening, which excludes one who eats after nightfall; the words teach something different.
R. Yochanan says tasteless saliva is that of a person who passed midnight without eating and was asleep.
Does this mean the matter depends on whether he slept?
A baraita says one who slept all day has saliva that is not tasteless, but one awake all night does, which conflicts with the sleep requirement; the dozing case is the explanation.
What are the circumstances of dozing?
Rav Ashi explains: asleep yet not fully asleep, awake yet not fully awake, answering when called and remembering only when reminded.
A baraita: one who rose early and learned aloud his chapter does not have tasteless saliva, since speech weakens the saliva.
How much speech removes the strength of saliva: R. Elazar's measure of most of the usual speech in three hours.
Mishna: liquid from split beans is made from naturally split beans and applied to the stain.
The Gemara suggests this supports Reish Lakish, but answers that the effect may come from the heat of the mouth rather than the saliva.
Baraita: R. Yehuda says split-bean liquid works only when boiling and before salt is added, so the mishna is not like him.
From where is it inferred that the word over indicates priority?
Proofs from the verses: R. Nachman bar Yitzchak cites Ahimaaz who overtook the Cushite; Abaye cites Genesis and Micah.
Mishna: urine that is a detergent is fermented urine; a baraita says three days.
R. Yochanan says that every measure of the Sages for blood stains needs a measure, since urine varies by age, sex, cover and season.
Mishna: each substance must be rubbed three times.
R. Yirmeya asks whether going and returning of the hand counts as one rubbing or two; the dilemma is left unresolved.
Mishna and two baraitot on applying the substances out of order: one says the second set counts, the other says the first counts.
Abaye says the baraitot do not disagree: the substances applied second count, and the first refers to the mishna's order.
Mishna: a woman with a fixed cycle based on a physical sensation, such as yawning, sneezing or abdominal pain, has a sufficient time.
The Gemara cites an earlier mishna on fixed cycles determined by days, to compare it with this one.
The Gemara explains the difference: there the cycles concern days, here they concern the body, as the mishna lists.
The mishna continues with sensation-based cycles, including a discharge that comes and goes.
Ulla, son of Rav Alai, comments on the case of a discharge that started and then stopped.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the mishna: she discharges impure blood in the midst of pure blood, such as non-red blood followed by red blood.
Mishna: a feverish shuddering or a similar sensation also establishes a fixed cycle.
Rabba bar Ulla explains the added phrase: it includes a woman whose head or limbs feel heavy, or who trembles or belches constantly.
Shmuel: two occurrences suffice for a fixed set of days, one for a physical sensation, but other sensations need three.
What did Shmuel intend to add by the phrase for sensations the Sages did not list?
Rav Yosef says it adds the heavy head, limbs, trembling and belching cases listed above.
Abaye objects: this is already in the mishna through Rabba bar Ulla's explanation, so what does it add?
Abaye explains the addition: a woman who ate garlic, onions or pepper and then saw blood, which needs three occurrences.
Rav Yosef says he did not hear this tradition of Shmuel's ruling on days and sensations.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he taught this ruling in connection with the mishna on the fifteenth and twentieth days.
Abaye says Rav Yosef taught that Shmuel's view is the statement of Rabban Gamliel son of R. Yehuda HaNasi, and the Sages differ.
Abaye recalls that Rav Yosef explained the two statements, one about sensations and one about days.
Why does Shmuel need to identify the mishna as Rabban Gamliel son of R. Yehuda HaNasi, rather than Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
Shmuel teaches that Rabban Gamliel son of R. Yehuda HaNasi holds in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Mishna: a woman accustomed to bleed at the beginning of her sensation has impure purities within it, and at the end has pure ones.
R. Yosei says even specific days and hours can establish a fixed cycle; R. Yehuda says the whole day is hers.
Asks: how so? What is the example of the days and hours?
R. Yosei gives examples: from the twentieth day, six hours, and beyond; R. Yehuda and R. Yosei prohibit or permit according to the hours of the day.
Objects from a baraita: R. Yehuda says the whole night is hers, which seems to conflict with the day rule.
Resolves it: she is used to seeing at the start of the day in one case and at the end of the night in the other.
One baraita: R. Yehuda prohibits her before her cycle and permits her after it.
Another baraita: R. Yehuda prohibits her after her cycle and permits her before it.
Resolves the two baraitot: each refers to the time she is accustomed to see blood, at the end of night or the start of day.
Rava rules that the halakha follows R. Yehuda.
Objects: did Rava really say so, since a baraita derives from the verse that Israelites must separate from their wives near their cycle?
R. Yirmeya derives from the verse a warning to Israelites to separate from their wives near their cycle, and Rava says how near: an onah.
What is meant by onah? Is it not another onah, and why is the second word needed?
The second word is needed: otherwise one would think the rule applies only to purity and not to the husband, and it is also needed for the other onah.
Mishna: a woman who was accustomed to see blood on the fifteenth day, and then changed to the twentieth day three times, establishes it as her cycle.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Stated case: a woman sees blood on the fifteenth of one month, the sixteenth of the next, and the seventeenth of the month after.
Rav says she has established a cycle by skipping a day; Shmuel says a skip must occur three times.
Shall we say Rav and Shmuel disagree like R. Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
Cites the baraita on a woman widowed twice: R. Yehuda HaNasi forbids a third marriage, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits a third but not a fourth.
Rejects the parallel: all agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rav and Shmuel differ on whether the first occurrence counts in the pattern.
Shmuel objects from a baraita on a woman who shifts from the fifteenth to the sixteenth and beyond, which seems to conflict with Rav.
Rav replies that the fifteenth was her established day, which is different; the baraita must teach that an established day is displaced only after three times.
Objects from a baraita on a woman who bled on the twenty-first, twenty-second and twenty-third, which seems to refute Shmuel.
Shmuel replies that the woman was used to bleeding on the twentieth, so there are three intervals; the baraita's choice of date proves it.
Rav Pappa's explanation of the mishna: three occurrences are needed to establish a cycle, but one occurrence requires caution.
What does Rav Pappa teach? The mishna already shows a single bleeding on another day requires caution.
Explains that the mishna's rule might apply only when she bleeds on a day within her menstrual days, and Rav Pappa limits the uprooting to three occurrences.
What does Rav Pappa's distinction add?
The mishna teaches that a woman establishes a cycle only after three times, excluding a one-to-one or two-to-two equivalence.
A baraita agrees with Rav Pappa: a woman used to bleed on the twentieth who shifts to the thirtieth is prohibited for both days, and so on.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Tail of the baraita: she is prohibited on the twentieth day, since her blood comes at its usual time.
Mishna: women compared to grapevines; R. Yehuda says a vine without fit grapes is a dry vine, as a woman without bleeding cannot bear children.
Explains durkati as a truncated generation and cites R. Hiyya and R. Meir: blood is good for a woman, and plentiful blood means plentiful children.
Chapter-ending formula introducing the next chapter.
Mishna on a young girl married before puberty or before she bled, and the rulings of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the torn hymen.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives from the mishna's distinction that the ruling applies even to a girl who has already bled.
A baraita states the same: Beit Hillel say the blood is attributed to the torn hymen until the wound heals, whether or not she had bled.
Until when can the blood be attributed to the torn hymen?
Rav says until she is noheret; Shmuel says he does not know that term and means as long as saliva is present due to intercourse.
What is the meaning of the term noheret that Rav used?
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains it through sitting and standing, the ground, and cushions, to determine whether the wound has healed.
Mishna: when her time has come, Beit Hillel say the blood is attributed to the torn hymen until the end of Shabbat.
Amoraim dispute: after daytime and nighttime intercourse, Rav says she has not lost her nights, while Levi says she has.
What is the meaning of four nights in the mishna, according to Levi?
Explains that four nights means four periods of intercourse, that the mishna teaches normal conduct for Rav, and that it permits intercourse on Shabbat ab initio, as Shmuel says.
Cites Shmuel's principle that a narrow breach may be entered on Shabbat, even though it dislodges stones.
Stated case: a man has intercourse, finds no blood, returns, has intercourse again, and finds blood.
R. Hanina says she is impure, while R. Asi says she is pure.
R. Hanina explains: if it were so, the blood would have come from the hymen at first, so it would have appeared earlier.
R. Asi explains: perhaps it happened as Shmuel said, that a man may have intercourse several times without blood.
The other Sage replies that Shmuel's case differs, since Rav's husband was a particular kind of man.
Rav rules: for a grown woman, the first night is given, but that applies only if she has not bled; if she has bled, only intercourse of mitzva is permitted.
Objects from a baraita on R. who gave a girl four nights within twelve months: did he give them all in her childhood?

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the mishna: the blood may be attributed to the torn hymen until the wound heals, so four nights is not the limit.
Objects that the four nights cannot all fall in the girlhood years of twelve months, since Shmuel says the transition takes only six months.
Rav Chinana bar Shelamya asks Rav: if a girl marries before puberty and her time comes under her husband, does she get the four nights?
Rav replies that all intercourse while she is still a girl counts as one act, and the rest complete the four nights.
Objects that if one night is given in girlhood, two in youth and one as a grown woman, the rule conflicts with how grown women are treated.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave one night in girlhood and three in youth; the six months are counted as two-month periods, giving three nights.
Story: Minyamin Saksana set out to act on Rav's ruling, died on the way, and Shmuel cited the verse that no harm befalls the righteous.
Rav Chinana bar Shelamya says in Rav's name that when a man's teeth fall out, his food diminishes.
Cites the verse from Amos about cleanness of teeth and lack of bread as support for Rav's statement.
Baraita: if a young woman sees blood while in her father's house, Beit Hillel say all the night is hers; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains a full period as one night and half a day.
Asks whether a full period truly requires all of one night and half a day.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita on impure winepresses and olive presses prepared for purity, which requires a different ritual sequence.

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita ruling on how long wine-press baskets must be set aside before reuse, and the twelve-month and season-based options.
Gemara explains the difference between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the first tanna as early versus late grape-ripening seasons.
Baraita continues with Rabbi Yosei's faster purification methods and Rabban Shimon's version in Rabbi Yosei's name.
Baraita states that the time frame for purity matters follows the time frame set for libation wine.
Gemara is surprised at the clause, asking whether the comparison should be reversed.
Gemara resolves the surprise by reading the comparison the other way round, from purity matters to libation wine.
Gemara asks what the actual length of the stated time period is.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yohanan's view that the period is either a day or a night.
Rabbi Hana and related transmitters report Rabbi Yohanan's view that the period is half a day and half a night.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak reconciles the two views by linking each to a different season's day and night lengths.
Gemara proposes applying the same reconciliation to niddah, reading Rabban Shimon's period as half a day and half a night.
Objection: the baraita explicitly says a night and half a day, so the proposed reading does not fit it.
Reply upholding Rabban Shimon by applying the seasonal distinction to his night-and-half-day formula.
Alternative explanation: marriage contracts require a longer window, so the marriage period differs from the purity period.
Rav and Shmuel both rule that the groom consummates the marriage as a mitzva and then separates from the bride.
Rav Hisda objects with a baraita about a virgin given four nights, which suggests the groom need not separate immediately.
Rava criticizes the objection's source, saying the mishna itself could have been cited for the refutation.
Gemara explains Rav Hisda's reasoning: a practical case decided by a sage is the preferable source.
Gemara states the difficulty this baraita poses for the rulings of Rav and Shmuel.
Reply: Rav and Shmuel followed the baraita's account of the Sages' vote establishing the groom's separation.
Ulla shows Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish reached the same conclusion, so the ruling rests on their authority too.
Rabbi Abba objects that a pious man would then never complete intercourse, which seems an unreasonable outcome.
Rav Ashi replies that no such decree exists, since the husband's own fear would make him withdraw early anyway.
Baraita: women who bleed over several nights must examine themselves, and Rabbi Meir follows Beit Shammai in stringency.
Rabbi Meir's criteria: menstrual blood is red, cloudy, and from the uterus, while hymenal blood differs in each respect.
Rabbi Yitzhak bar Rabbi Yosei reports Rabbi Yohanan's view that Rabbi Meir alone distinguishes blood types, while the Sages treat all as one.
Baraita: a woman who bleeds after intercourse may resume relations for three cycles, then must wait until divorce.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah case of a divorcee who remarries and again bleeds from intercourse, with the three-time limit on relations.
Mishnah continues the case of the remarried woman, who must examine herself before resuming relations after the presumption arises.
Mishnah describes the examination with a tube and cosmetic brush, and how the blood's place of origin is read from the cloth.
Mishnah adds that a wound or a fixed menstrual cycle may explain the bleeding, so she is pure in those cases.
Mishnah says a woman is believed that she has a uterine wound when the blood differs in appearance; this is Rabbi's view.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds wound blood from the uterus is impure, while the Sages testified it is pure by tradition.
Gemara asks what the practical difference is between the Sages and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Ulla explains the difference: whether the uterine place itself is impure, so blood passing through it is impure even from a wound.
Gemara asks whether the inserted tube would itself scratch the woman and cause bleeding.
Shmuel answers that the baraita means a lead tube with its inserted end folded so it does not scratch.
Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yohanan that she should test herself after the third act with her first husband instead of divorcing.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that it is better she not test herself, since not all fingers are equal in their effect.
Reish Lakish presses that she should test herself after the first act with her third husband, since she is then presumed to bleed.
Rabbi Yohanan answers again that not all forces are equal, so the bleeding may be due to the manner of intercourse.
Narrative of a woman bleeding from intercourse whom Abdon frightened, after which congealed blood fell out and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declared her cured.
Narrative of another woman, whom Rav Dimi frightened without result; Shmuel says a woman who is filled with blood has no cure.
Narrative of a woman bleeding after purification whom Rabbi Yohanan advises to bathe in a river and tell her friends.
Alternative version of Rabbi Yohanan's advice: the woman should either reveal the matter to her friends or ask them to pray for her.
A baraita on the leper's announcement of his impurity is cited as a source for publicizing one's affliction so others pray for mercy.
Rav Yosef reports a similar case in Pumbedita in which the woman was cured after the same advice.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, reports Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's decree for remote fields where women could not distinguish menstrual days from ziva days.
Rabbi Zeira says Jewish women were stringent, sitting seven clean days even for a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed.
Rava has Shmuel teach a ruling: a woman who miscarries after two days of labor must count seven clean days.
Gemara explains Rava's reasoning: a miscarriage requires blood to open the womb, so blood must have flowed.
Rav Pappa challenges why the ruling specifies two days, since any blood would trigger the stringency Rabbi Zeira describes.
Rava replies that his ruling is a Torah prohibition, while Rav Pappa's point concerns only a custom of stringency.
A mnemonic list is given to organize the following halakhot on betrothal, purification, and immersion.
Rava rules that a woman who has accepted a proposal must count seven clean days before she may marry.
Narrative: Ravina arranges his son's marriage to Rav Hanina's daughter and delays the wedding by a week.
Rav Hanina asks Ravina what the purpose of the extra week of delay is.
Ravina replies that his delay follows Rava's ruling that an accepted proposal requires seven clean days before immersion.
Rav Hanina objects that Rava may have spoken only of an adult woman who has seen blood, not a minor girl.
Ravina replies that Rava stated explicitly that there is no difference between an adult woman and a minor girl.
Gemara gives the reason: a minor girl also desires marriage, so the same risk of bleeding applies to her.
Rava states the halakha for a woman about to immerse in a ritual bath for purification.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A woman may not wash her hair with natron or sand before immersion, since both leave residue that would interpose.
Ameimar in Rava's name: a woman washes her hair only in hot water, not cold, even hot water heated by the sun.
The reason given is that cold water hardens the hair and leaves the dirt in it.
Rava teaches that a man should instruct his household that a woman must rinse her creases before immersing.
Objection from a baraita: creases and concealed places need not be reached by water, so rinsing them seems unnecessary.
Reply: such places must still be suitable for immersion, following Rabbi Zeira's principle about mingling in a meal offering.
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required a maidservant to re-immerse when a bone was found between her teeth.
Rava rules that if an interposition is found after immersion, re-immersion depends on whether it was near the washing.
Another version of Rava's ruling ties the requirement to whether she washed on the same day as immersing.
Gemara asks what the practical difference is between the two versions.
The difference concerns washing close to immersion, and whether washing by day and immersing by night is sufficient.
Rava rules that a woman may not stand on submerged earthenware vessels while immersing.
Rav Kahana explains the reason is a decree against immersing as in bathhouses, so standing on a wooden plank is permitted.
Rav Hanan of Neharde'a rejects that reason and says the real concern is fear of falling, which applies to planks too.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak states that a woman may not immerse herself while standing in this way.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A woman may not immerse in a port where mud may cling to her, since one cannot be sure it was absent during immersion.
Narrative: Shmuel's father prepared ritual baths for his daughters by filling pits with rainwater and laying mats in the river.
Rav rules that a woman who handled a cooked dish before immersing has an ineffective immersion, by the same reasoning as the mud.
Rami bar Abba rules that bloodletting incisions interpose only after three days, once a hard scab has formed.
Mar Ukva rules that moist eye mucus does not interpose, while dry mucus does, from the point it begins to turn yellow.
Shmuel rules that eye shadow inside the eye does not interpose, while shadow on the eye does, unless the eyes constantly blink.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that opening or tightly closing the eyes during immersion makes the immersion ineffective.
Reish Lakish rules that a woman must immerse in the posture of her natural stance, without forcing her limbs.
Reish Lakish supports this by citing the mishnah's description of how a man and a woman appear when examined for a leprous mark.
Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that a single hair tied in a knot interposes and invalidates an immersion.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan rules that two or more hairs knotted together do not interpose, and that only a single hair does.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains the Torah-law and rabbinic distinctions between interposing substances based on whether the person minds them.
Gemara asks why the Sages did not also decree against minority-covering substances the person does not mind.
Reply: that prohibition is already a decree, and one should not add a decree to prevent violating another decree.
Rav rules that a niddah immersing on time may do so only at night, while an off-time immersion may be by day or night.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that both on-time and off-time immersion must be at night, so the daughter does not follow her mother by day.
Rav reverses himself, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi reports that all immersions of a niddah must be at night for the same reason.
Rav Idi decrees in Neresh that women may immerse by day on the eighth day, because lions roamed the area at night.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov decrees in Pappunya that women may immerse by day on the eighth day, because of thieves at night.
Rav Yehuda decrees in Pumbedita that women may immerse by day on the eighth day, because of the cold at night.
Rava decrees in Mehoza that women may immerse by day on the eighth day, because of untrustworthy gatekeepers.
Rav Pappa asks Rava and Abaye whether, since all menstruants now count as uncertain zavot, they may immerse by day on the seventh day.
Rava and Abaye reply that the seventh-day immersion is barred according to the view of Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita cites the verse in Leviticus 15:28 and explains how it bears on counting seven clean days before purification.
Rabbi Shimon reads the phrase and after that she shall be pure as permitting immersion once she has examined herself on the seventh day.
The Sages prohibit this practice, lest a later discovery of bleeding on the seventh day cause intercourse while impure.
Rav Huna rules that a woman may wash her hair on Sunday and immerse on Monday night.
Proof: women often wash on the eve of Shabbat and immerse only after Shabbat ends, a similar interval.
Rav Huna rules that a woman may wash her hair on Sunday and immerse on Tuesday night.
Proof: women often wash on the eve of Shabbat and immerse after a festival following Shabbat, the same interval.
Rav Huna rules that a woman may wash her hair on Sunday and immerse on Wednesday night.
Proof: women often wash on the eve of Shabbat and immerse after two Rosh HaShana days following Shabbat, the same interval.
Rav Hisda replies that Shabbat cases cannot prove the weekday halakha, since alternatives exist only where immersion is possible.
Rav Yeimar agrees with Rav Huna except for Wednesday, arguing that one could wash at night after Rosh HaShana and immerse that night.
Mareimar teaches that the halakha follows Rav Hisda, and also follows Rav Yeimar's explanation for the Rosh HaShana case.
Dilemma raised: may a woman wash her hair at night and immerse that same night?
Mar Zutra prohibits it, fearing haste, while Rav Hinnana from Sura permits it.
Rav Adda objects to Rav Hinnana with the incident of Abba Mari's wife, who refused immersion and had no reason to hurry.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak tells the woman to return tomorrow, then rebukes her for lacking the means to wash her hair in time.
Rava teaches that a woman may wash her hair on the eve of Shabbat and immerse after Shabbat ends.
Rav Pappa objects that Ravin's letter ruled the opposite, forbidding washing on the eve of Shabbat for post-Shabbat immersion.
Quoted halakha from Ravin's letter: a woman may not wash on the eve of Shabbat and immerse after Shabbat.
Rav Pappa objects that washing by day and immersing at night violates the requirement that immersion follow washing immediately.
Rava retracts his earlier teaching, calling it a mistake of his own.
Rava introduces the corrected version, attributed to Rabbi Yohanan, that a woman may not wash on the eve of Shabbat for post-Shabbat immersion.
Rabbi Yohanan's ruling is restated, with the principle that immersion must be immediately after washing, so daytime washing fails.
The Gemara lists two apparently conflicting halakhot on whether washing is permitted by day or only at night.
The Gemara notes the two halakhot contradict each other and calls the contradiction difficult.
The contradiction is resolved: daytime washing applies when immersion is possible soon after, and night-only washing when it is not.
Mishnah: a woman who examined herself on the seventh morning and found pure, but skipped the evening check, is presumed pure.
Mishnah continues: if she found herself impure in the morning, or the evening check is missed, the presumptive status applies, and a fixed cycle suffices.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a woman who did not examine herself in a pure state from minha onward is presumed impure.
The Sages hold that even with two earlier examinations, a woman who missed the evening check is presumed pure after a later finding of impurity.
The dispute is stated: Rav says she is a definite greater zava, while Levi says she is an uncertain greater zava.
The Gemara asks which mishnah clause the dispute concerns, since the first clause makes her pure and the second makes the case unsuitable.
The dispute is restated as a separate halakha, unconnected to the mishnah, about a woman found impure on the seventh day.
The dispute is stated again: Rav holds she is a definite zava, and Levi holds she is an uncertain zava.
Rav's reasoning: she was impure at first and impure again, so her impurity is definite.
Levi's reasoning: she may have stopped bleeding in between, so her status as a zava is uncertain.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Levi's baraita: a woman examined herself, found ambiguous results, and is a doubtful zava who transmits impurity
Proposes this baraita refutes Rava's view that a woman does not transmit impurity for a twenty-four-hour period
Asks why the refutation of Rava is raised again when a conclusive refutation was already cited earlier
Rava could say the mishna refers to the case of a young woman who saw blood before marriage in her father's house
The ruling is needed to exclude the thought that interrupted days reset her cycle so no retroactive impurity applies
The mishna teaches that a woman with a fixed menstrual cycle on the day she found blood is not retroactively impure
Proposes this refutes Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya's report of Shmuel that a woman cannot establish a fixed cycle during ziva days
Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya meant only a leniency: one missed cycle uproots it, and her menstrual blood is removed during ziva days
Rabbi Yehuda says that a woman who did not examine herself at minḥa time on the seventh day is presumed impure
A baraita objects: Yehuda's view would be fine only if her hands stayed in place, so why not count the first day
Asks whether anyone holds that an examination on the first day alone is sufficient
A baraita reports Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asking Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon about a woman who examined herself on the seventh day
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon rule that she has a presumptive status of purity until she discovers she is impure
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks the same about examinations made on the sixth, fifth, fourth, third and second days
They reply that there is no difference between those days and the first day in this respect
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states that he erred by not asking about a woman who examined herself on the first day
Argues by analogy: if the other days leave her presumptively pure, the first day must do so too
Asks what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held initially, since he did not ask about the first day
He held that her uterus is still open right after bleeding began, so an examination that day is ineffective
The mishna introduces a zav or zava who examined on the first and seventh days and not on the days between
Rabbi Eliezer holds that such a person keeps a presumptive status of purity
Rabbi Yehoshua holds that only the first and seventh days count, so five more days must be counted
Rabbi Akiva holds that only the seventh day counts, so six more days must be counted
Rabbi Eliezer tells Rabbi Yehoshua that his view counts at intervals rather than on consecutive days
The Torah requires purification only after seven consecutive clean days, so no impurity may separate the counted days
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that Eliezer also counts at intervals in the cases of a zav's emission and a nazirite
Cites the verse on a nazirite's earlier days being void to support counting with intervening impurity
Rabbi Eliezer replies that the verse on a zav's emission limits the overturned count to one day, a special case
A nazirite under overhanging boughs is impure by rabbinic decree only, and rabbinic halakha cannot be confused with Torah law
In the zava's case, the first day might be confused with a situation where she certainly bled on intermediate days
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon hold Eliezer's view most correct, and the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer
A dilemma: a zav or zava examined on the first and eighth days and not in between, what is the status

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the halakha by Rabbi Eliezer's view when examinations occur on the first and seventh days, or only the first day
Rav holds that the first-and-eighth case equals first-and-seventh: the beginning examination suffices without the end
Rabbi Ḥanina holds that both the beginning and end examinations are required, so Eliezer would permit no counting here
A baraita on the first-and-eighth case seems to contradict Rav, since its Sages would include Eliezer
Asks who the agreeing Sages in the baraita are, if not Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
They are Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, who both exclude the first day, so no contradiction arises
Rav Sheshet reports Rav's ruling that a woman who examines on her third day counts that day among the seven clean days
Asks why a niddah needs counting at all, and proposes the ruling must concern a zava instead
Rav Sheshet challenges Rav Yirmeya: is Rav's ruling like the Samaritans, who count the day ziva stops
Rav Yirmeya replies that Rav's ruling excludes the third day itself, so the counting starts after it
Rav Sheshet objects that this would be obvious and need no statement
Rav Yirmeya explains it is needed when she examined clean after the third day and waited until the seventh
Rav teaches two rulings: a beginning examination suffices without an end, and an end examination suffices without a beginning
Rav Yirmeya explains both rulings are needed so the presumptive-purity principle is not wrongly extended to the end case
Asks whether this explanation really holds, given an earlier discussion about Rav Yehoshua ben Levi
Ravin reports Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina objecting to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view on a possible miscarriage
Ravin replies that the miscarriage's timing is unknown, so she immerses only at night while counting her clean days
If we did not require counting before us, she should immerse by day too, since she might have already counted
So we must conclude that the seven clean days must be counted before the court, which is why she is not told to immerse by day
Rejects that conclusion: the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, while Rav follows Rabbi Eliezer, who does not require it
Asks from where the Rabbis' view is known, that the clean days need not be counted before the court
Cites a baraita on a forgetful woman who saw blood on one day, who must immerse nine times
Explains the baraita's rule: seven and two immersions for the unknown case, and eleven if she saw blood at twilight
Asks what the purpose of the eleven immersions is, given the baraita's counts
Rav Yirmeya of Difti explains the twilight case: she came before the court at twilight, so eight plus three immersions
If she says she saw no blood at all, the baraita requires fifteen immersions
Rava says this ruling is illogical, offering the Galahi custom of unequal shepherding as an analogy
Relates the Galahi incident: an orphan slaughtered the oxen and gave the townspeople one or two hides each
The townspeople ask the orphan what he means by this distribution
The orphan replies that the end of the law mirrors its beginning, so the one without an ox receives more
Argues by analogy that if nine or eleven immersions suffice when she saw blood, fifteen is illogical when she saw none
Rather, the baraita means she saw blood but cannot say how many days or whether it was menstrual or ziva blood

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita requires eight daytime immersions for ziva, since she may have bled on the day she came before the court
Raises the difficulty that ziva still calls for eight immersions, given the possibility of a greater zava
Resolves it: in both cases she immerses seven times for menstruation and eight times for ziva
Asks why the baraita totals only fifteen immersions when some cases require sixteen
The baraita states the fixed eight ziva immersions, while the menstrual count is given only at its minimum of seven
If seven clean days had to be counted before the court, why would all these immersions be needed at all
So the baraita must follow the Rabbis, who do not require the seven days to be counted before the court
Rav Aḥa son of Rav Yosef objects: resolve the baraita the same way, reading it as a woman who counted but cannot recall how many
Proposed revised baraita: a woman who counted but does not know how many days or which kind of days gets fifteen immersions
Asks whether a woman who counted cannot have counted at least one clean day, making the eighth immersion unnecessary
Revises the case: she does not know whether she counted any clean days or none, so she has not yet counted at all
Mishna: corpses of zav, zava, niddah, woman after childbirth and leper transmit impurity by carrying until the flesh decays
Beit Shammai hold all women who die are treated as niddot, so their garments require immersion
Beit Hillel hold only a woman who died in niddah impurity is treated as a niddah after death
Asks what carrying means, since every corpse would otherwise impart impurity by carrying, making the rule superfluous
Carrying means imparting impurity through a very heavy stone, a unique rule for zavim and niddot sitting over vessels
Cites Daniel 6:18, where a stone was placed upon the mouth of the den, to support the term mesama
Asks the reason the Sages decreed that these corpses impart impurity through a heavy stone
Rav says it is a decree lest such a person faint on the stone and be mistaken for dead
A baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: these corpses impart impurity through a stone until the belly bursts
The mishna's ruling is recited: a dead gentile is ritually pure and cannot transmit impurity by carrying
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explains: a gentile's living impurity is rabbinic, so it does not extend to his corpse
Alexandrians asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥinnana twelve questions, in four groups of three of wisdom, aggada, ignorance and conduct
First question of wisdom: until when do such corpses transmit impurity by carrying
Rabbi Yehoshua answers: until the flesh decays, as the mishna teaches
Second question: what is the status of a divorcee's daughter from a forbidden remarriage regarding marrying a priest
Asks whether a fortiori reasoning can be applied to the case
A fortiori argument: a widow of a High Priest has a flawed son, so this daughter's son should be flawed too
Refutes the argument: a widow of a High Priest is herself disqualified from teruma, which a remarried divorcee is not
Rabbi Yehoshua begins his reply to the second question, which continues on the next daf

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Deuteronomy 24:4: the remarried divorcee is an abomination, but her children are not, so they may marry priests
Third question: two leper offerings were mixed and one died, so what is the status of the surviving leper
Rabbi Yehoshua replies: he transfers his property to others and becomes poor, bringing a bird sin offering
Objects that a leper must still bring a guilt offering, which cannot be brought in a case of uncertainty; Shmuel says it was already sacrificed
Rav Sheshet challenges that a great man like Shmuel would not say such a thing
Asks in accordance with whose opinion Shmuel's solution holds
If it follows Rabbi Yehuda, a leper who fixed a guilt offering while wealthy cannot bring a bird sin offering when poor
Cites a mishna on a leper whose wealth changed, which Rabbi Shimon resolves by the sin offering
Rabbi Yehuda holds that everything follows his status when the guilt offering was brought
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov holds that everything follows the bird offering brought at the start of purification
If Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, another animal could be brought as guilt offering with a stipulation, so why assume it was sacrificed
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon: the leper brings guilt offering and oil on the eighth day, stipulating that the animal is a peace offering if not a leper
States that a guilt offering of uncertain status requires a stipulation, continued on the next daf

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon's view: the leper's guilt offering is slaughtered in the north and eaten by priestly males for one day and night
The Rabbis did not concede to Rabbi Shimon, because it brings offerings into a status more prone to disqualification
Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon on one point but disagrees on another, denying the stipulation for a guilt offering
First Alexandrian aggada question: one verse says God has no pleasure in death, another says God desired to kill
Rabbi Yehoshua: one verse refers to sinners who repent, the other to sinners who do not repent
Second aggada question: one verse says God shows no favor, another says God shows favor
Rabbi Yehoshua: the favor is shown before sentencing, while the other verse refers to after sentencing
Third aggada question: one verse says God chose Zion, another says the city provoked His anger
Rabbi Yehoshua: the first verse refers to before Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, the second to after
First ignorance question: does Lot's wife, turned into a pillar of salt, transmit ritual impurity as a corpse
A corpse transmits impurity, but a pillar of salt does not, even if it was formerly a person
Second ignorance question: does the Shunammite's son, revived by Elisha, transmit impurity as a corpse
A corpse transmits impurity, but a living person does not, even one who had been dead temporarily
Third ignorance question: will the resurrected dead require sprinkling on the third and seventh days
Rabbi Yehoshua: when they come to life we will clarify the halakha, or Moses will tell us when he comes with them
First behavior question: what should a person do to become wise
Rabbi Yehoshua: increase sitting in the study house and minimize business dealings
Objection: many people did so and it did not help them become wise
They should pray for mercy from the One to whom wisdom belongs, citing Proverbs 2:6
Rabbi Ḥiyya's parable of a king feasting his servants and sending food to loved ones illustrates that God gives wisdom to whom He loves
Asks what Rabbi Yehoshua taught by saying one should increase study, since wisdom comes through prayer
Prayer without study does not suffice, so both are needed
Behavior question: what should a person do to become wealthy
Rabbi Yehoshua: increase business dealings and conduct them faithfully
Objection: many did so and it did not help them become rich
They should pray for mercy from the One to whom wealth belongs, citing Haggai 2:8
Asks what Rabbi Yehoshua taught by saying one should conduct business, since wealth comes through prayer
Prayer without honest business does not suffice, so both are needed
Behavior question: what should a person do to have male children
Rabbi Yehoshua: he should marry a woman fit for him

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes Rabbi Yehoshua's advice: one should sanctify himself by modesty during intercourse
Objection: many people did so and it did not help them to have sons
Rabbi Yehoshua: they should pray for sons from the One to whom children belong, citing Psalms 127:3
Asks what Rabbi Yehoshua taught by saying one should marry well and be modest, since prayer is the path
Prayer without marrying well and modesty does not suffice, so all are needed
Asks what act is rewarded by the fruit of the womb in Psalms 127:3
Rabbi Ḥama son of Rabbi Ḥanina: a man who holds back semen so his wife emits first is rewarded with children
Beit Shammai hold that all women who die are treated as menstruating women
Asks what the reasoning of Beit Shammai is
Beit Shammai derive it from Esther 4:4, where the queen was greatly distressed
Rav explains that the verse teaches she began to menstruate from fear, as her bodily openings relaxed
Likewise a dying woman sees blood out of fear of the Angel of Death
Objects: a mishna teaches that fear removes menstrual blood, so the derivation seems contradicted
Not difficult: prolonged anxiety contracts the muscles and stops blood, while sudden fear relaxes them and lets it flow
If fear explains it, Beit Shammai should also say all dying men are zavim, yet they disagree on men
A zav's impurity applies only to a discharge not caused by circumstances beyond his control, so fear would not make him impure
Rather, Beit Shammai's reason is a different one, as a baraita explains
Baraita: utensils used by menstruating women who died were immersed, and this was relaxed to protect the living women's honor
Similarly, utensils used by dying zavin were immersed until this was relaxed for the living zavin's honor
Mishna: a quarter-log of blood emitted after a woman's death imparts impurity as a menstrual blood spot and in a tent
Rabbi Yehuda holds that this blood is not impure as a spot, because it was displaced after she died
Rabbi Yehuda concedes that if she was sitting on the birthing stool and the blood came out while alive, it is impure as a spot
Rabbi Yosei holds that such blood does not impart impurity in a tent, since it did not come from a corpse
By inference, the first tanna may hold that blood emitted after death is impure as a menstrual spot, which seems unreasonable
Ze'eiri: even the first tanna agrees such blood is not a spot; the dispute is whether the uterus is impure after death
By inference, the first tanna may hold that such blood also imparts impurity in a tent
Rav Yehuda: the dispute concerns blood of submission, which is a mixture of blood from life and from after death
Asks what blood of submission is, as taught in a baraita
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yehuda: a killed person's uncertain blood, partly before and partly after death, is blood of submission
The Rabbis say this is an uncertain case of Torah impurity: impure in a private domain, pure in a public domain
Asks again what blood of submission is, if not the case just described
Blood still flowing after death, with uncertainty whether the majority was emitted alive or dead, is blood of submission
Rabbi Yehuda: blood of a killed man dripping into a hole is impure, because the drop of death is mixed in it
The Rabbis deem it pure because the drop of death is not mixed with it

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes the case: the first drop and the drops after it are separated from one another, not in a steady stream
Asks how Rabbi Yehuda responds to the Rabbis' challenge to his position
Rabbi Yehuda follows his own principle that blood does not nullify blood
Rabbi Shimon: for one crucified on wood, a quarter-log found beneath him is impure
Rabbi Yehuda deems it pure: the blood that fell earlier was from life and the death drop stayed on the wood
Challenges Rabbi Yehuda to apply the same reasoning to a man killed on a bed with blood dripping into a hole
The bed case differs, since the blood seeps through the bed onto the floor
Mishna: a woman after birth in her blood-of-purity period may pour water to rinse the Paschal offering from a vessel
The Sages later ruled she is like one impure by a corpse, who renders sacred items impure, in accordance with Beit Hillel
Beit Shammai say she is even like one impure by a corpse, rendering non-sacred vessels impure
Infers from the mishna that water prepared with sacred-level purity is treated like sacrificial food
Objects that the mishna's latter clause shows non-sacred items prepared with sacred purity are not like sacrificial food
Asks whose opinion the latter clause of the mishna expresses
Baraita of Abba Shaul: one who immersed that day renders two sacred items impure and disqualifies a third
Beit Shammai concede to Beit Hillel that she may eat second tithe and separate ḥalla from her dough
Beit Shammai also concede that a drop from her saliva or blood of purity on teruma is pure
Dispute: Beit Shammai require immersion at the end of purity, Beit Hillel do not
Explains the concession: one who immersed during the day may eat second tithe immediately after ascending
The untithed dough is not like ḥalla, so it is not rendered impure by her contact
It is a mitzva to separate teruma from produce nearby the produce it exempts, ab initio
The mishna must teach that the vessel may be named ḥalla, since no decree prevents touching it from outside
Cites a mishna in Tevul Yom: liquids from one who immersed that day are like those he touches and do not impart impurity
Asks what the basis of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is
Rav Ketina: they differ on whether an immersion long past remains valid, thirty-three or sixty-six days after birth
Mishna: a woman who sees blood on the eleventh day immerses the eve of the twelfth and then has intercourse
Beit Shammai say she retains the status of a zava, so she and her husband transmit impurity and owe sin offerings

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Hillel say she is exempt from the sin offering, since the twelfth day is unfit for a zava's flow
Describes the case: she immersed the day after the eleventh, had intercourse on the twelfth, and then saw blood
Beit Shammai say she renders bedding and seats impure by rabbinic law but is exempt from the offering
Beit Hillel say the husband is a glutton for not waiting until the twelfth day ended
Beit Hillel concede that if she saw blood within the eleven days and had intercourse without a clean day, both owe an offering
If she immersed after a partial clean day, her conduct is wayward and the status of her items depends on later bleeding
Baraita: both schools agree that a night immersion is invalid and that an unwaited immersion renders items impure and brings an offering
They disagree only on the eleventh day: Beit Shammai hold an offering is owed, Beit Hillel exempt her
Beit Shammai challenge Beit Hillel: if the eleventh day equals other days for impurity, it should equal them for offering
Beit Hillel reply: liability in the middle days arises because the next day combines with the bleeding, which does not happen on the eleventh
Beit Shammai retort: apply the same method consistently, equating impurity and offering in both directions
Beit Hillel: a decree of stringency for impurity does not justify leniency that would bring an unnecessary offering
Beit Hillel show Beit Shammai's own position on the twelfth day contradicts their method
Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai agree to equate for stringency only, so the same should hold in this case
Rav Huna explains Beit Shammai: even without bleeding after immersion, the items are impure by rabbinic law
Rav Yosef asks what Rav Huna is teaching, since the mishna already states this
Cites the mishna's ruling on the twelfth-day case and infers the same rabbinic impurity for a later bleeding case
Rav Kahana: Rav Huna teaches that Beit Shammai impute impurity even without actual bleeding, unlike the mishna's case
Rav Yosef refutes Rav Kahana: a sighting on the twelfth day is only a niddah sighting, comparable to a clean-day case
Abaye objects that a decree on a niddah sighting is reasonable only if blood was seen, not when none was seen
Cites a mishna in Zavim: Beit Shammai liken a man's single sighting of ziva to a clean-day woman, and Beit Hillel to a seminal emission

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if one moves a zav's first discharge, its impurity depends on whether a second discharge follows, per Beit Shammai; Beit Hillel deem it pure
Items lying or sitting between the two sightings are impure only if a second discharge is seen, per Beit Shammai; pure per Beit Hillel
Abaye cites the baraita's first clause, which Rav Kahana found difficult for Rav Huna's reading of Beit Shammai
Rav Huna explains: the man resembles one who has intercourse with a woman observing a clean day after immersing
Asks why the man does not render bedding impure while the woman does
He rarely sees blood, so no decree applies to him; she often sees blood, so the decree applies to her
Asks why her bedding is impure while the man who lies with her is not
Bedding and seats are often sat on so they become impure, while intercourse is rare and does not
Difficulty: the mishna's latter clause seems to be agreed by all, which would conflict with Rav Huna
That clause follows only Beit Hillel, as a baraita shows Rabbi Yehuda rebuked them for calling this wayward conduct
Rejects that Rabbi Yehuda meant intercourse with a menstruating woman or a zava
Rabbi Yehuda meant a man intending intercourse with a woman observing a clean day, so the latter clause follows Beit Hillel
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the tenth day is like the ninth and requires a clean day observance
Reish Lakish: the tenth day is like the eleventh and requires no observance, since three bleeding days cannot fall in the eleven
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya tells Rabbi Akiva the eleven-day rule is a halakha transmitted to Moses at Sinai, not derived from verses
Asks what the halakha about the eleven days refers to, per Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the eleventh day alone is exempt from observance; Reish Lakish: two halakhot distinguish the eleventh day
Asks whether these are Sinai halakhot, and answers that they are derived from verses
Baraita: one who sees blood three days at the start of menstruation is not a zava, by the verse in Leviticus 15:19
Cites Leviticus 15:19 as limiting zava status to one day of blood, with the verse's inference continuing on the next daf

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Leviticus 15:25 as the scriptural source for zava rules on bleeding near menstruation.
The baraita teaches that a zava is one who bleeds close to her menstrual days, not during them.
Asks from where bleeding one day separated from menstruation is also included.
Brings the same verse, Leviticus 15:25, to support including bleeding beyond the menstrual time.
Restates that the verse yields only one day of separation, so further days need another derivation.
Asks from where bleeding after more than one day of separation is derived.
Asks from where separations of two through ten days are included as zava cases.
Argues by analogy from the fourth day to the tenth day, bringing the tenth day into the count.
Asks from where the eleventh day after menstruation is included.
Cites the verse not in her menstrual time to limit the zava period to eleven days.
Objects that the twelfth day might also be included, and the baraita rejects that possibility.
Asks what justifies including the eleventh day while excluding the twelfth day.
Explains that the eleventh day is fit for the seven clean days, while the twelfth day is not.
Asks from where bleeding on two days, or on only one day, makes her impure.
Cites the plural days and all the days of impurity verses to support the two-day and one-day rules.
A zava renders impure one who lies with her, unlike a zav, according to the wording she is impure.
Raises an a fortiori argument that a zav should also render impure a partner, challenging that distinction.
Upholds the distinction, citing the verse she is impure to show only a zava transmits impurity to her partner.
Asks from where a zava transmits impurity to items she lies or sits on.
Cites Leviticus 15:26 about the bed she lies on being impure like her menstrual bed.
Asks how the three-day, two-day and one-day rules apply to transmitting impurity to items.
Brings the verses on the plural days and all the days of discharge to include shorter bleeding.
Asks from where a zava counts one clean day for each single day of bleeding.
Cites the verse her days shall be for her to show she counts one clean day.
Argues by a fortiori that she should count seven clean days after two days, as a zav does.
Replies that the verse limits her counting to her one day, even after two days of bleeding.
Asks whether the halakhot of the eleven days derive from verses rather than a tradition from Sinai.
Rabbi Akiva derives these halakhot from verses, while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds a Sinai tradition.
Rav Shemaya proposes that daytime bleeding makes her a zava, while night bleeding makes her a niddah.
Rabbi Abba rejects this, citing the verse beyond menstrual time to show night bleeding makes her a zava.
Asks when the close time occurs, and why nighttime bleeding is still called zava.
Teaches that one who studies halakhot daily is guaranteed a place in the World-to-Come.
Cites Habakkuk 3:6 and reads halikhot as halakhot to support the value of studying halakha.
The closing formula that ends the chapter and the tractate Niddah.
